Kecira et al. 1 3 863 Page 2 of 12 Graphical abstract Keywords Oxygen functional groups · Electrochemical performance · Biomass-based activated carbon · Supercapacitor · Energy storage 1 Introduction The world is facing an energy crisis due to the scarcity of primary resources. It is therefore, important to develop clean and renewable energy sources by improving high-perfor￾mance energy storage technology [1, 2]. Electrochemical capacitors (ECs), also called supercapacitors, have garnered a great deal of interest among many technologies for energy storage, due to their high power density, rapid energy stor￾age rate, and long life cycle [3, 4]. Consequently, electro￾chemical capacitors are gradually finding their way into applications such as electric vehicles, portable electronics, heavy-duty machinery, storing the energy produced by solar cells and other fields [5–8]. The supercapacitor’s ultimate performance is significantly influenced by the electrode material and electrolyte [9, 10]. The development of highly efficient electrode materials with a high energy density is one important challenge [9, 11]. Supercapacitors can be divided according to their charge storage mechanism into three types; (i) Double-layer capacitors, which are associated with electrostatic charge accumulation. They are character￾ized by rectangular CV curves and triangular GCD curves; (ii) Pseudo-capacitors, where charge storage comes from surface faradic reactions and the intercalation mechanism. They behave like EDLC materials, with almost rectangular CV curves and quasi-triangular GCD curves; Finally, (iii) Battery-type SCs, where reactions are controlled by ionic diffusion from the electrolyte, with a phase transformation reflected in the CV curves by obvious redox peaks, leading to the appearance of the potential plateau in the GCD curves [12, 13]. Carbon electrode materials such as graphene, carbon nanofibers, carbon nanotubes, and activated carbon have generally demonstrated promise as active materials for supercapacitors [11, 14]. Within these materials, activated carbon is most frequently utilized as an electrode due to its high surface area, chemical stability, environmental friend￾liness, relatively low cost and well-established scalability [15, 16]. One of the major challenges for high performance elec￾trochemical capacitors is the wettability of activated carbon. Coating the surface of activated carbon with oxygen func￾tional groups (OFGs) improves surface area utilization and capacitance at high current densities [15]. For instance, the effect of oxygen functional groups such as carboxyl, phe￾nol, carbonyl, and quinone on electrochemical behavior of incompletely reduced graphene oxides (RGOs) was studied by Young Joon Oh et al. [17], revealing a specific capaci￾tance of 220 F g−1 at the scan of 5 mV s −1. Xi-ran Li and his team modify activated carbon by (NH4)2S2O8 oxidation [18],

Synthesis of oxygen‑functionalized biomass‑based activated carbon as supercapacitor with… 1 3 Page 3 of 12 863 which enables them to improve the specific capacitance up to 142.0 F g−1 at 1 A g−1 (compared to 122.0 F g−1 for AC). It has been established that oxygen-containing func￾tional groups (OCFG) scan produce pseudo-capacitance by a reversible redox reaction, increasing the total capaci￾tance [19, 20]. Therefore, there is still a need for advanced research to optimize AC with high surface area and excel￾lent wettability [21]. Additionally, the oxygen treatment encouraged the creation of the oxygen-containing functional groups (OCFGs) on the surface of AC, allowing it to be more wettable. Utilizing biomass for the production of activated carbon presents an eco-friendly and renewable approach to energy storage technology. With proper process optimization and consideration of material properties, biomass-derived AC has the potential to contribute to sustainable energy storage solutions. The surface of activated carbon prepared from biomass was modified in this study using oxygen as an oxi￾dizing agent at various temperatures, in the aim of produc￾ing activated carbons with different oxygen contents and to apply these materials as electrodes for the supercapacitors. The relationship between the number of oxygen-functional groups and specific capacitance was investigated. The results obtained demonstrate the improved capacitive performance of oxygen-functionalized activated carbons, confirming the important effect of oxygen functional groups in enhancing the properties of activated carbons. As a result, oxygen￾functional biomass activated carbons have great potential as electrode materials for supercapacitors [22]. 2 Experimental 2.1 Chemicals and apparatus All chemical substances employed in this work were of ana￾lytical grade, they were therefore, used as they are, with￾out further purification. From Sigma Aldrish-USA: H3PO4 (85%), HCl (38%), NaOH (>99%), NaCl (>99%,). Ultrapure distilled water was used in all the experiments. 2.2 Preparation and characterization of functionalized activated carbon The activated carbon was prepared via chemical activation using apricot stones as a precursor, the latter was obtained from the N’Gaous region in the wilayah of Batna, in east￾ern southern Algeria. All fabrication steps were conducted by Z. Kecira and co-workers and are described in detail elsewhere [23]. Briefly, the biomass was impregnated with phosphoric acid (1 g H3PO4/1 g biomass) [23]. The impregnated sample was then carbonized at 673 K under N2 flow. The resulting material was cleaned using distilled water until a steady pH was achieved. The resulting acti￾vated carbon was named AC. Functionalization of the prepared activated carbon was carried out to introduce oxygen functional groups by oxygen treatment (OCFGs), which was capable of increasing the electrochemical performance of AC-based supercapacitor. The prepared AC was placed into the horizontal furnace and heated at 10 °C per minute, in N2 flow (20 L per hour), from ambient temperature to the required oxidation temperature. The nitrogen stream was then replaced with the oxidative gas (O2) (flow=20 L per hour) and the treatment was prolonged at different temperatures in the range of 473, 523, 573 and 623 K for 4 h. Following that, the system was cooled to room temperature under N2 flow (20 L/h). The oxidized ACs were then labeled as OAC473, OAC523, OAC573 and OAC623, respectively. N2 adsorption adsorption–desorption isotherms were con￾ducted using a micromeritics ASAP 2010 device at 77 K to identify the textural characteristics of each ACs-based elec￾trode [23]. Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) pictures (FEI Quanta 250) equipped with EDX-ray Tube were used to study the morphology and presence of main elements in the produced carbons (EDX). The FTIR spectra were captured with a Pekin-Elmer Spectrum. According to Boehm method [23–26], 0.05 M NaOH aqueous solution was used to titrate the total acidic oxygen surface groups. Thermogravimetric analysis (TGA) was used to determine the samples’ ther￾mal stability using a handmade device. 200 mg of the mate￾rial were heated at a rate of 10 °C min−1 under nitrogen flow from 25 to 1000 °C. XPS analysis were conducted by ESCALAB Xi+from Thermo Scientific highlighting a mon￾ochromatic Al K Alpha X-ray source (1486.68 eV). 2.3 Electrodes preparation and electrochemical measurements The experiments were carried out in a closed vessel with a three-electrode setup composed of a platinum plate as the auxiliary electrode, and a saturated calomel electrode (SCE) as the reference [27, 28]. The working electrode is a pre￾pared oxygen-functionalized AC (OFAC). The quantity of OFAC was adjusted and fixed with 24.8±3 mg, inserted in a Teflon tip in contact with a graphite pencil that serves as an electronic conductor (Fig. 1). The Cyclic voltammetry (CV), the Galvanic cycle test (GC) and the electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) analyses are performed using an electrochemical interface (Solartron, Si: 1287-1260) controlled by the CorrView software and impedance/Gain- phase analyzer (SI 1260) controlled by the Z-View software which was also used to analyze and fit the impedance data.

The produced activated carbon's external surface seems visually to have a variety of cavities of various sizes and shapes dispersed throughout the surface (see Fig. 3). TGA plot reveal a first mass loss above 150 °C, attributable to the removal of water physisorbed in the micropores and mesopores. The dissolution of the oxygenated surface groups can be used to explain the second minor mass loss that was seen at the plateau between 150 and 450 °C. To qualitatively examine the impact of oxidation on sur￾face chemical functionalities, Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy (FTIR) was used [30, 31]. Figure 5 displays the spectra that were obtained for the unmodified AC and different modified samples. The samples’ identical FTIR spectra indicate that the alteration technique did not affect the chemical groups’ species but rather their intensities. All spectra show a broad absorption band at 3600–3050 cm−1, with a high near 3400 cm−1 due to O–H stretching of hydroxyl groups, carboxyl groups, and adsorbed water [1, 29]. The bands near 2925 and 2858 cm−1 are caused by aliphatic C-H stretching vibra￾tions. Stretching vibrations -C=C- in aromatic rings affect the bands at 1600 cm−1 and 1550 cm−1, which are ampli￾fied by the presence of phenolic groups [15]. Stretch￾ing vibrations of -CH3 between 1400 and 1300 cm−1 are associated with methyl structures. The bands identified in the 1200–950 cm−1 range correspond to C-O single bond stretching modes [32]. It is noteworthy that the spectra of OAC623 show sharper peaks than those of the other materials, which could be attributable to the presence of acid groups. The two mechanisms can work together simultaneously according to the nature of the electrode materials. It is widely acknowledged that the electrode material is one of the most important factors influencing supercapacitor performance. A large number of carbon-based electrode materials, such as AC [10–12], mes￾oporous carbon [13–15], graphene [16–18], carbon nanofibers [19,20], carbon nanotubes [21,22], xerogels [23–27], and carbide-derived car￾bons [28–30], have been widely explored by scholars. Among these carbon-based electrode materials, AC is widely used as an EDLC elec￾trode material due to its high specific surface area, somewhat control￾lable pore size distribution, excellent electrical conductivity, high physicochemical stability, high mechanical strength, high chemical polarity, and moderate cost. Historically, most commercial AC materials have been produced from petroleum residues, coal, peat, lignite, and so on. However, these limited and non-renewable precursors are clearly associated with high production costs and much environmental pollu￾tion. Hence, researchers have turned their attention to developing biomass-derived AC materials due to the abundance, low cost, and renewable and eco-friendly nature of such sources [31]. Giant reed, also known as Phragmites communis, Phragmites australis, or Arundo donax Linn, is a perennial, rhizomatous, and herbaceous plant of the Poaceae family distributed globally in Asia and the Mediterranean regions of North Africa, southern Europe, and the Middle East [32,33]. Because of its rapid growth, strong capacity to adapt to different envi￾ronments, and low input requirements, the biomass productivity of giant reed can reach 30–40 t/ha, which makes it a low-cost and sustainable feedstock for the production of biofuels, chemicals, and bioenergy [33, 34]. However, most of the biomass residues generated from giant reed every year are burnt on site, which results in serious environmental pollution and a waste of biomass resources. Fortunately, in the last few decades, some studies have been conducted to explore the application of AC derived from giant reed through physical activation (CO2 or steam), chemical activation (H3PO4, ZnCl2, KOH, etc.), and microwave heating [35–38]. For example, Arundo donax (giant reed) was used as the carbon source to study the effects of carbonization temperature, weight ratio of H3PO4 to precursor (R), and carbonization time on the pore structure of AC [35]. The results showed that the order of influence of activation factors on the surface properties was: carbonization temperature > R > carbonization time. The maximum surface area reached 1312 m2 g− 1 at 500 ◦C, an R of 2 g g− 1 , and 0.25 h. Both the specific surface area and the pore volume decreased on increasing the carbonization temperature above 550 ◦C or R beyond 2.5, which may have been related to contraction of the carbon structure and collapse of the pore structure. Üner and Bayrak investigated AC derived from Arundo donax with ZnCl2 as chemical activator [36]. They obtained AC samples by simultaneously varying activation parameters, such as impregnation ratio, carboniza￾tion time, and carbonization temperature. The maximum specific sur￾face area achieved was 1785 m2 g− 1 at a carbonization temperature of 400 ◦C, an impregnation ratio of 1.5, and a carbonization time of 2 h. Dai et al. prepared hollow AC from reed straw as the precursor with KOH as the activating agent [37]. The specific surface area reached 2387 m2 g− 1 by applying a mass ratio of KOH to carbonized reed straw of 3 at 700 ◦C for 1 h. Sun et al. discussed two kinds preparation methods for obtaining AC from Arundo donax Linn, a conventional H4P2O7 activation method and a microwave heating technique [38]. The AC obtained by micro￾wave heating showed a larger specific surface area of 1567 m2 g− 1 and a higher micropore surface area of 631 m2 g− 1 compared with that ob￾tained by H4P2O7 activation [38]. However, there have been few studies on utilization of the waste residue that remains after extraction of the water-soluble chemical components, such as glucose, sucrose, and fructose, from reeds. In this study, waste residue from the remains of extracted reed (reed residue waste) has been used as a precursor. AC materials have been prepared at different pyrolysis temperatures and then chemically activated with KOH. The influence of pyrolysis tem￾perature on the electrochemical performances of the as-prepared AC materials as supercapacitor electrodes has been studied. 2. Experimental 2.1. Materials Reed residue waste was purchased from Shengquan Group (Jinan, China). Potassium hydroxide (KOH) was purchased from Aladdin re￾agent Co., Ltd. (China). All chemical reagents were used as received without further purification. 2.2. Synthesis of AC materials Reed residue waste was placed in a quartz tube furnace and heated at a rate of 10 ◦C min− 1 to 500, 600, 700, or 800 ◦C under a flow of N2 at 200 mL min− 1 and maintained at the final temperature for 2 h. The as￾prepared carbonization products were mixed with KOH, placed in a tubular furnace, and again heated at a rate of 10 ◦C min− 1 under N2 at a flow rate of 200 mL min− 1 and maintained at the final temperature of 800 ◦C for 2 h. The mass ratio of as-prepared carbonization product to KOH was 1:5. The obtained products were washed with deionized water until the washings were neutral, and then dried in a vacuum oven at 70 ◦C for 24 h. The samples are denoted as C/500 ◦C, C/600 ◦C, C/ 700 ◦C, and C/800 ◦C, respectively. 2.3. Characterization of the AC materials The properties of the AC samples were determined by applying a series of topographic analysis methods. N2 adsorption/desorption iso￾therms were recorded at 77 K on a Micromeritics ASAP 2020 analyzer. The specific surface areas and pore volumes of the AC samples were determined through Brunauer–Emmett–Teller (BET) measurements. The pore size distribution (PSD) was plotted by applying a non-local density functional theory (DFT) method. A JSM-6700F scanning elec￾tron microscope (SEM; JEOL, Tokyo, Japan) was used to inspect the morphologies of the AC samples. Raman spectroscopy was conducted with a Bruker spectrometer (Bruker Corporation, Germany) with an excitation wavelength of 532 nm to study the microstructures of the AC samples. X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS, ESCALAB 250Xi, Thermo Fisher, USA) was conducted using a monochromatic Al-Kα source. 2.4. Preparation of electrodes The preparation method for the working electrode involved the following steps. First, AC (80 wt%) was mixed with acetylene black (>99.9%, 10 wt%) and poly(vinylidene fluoride) (PVDF, Sigma-Aldrich, 10 wt%) in N-methyl-2-pyrrolidone (NMP, Sigma-Aldrich) to obtain a homogeneous mixture. Second, the paste-like mixture was uniformly coated on Ni foam of dimensions 1 × 1 cm2 . Third, the resulting elec￾trode (with a mass loading of active material of approximately 2.4 mg) was dried in a vacuum oven at 80 ◦C for 24 h. 2.5. Electrochemical measurements Electrochemical experiments were carried out with an electro￾chemical workstation (CHI 660E, Shanghai, China) to assess the relevant properties of the AC samples. The test conditions were as follows: con￾ventional three-electrode system with 6 M aqueous KOH solution as the electrolyte, a platinum sheet as the counter electrode, and a saturated calomel electrode (SCE) as the reference. Cyclic voltammetry (CV) tests were conducted at scanning rates of 1, 2, 5, and 10 mV s − 1 . Galvano￾static charge–discharge (GCD) measurements were made at current densities of 0.25, 0.5, 1, 2, and 5 A g− 1 . The potential window ranging from − 1.0 V to 0 V was selected for CV and GCD tests. Electrochemical impedance spectra (EIS) were obtained in the frequency range 100 D. Zhang et al.

Journal of Physics and Chemistry of Solids 178 (2023) 111318 3 kHz–10 mHz with an alternating current (AC) amplitude of 5 mV. Generally, the specific capacitance (C, F g− 1 ) of a supercapacitor can be calculated from a GCD plot according to Eq. (1). C = IΔt mΔV (1) E = 1 2 CΔV2 (2) P = E Δt (3) here, I is the discharge current (A), ΔV and Δt refer to the voltage window (V) and the discharge time (s), respectively, m (g) is the mass of active material, E (W h kg− 1 ) is the energy density, and P (W kg− 1 ) is the power density. 3. Results and discussion 3.1. Characterization of carbon materials Fig. 1 shows the N2 adsorption/desorption isotherms and PSD plots acquired to investigate the porosities of samples C/500 ◦C, C/600 ◦C, C/ 700 ◦C, and C/800 ◦C. It can be observed that almost all of the AC samples displayed type I N2 adsorption/desorption isotherms at 77 K, according to the IUPAC classification [39], demonstrating the presence of a large amount of micropores with average pore diameter less than 2 nm. All of the isotherms display a sharp increase in nitrogen uptake at relative pressures below 0.1 P/P0, accompanied by an almost horizontal plateau, indicating a high adsorption amount and abundant cumulative space for electrons due to a large number of micropores [39,40]. As can be seen in Fig. 1(a), compared with C/600 ◦C and C/800 ◦C, relatively obvious hysteresis loops with typical characteristics of type IV isotherms were observed for C/500 ◦C and C/700 ◦C. Table 1 lists the specific surface areas and pore structure parameters of the AC samples. C/600 ◦C displayed the highest specific surface area (2074.72 m2 g− 1 ) and the largest total pore volume (0.930 cm3 g− 1 ). For C/500 ◦C, C/700 ◦C, and C/800 ◦C, the specific surface areas were 1099.45, 1499.76, and 1033.38 m2 g− 1 , and the pore volumes were 0.592, 0.789, and 0.452 cm3 g− 1 , respectively. It is generally acknowledged that the electro￾chemical performance of a supercapacitor not only depends on its spe￾cific surface area, but also its pore framework (porosity and PSD). PSD plots of the AC samples obtained at different pyrolysis temperatures are shown in Fig. 1(b). C/600 ◦C displayed a smooth curve with the pore size centered at around 2 nm, implying that such a micro/meso hierarchical porous structure is beneficial to achieve excellent performance in supercapacitors [41]. The micropore volume gradually decreased as the pyrolysis temperature was increased from 600 ◦C to 800 ◦C due to collapse or amalgamation of the micropore structure [42,43]. Further￾more, the order of average pore diameters can be seen in Table 1; C/800 ◦C (2.56 nm) > C/700 ◦C (2.10 nm) > C/600 ◦C (1.79 nm). Other data related to mesopore area and the average diameters of mesopores are collected in Table S1. The surface morphologies of the AC samples characterized by SEM are shown in Fig. 2. It can be seen that C/500 ◦C was composed of a large number of diffuse spherical particles [Fig. 2(a)]. When the pyrolysis temperature was increased to 600 ◦C, a fluffy Hemistepta lyrata-like structure with abundant pores was observed [Fig. 2(b)]. The presence of a large number of micropores (<2 nm) contributes to a high specific surface area, which is beneficial for high electrical double-layer capac￾itance due to abundant adsorption sites for ions [44]. Mesopores (2–50 nm) allow ions to easily access inner micropores by shortening their diffusion distance and reducing diffusion resistance [45]. Moreover, a small number of macropores (>50 nm) favor ion transport as ion-buffering reservoirs [46,47]. On further increasing the pyrolysis temperature to 700 ◦C and 800 ◦C, the fluffy Hemistepta lyrata-like structure disappeared, being replaced by clusters or chunks of spherical particles [Fig. 2(c and d)]. These observations are consistent with the BET results. Additionally, Raman measurements were carried out to further validate the structures of C/500 ◦C, C/600 ◦C, C/700 ◦C, and C/800 ◦C (Fig. 3). Two prominent D-band and G-band peaks due to amorphous carbon were seen for all of the samples. The D-band (ca. 1340 cm− 1 ) can be attributed to disorder or defects in a graphitic structure with A1g symmetry. The G-band (ca. 1590 cm− 1 ) corresponds to an in-plane stretching vibration of sp2 bonds of carbon in the graphite lattice mode E2g [44,48]. The intensity ratio of the D- and G-bands (ID/IG) is often used to represent the degree of disorder or defects in carbon ma￾terials. A higher ratio reflects a lower degree of graphitization [48,49]. The Raman spectra (Fig. 3) indicated partial graphite characteristics for all four samples. C/500 ◦C displayed the highest intensity ratio (ID/IG = 1.95), reflecting the lowest degree of graphitization and the highest content of disordered carbon material. This observation was consistent with the SEM image [Fig. 2(a)]. The ID/IG values of C/600 ◦C, C/700 ◦C, and C/800 ◦C were 1.65, 1.58, and 1.62, respectively, suggesting that the AC samples prepared at higher temperatures possessed higher de￾grees of graphitization and excellent electronic conductivity. Moreover, there were no significant changes in the ID/IG ratio when the pyrolysis temperature exceeded 600 ◦C. Therefore, based on the above analysis, 600 ◦C was identified as an appropriate pyrolysis temperature for pre￾paring high-performance carbon-based electrodes, and C/600 ◦C was selected for further studies. The main elemental composition and the valence states of the ele￾ments present were analyzed by XPS. A survey spectrum of C/600 ◦C is shown in Fig. 1S(a), which indicates the presence of C and O. A deconvolution of the O 1s pattern is displayed in Fig. 1S(b). Peaks at binding energies of around 531.0, 532.3, 533.9, and 535.6 eV may be ascribed to oxygen double-bonded to carbon in carbonyl and quinone￾like structures [50,51], oxygen singly-bonded to carbon in aromatic rings as in phenols and ethers [50,51], hydroxyl groups, and adsorbed Fig. 1. Journal of Physics and Chemistry of Solids 178 (2023) 111318 4 water, respectively. This implies the presence of multiple functionalities, providing improved hydrophilicity. 3.2. Electrochemical performances of the AC samples To assess the performances of the materials in supercapacitor elec￾trodes, data from CV, GCD, EIS, and cyclic life tests were combined to provide information at different current densities and scan rates, and to assess the degree of capacitance retention after successive char￾ging–discharging. Fig. 4(a) shows voltammograms of the AC samples at a scan rate of 1 mV s − 1 . The specific capacitance of a supercapacitor electrode is proportional to the integrated area of its voltammogram. Among the AC samples derived from reed residue waste, C/600 ◦C with the largest integral area showed the highest capacitance. All of the voltammograms display a quasi-rectangular shape without obvious distortion, except that for C/600 ◦C, demonstrating that the AC samples showed ideal electrical double-layer capacitive behavior to meet ion￾transfer/diffusion responses. Voltammograms for C/600 ◦C acquired at different scan rates ranging from 1 mV s − 1 to 10 mV s − 1 are plotted in Fig. 4(b). They maintain the quasi-rectangular shape with slight distortion as the scan rate is increased, indicating that a C/600 ◦C electrode with good ion-transport capability and an accessible surface area would be suitable for rapid charge–discharge operations due to its porous structure [50–52]. Journal of Physics and Chemistry of Solids 178 (2023) 111318 5 wide hump due to reversible pseudocapacitive reaction can be observed between − 0.8 and − 0.4 V in the voltammograms of C/600 ◦C. Fig. 4(c) compares the GCD profiles of the AC samples prepared at the different pyrolysis temperatures, from which it is apparent that C/600 ◦C dis￾played the longest discharge time, suggesting the highest specific capacitance. All of the GCD plots acquired at a current density of 1 A g− 1 showed a similar isosceles triangle shape, with only slight deviations from linearity. However, no discernible amperometric IR drop was observed, demonstrating excellent capacitance behavior and outstanding electrochemical reversibility [53]. Furthermore, the char￾acteristics and relatively longer discharge time of the GCD plot of C/600 ◦C are broadly consistent with both the EDLC and pseudocapa￾citive performances [54,55]. Table 2 lists the specific capacitances of the C/500 ◦C, C/600 ◦C, C/700 ◦C, and C/800 ◦C electrode materials at different current densities in a three-electrode system according to Eq. (1). Among these four samples, at the same current density of 1 A g− 1 , C/600 ◦C displayed the highest specific capacitance (228.1 F g− 1 ), far exceeding those of C/800 ◦C (122.1 F g− 1 ), C/700 ◦C (125.1 F g− 1 ), and C/500 ◦C (139.0 F g− 1 ). GCD plots of C/600 ◦C at current densities of 0.25, 0.5, 1, 2, and 5 A g− 1 are shown in Fig. 4(d), from which the specific capacitances were evaluated as 307.5, 246.4, 228.1, 217.0, and 199.1 F g− 1 , respectively, according to Eq. (1). These values are higher than those of C/500 ◦C, C/700 ◦C, and C/800 ◦C (Table 2). It is also evident from Table 2 that the specific capacitances of all four samples decreased with increasing current density, implying that the electrolyte ions had insufficient time to penetrate the inner micropores of the electrode at high current densities [56–58]. At a current density of 5.0 A g− 1 , the specific capacitance of C/600 ◦C still remained as high as 199.1 F g− 1 , with a retention of 64.7%, demonstrating a good ability for fast ion transport. Fig. 5 shows the energy densities of the four samples at different power densities. It is obvious that the energy densities of C/600 ◦C were much higher than those of the other samples. Accord￾ingly, C/600 ◦C reached a maximum energy density of 42.7 W h kg− 1 at a power density of 122 W kg− 1 . Furthermore, a prominent energy density of 27.65 W h kg− 1 still remained at a power density of 2513.6 W kg− 1 . These good results prove that C/600 ◦C shows excellent electro￾chemical performance as a promising supercapacitor electrode due to its hierarchical porous structure. Fig. 4. Journal of Physics and Chemistry of Solids 178 (2023) 111318 6 EIS was also carried out to evaluate the electrochemical properties of the supercapacitor electrodes, especially their ion-transfer kinetics. The results are shown in Fig. 6(a), in which the inset shows an enlargement of the lower portion. As shown in Fig. 6(a), the Nyquist plots were composed of three parts: an almost vertical straight line representing ideal double-layer capacitance in the low-frequency region, an incom￾plete semi-circle representing the charge-transfer resistance (Rct) in the high-frequency region, and a real-axis intercept representing the inter￾nal resistance (often called equivalent series resistance, ESR) [59,60]. The ESRs of C/500 ◦C, C/600 ◦C, C/700 ◦C, and C/800 ◦C were 0.6 Ω, 0.6 Ω, 0.55 Ω, and 0.55 Ω, respectively, while the small diameters of the semi-circles demonstrated low Rct, except for C/800 ◦C. All of the samples displayed an almost perpendicular line, demonstrating ideal capacitive behavior. To further assess long-term cycle life of the AC samples for practical application as supercapacitor electrodes, their cycling stability was monitored by GCD at a current density of 5 A g− 1 over 8000 cycles. As shown in Fig. 6(b), the specific capacitance of C/600 ◦C still retained >98% of its original value, even after 8000 charge/discharge cycles, indicating excellent electrochemical cycling stability. Moreover, C/600 ◦C exhibited a higher initial capacity due to its higher specific surface area providing a large number of adsorption sites for electrolyte ions. It can be seen that the main capacitance decayed during the first 500 cycles, and then the capacitance values remained almost unchanged during the rest of the test. This phenome￾non can be rationalized in terms of irreversible electro-oxidation re￾actions (such as carbon oxidation) at the beginning of prolonged cycling [61]. The performance of our AC is compared with those of other biowaste-based AC materials as supercapacitor electrodes in Table S2. 4. Conclusions In summary, Hemistepta lyrata (bunge flower)-like porous carbon (C/ 600 ◦C) with excellent electrochemical performance has been prepared from reed residue waste by pyrolytic carbonization at 600 ◦C followed by chemical activation with KOH. C/600 ◦C displayed the highest spe￾cific capacitance of 228 F g− 1 , compared to other AC samples prepared at different pyrolysis temperatures, at the same current density of 1 A g− 1 . Moreover, C/600 ◦C exhibited a higher energy density of 42.7 W h kg− 1 , a higher power density of 2513.6 W kg− 1 (in the voltage range − 1 to 0 V), and longer cycling stability (less than 2% loss of its initial capacitance after 8000 cycles). We conclude that the biomass-derived hierarchical porous carbon described here may be considered as a promising low-cost and high-performance supercapacitor electrode material. The electrochemical perform￾ance was carried out in 1 M H2SO4 and poly(vinyl alcohol)− KI−H2SO4 polymer gel electrolytes, with the specific capacitance of 500 F g−1 at 1 mV s −1 and specific energy of 36.11 Wh kg−1 . 19 Bhat et al. derived activated carbon from the leaves and stems of the cilantro plant using KOH as the activating agent, designing an electrode for use in super￾capacitors and a cartridge for water filtration. In a 6 M KOH solution, the electrode demonstrated a specific capacitance of 162.4 F g−1 at a current density of 1 A g−1 in 6 M KOH solution.20 Hu et al. grew a layer of Ni−Co double hydroxides on the surface of a rice husk activated-carbon-coated Ni foam electrode; it delivered the specific capacity of 8542.5 mF cm−2 at 2 mA cm−2 current density.21 Shaku et al. activated marula nutshell waste using KOH and used it for supercapacitor applications. It exhibited the capacitance of 248 F g−1 and energy density of 28.4 Wh kg−1 in 2.5 M KNO3 electrolyte solution.22 Luo et al. prepared cotton-based activated carbon fiber and reached the highest specific surface area of 2304.8 m2 g−1 by a KOH activation agent.23 Gogoi et al. prepared the electrode material by mixing Cu2O with spent tea waste￾derived carbon, exhibiting the specific capacity of 1202.2 C g−1 in 3 M KOH electrolyte solution. The asymmetric device fabricated using a PVA gel electrolyte had the capability of supplying an energy density of 112.8 Wh kg−1 at 1521.5 W kg−1 power density.24 Lu et al. prepared rapeseed-meal-derived activated carbon (RMAC) by hydrothermal carbonization and high-temperature activation. The effects of different activation temperatures on the performance of RMAC were investigated. Co-doped RMAC-800 using N, O, P, and S exhibits a specific surface area of 3291 m2 g−1 and a specific capacitance of 416 F g−1 at 1 A g−1 current density.25 Peng et al. derived the rapeseed stalk activated carbon (RSAC) by N and O co￾doping, which exhibits a specific surface area of 3085 m2 g−1 and a specific capacitance of 357.7 F g−1 at a current density of 0.25 A g−1 . 26 Sun et al. utilized the mango seed precursor for deriving activated carbon by the N and O co-doped KOH activation process. Activated carbon delivers a specific capacitance of 402 F g−1 at a current density of 1 A g−1 with a specific surface area of 1815 m2 g−1 . 27 The coconut tree (Cocos nucifera) is most abundant in southern India, producing nutritious edible seeds, healthy and refreshing drinks, oils, ropes, brooms, fibers, etc. The coconut tree belongs to the family Arecaceae, and it contributes every inch of its life to become more useful for humankind. Coconut husk (CH) and coconut tree husk (CTH) are two different sorts of biomass obtained from coconut trees (shown in Figures S1 and S2 of the Supporting Information). Coconut husk (coconut fiber) helps make products, such as ropes, mats, carpets, brushes, etc. Coconut tree husk is one of the products obtained from coconut trees that has been used for fire in traditional kitchens; there is no other specified use that it has. Therefore, it will be one of the attractive environmentally friendly precursors for activated carbon electrode materials. Producing activated carbon is a two-step process: (1) Carbonization: The carbon-rich material is carbonized at low temperatures. (2) Activation: Activation is performed at high temperatures through physical or chemical activation proce￾dures. The surface is modified using air, steam, or oxygen at high temperatures in physical activation. In chemical activation, biomass-derived carbonized carbon is mixed with an activating agent, such as salt, base, or acid, in an inert atmosphere.28 In biomass-derived carbon, the porous nature may occur inherently or form the porous structure easily.29 Because of the fast electrolyte ion diffusion, mesopores can store more charges than micropores. By reduction of ion scattering, micropores can improve the rate capability. High ion adsorption will happen at the macropores; as a result, it acts as an ion reservoir. The high performance of the supercapacitor is due to the combined effect of all three types of pores in the biomass-derived carbon materials.1 In some of the recent literature, coconut husk is used as a biomass for energy storage applications. In this work, one of the agricultural wastes, coconut tree husk biomass, is used as a sustainable and environmentally friendly precursor for preparing activated carbon for the first time. Through a chemical activation process, various activating agents assisted AC generated from biomass. The diffraction planes, graphitic structure, morphology, porosity, surface elemental composi￾tion, and chemical bonding states of all AC samples are initially analyzed. The charge storage performance of all AC samples is Figure 1. Synthesis procedure of chemically activated AC samples from coconut tree husk. studied using the three-electrode system in a 2 M KOH aqueous solution; the AC3 electrode exhibits better charge storage performance than the other electrodes. Further, using the AC3 electrodes, a symmetric device is fabricated with aqueous and gel electrolytes and examined using a two￾electrode system. ■ EXPERIMENTAL SECTION Chemicals and Reagents. Coconut tree husks were collected from coconut trees in Kanyakumari district in Tamil Nadu, India. Potassium carbonate (K2CO3), potassium hydroxide (KOH), potassium permanganate (KMnO4), potassium chloride (KCl), potassium bromide (KBr), potassium iodide (KI), nitric acid (KNO3), and hydrochloric acid (HCl) were purchased from Merck (P), Ltd. Poly[vinyl alcohol] (PVA) was purchased Alfa Aesar (P), Ltd. All chemicals were used for synthesis without any further purification. Synthesis of Biomass-Derived Activated Carbon. The coconut tree husks were first washed using HCl and double-distilled (DD) water to remove the dust and inorganic impurities, then cut into small pieces, and dried at 60 °C for 12 h to remove the water contents. After drying, the pieces were kept inside a muffle furnace for carbonization in an air atmosphere at 350 °C for 1 h. The carbonized powder was purified several times using HCl, HNO3, and DD water until approaching the neutral pH. The above powder is known as carbonized carbon (CC). The next step is called the chemical activation process, in which activating agent K2CO3 and the carbonized carbon material were mixed in a 2:1 weight ratio until a homogeneous slurry was formed. The above slurry was heated inside the tubular furnace with an Ar environment up to 800 °C at a heat rate of 5 °C min−1 and maintained at 800 °C for 2 h. Then, the sample was allowed to reach room temperature; the collected sample was washed using HCl, HNO3, and DD water. After cleaning, the sample was dried in a vacuum oven at 80 °C for 12 h and denoted as activated carbon sample (AC1). In the above synthesis procedure, instead of K2CO3 activating agent, KOH, KMnO4, KCl, KBr, and KI activating agents were used, and the samples are denoted as AC2, AC3, AC4, AC5, and AC6, respectively. Figure 1 represents the synthesis procedure of activated carbon from the coconut tree husk biomass. The possible activation mechanism that may occur between the different activating agents and carbonized carbon under gasification conditions (during the activation process) at various temperatures is explained in section 1 of the Supporting Information. Material Characterization. The X-ray diffraction (XRD) pattern was obtained using a Cu Kα1 radiation-equipped Rigaku Ultima III powder X-ray diffractometer encountering at 40 kV for a 2θ range of 20−80°. From the XRD pattern, the diffraction planes of AC samples were identified. Using Raman spectroscopy (LabRAM HR Evolution, Horiba, Ltd., Japan) with a micro-Raman spectrometer (exciting wavelength of 523 nm), the disorder and graphitization degree of each sample were identified. Field emission scanning electron microscopy (FE-SEM) and high-resolution transmission electron microscopy (HR-TEM) were used to analyze the morphology of the AC samples. A Carl Zeiss (Hebron, KY, U.S.A.) Sigma FE-SEM apparatus with a Gemini column (resolution of 1.5 nm) was employed to entrap the surface morphology. Using a Bruker (Germany) Nano XFlash detector, the energy-dispersive X-ray analysis (EDAX) and elemental mapping of AC were carried out. A 300 kV transmission electron microscope (Technai G2 Twin) was used to take the HR-TEM picture of the AC3 sample. A Thermo Scientific K-Alpha X-ray photoelectron spectroscope was used to examine the chemical bonds on the surface of the electrode material. Quantachrome Nova 2200e V11.05 equipment was used to quantify the specific surface area, pore size distribution, and N2 adsorption/desorption isotherm of the synthesized material using Brunauer−Emmett−Teller (BET) and Barrett−Joyner−Halenda (BJH) studies. Electrochemical Measurements. Using the Biologic SP-200 electrochemical workstation, the electrochemical performances of AC samples were investigated in three- and two-electrode configurations. Active material (AC), binding agent [polyvinylidene fluoride (PVDF)], and conductive material (carbon black) were mixed with a few drops of 1-methyl-2-pyrrolidone (NMP) in an 8:1:1 ratio, and the resultant mixture was sonicated around 15 min to make a uniform slurry. The slurry of the active material was coated on the pre-cleaned graphite sheet substrate using the drop-casting method. A 1 cm2 area of graphite sheet was coated with the active material and used as the working electrode after drying 60 °C for 12 h. The mass loaded on the graphite sheet is 0.8 mg cm−2 . The reference and counter electrodes were Ag/AgCl and Pt wire, respectively. For the galvanostatic charge−discharge (GCD) study and cyclic voltammetry (CV) study, 2 M KOH was used as the electrolyte solution with a potential range of 0.0−0.5 V. In the same three-electrode system, an electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) study was performed in the frequency range of 100−0.1 Hz. Symmetric Device Fabrication. Two types of symmetric devices were fabricated using the KOH electrolyte and PVA/KOH gel electrolyte as the two electrolytes with the same electrode materials. Figure 2. (a) Aquous electrolyte symmetric device: The AC-coated two graphite sheets act as the positive and negative electrodes with 2 M KOH as an electrolyte solution. (b) Gel electrolyte symmetric device: To synthesize the PVA/KOH gel electrolyte, 20 mL of DD water was heated to 70 °C. A 1 g portion of PVA was mixed with the above￾heated solution with continuous stirring for 15 min, and a 2 M KOH solution was mixed drop by drop in the above solution. Then, the final solution was heated at 70 °C to obtain a viscous liquid. After it reached room temperature, the PVA/KOH transparent gel electrolyte was sandwiched between the two AC-coated graphite sheet electrodes. ■ RESULTS AND DISCUSSION XRD Analysis. Figure 2a shows the XRD patterns of AC1, AC2, AC3, AC4, AC5, and AC6 samples. All of the carbon samples show similar XRD patterns, with two peaks around the 2θ values of 24−25° and 43−45°. The two peaks around 24° and 43° correspond to all sample (002) and (100) planes, implying that all samples are in amorphous structures. The broad diffraction peak at low 2θ corresponds to the disturbed structure of carbon, and the peak at high 2θ corresponds to the limited graphitization degree of the carbon sample.30 All activated carbon diffraction peaks are wide and weakly intense, suggesting the amorphous and small crystalline nature of the samples.31 Raman Analysis. Raman analysis was used to examine the graphitic structure of the AC samples. Raman spectra of all AC samples (AC1, AC2, AC3, AC4, AC5, and AC6) are shown in Figure 2b. All of these samples exhibit two peaks in the ranges Figure 3. FE-SEM images of (a) CC, (b) AC1, (c) AC2, (d and e) AC3, (f) AC4, (g) AC5, and (h) AC6 samples, (i) EDAX spectrum, (j and k) elemental mapping, and (l) HR-TEM image of the prepared AC3 sample. of 1340−1350 cm−1 (D band) and 1590−1600 cm−1 (G band), which disclose the crystallography and structure of the carbon materials. D and G bands in AC materials correspond to the sp3 - and sp2 -hybridized phases of carbon. The defect amount in the carbon material is ascribed to the intensity of the D band (disordered or defective graphite band), which is used for electrochemical reactions as an active site for ion adsorption. The G band (crystalline graphite band) reveals the graphene property of the carbon material, which helps improve the electrical conductivity.32 ID and IG represent the intensity of D and G bands. The large value of ID/IG shows the presence of a large number of active sites with less electrical conductivity; on the other hand, the small value of ID/IG indicates the high electrical conductivity with less active sites. The ID/IG ratio for AC1, AC2, AC3, AC4, AC5, and AC6 samples is 1.09, 1.10, 1.01, 1.08, 1.05, and 1.11, respectively. Different activating agents affecting the number of defects and the graphitic nature of the sample lead to different ID/IG ratios. The lowest ID/IG ratio carbon material is suitable for electrode application because of its high electrical conductivity.33−35 From the above results, the AC using KMnO4 activating agent exhibits a low ID/IG ratio, which is favorable for fast electrochemical charge transfer. FE-SEM, EDAX, and TEM Analyses. FE-SEM analysis of all carbon samples was performed to reveal the morphology and microstructure of the prepared samples. The results are displayed in panels a−h of Figure 3. Figure 3a represents carbonized carbon (CC), which has layered structures that are closely overlapped with each other with no pores. The layered structure that existed before chemical activation completely collapsed, and various morphologies were created on the basis of different activating agents, as depicted in panels b−h of Figure 3. Figure 3b shows the morphology of AC1 samples, which has the collapsed layer structure, and the layers do not overlap together; as a result, it will have more surface area than CC. Figure 3c indicates the morphology of the AC2 sample, in which layered structures collapsed and develop an agglom￾erated microsphere-like morphology. Figure 3d exhibits the developed pores on the surface of the AC3 samples during chemical activation; in addition to that, these pores will help to enhance the interaction of electrolytes with the active material. The high-magnification FE-SEM image of the AC3 sample is shown in Figure 3e. This interconnected porous structure will provide more surface area during the charge storage process; therefore, the sample activated using KMnO4 activating agent exhibits better electrochemical performance. Panels f, g, and h of Figure 3 proclaim the morphology of AC4, AC5, and AC6 samples, in which the layered surface of CC is busted to make a cactus-like morphology during the chemical activation process. All of these samples exhibit different cactus-like morphologies for different chemical activating agents. Figure 3i illustrates the EDAX spectrum of the as-prepared AC3 sample, which verifies the presence of C and O elements. From EDAX analysis, the AC3 sample has 88.4 atomic percentage carbon and 11.6 atomic percentage oxygen. This indicates that the prepared sample is clean and free of impurities. The EDAX spectra and atomic and weight percentages of all other samples are shown in Figure S3 of the Supporting Information. The elemental mapping of the AC3 sample is displayed in panels j and k of Figure 3; the mapping of C (red) and O (blue) represents the elements that are evenly dispersed across the surface of the material. The TEM image of the AC3 sample is shown in Figure 3l, which exhibits a high degree of linked pores across the AC3 sample. This structure increases the surface wettability and specific surface area of the sample, promoting the quick movement of ions inside the pores.33 Figure 4. (a) Nitrogen adsorption/desorption isotherm of the AC3 sample, (b) pore size distribution of all AC samples, (c) XPS survey spectrum, and deconvoluted high-resolution XPS spectra of (d) C 1s and (e) O 1s for the AC3 sample. BET Analysis. All carbon samples were assessed for surface area and porosity using the BET technique, which involves nitrogen adsorption−desorption isotherms. Before the meas￾urements, all samples were degassed at 300 °C under vacuum for 5 h. The BJH method and BET equation were used to determine the pore size distribution and specific surface area of the sample. Figure 4a shows the N2 adsorption−desorption curve for the AC3 sample. The N2 adsorption/desorption curve for all other samples (AC1, AC2, AC4, AC5, and AC6) is displayed in Figure S4 of the Supporting Information. All activated carbon samples exhibit type IV isotherms [classi￾fications based on the International Union of Pure and Applied Chemistry (IUPAC)] with a loop of hysteresis. The curve for isotherms quickly rises at lower relative pressures (P/P0 < 0.1) depicting the presence of micropores. The hysteresis loop in the relative pressure (0.1 < P/P0 < 0.9) indicates the presence of a large number of mesopores; a slight upward inclination in the high relative pressure (P/P0 > 0.9) corresponds to less macropores. All activated carbon samples combine micro-, meso-, and macropores; these hierarchical pore structures would support high-performance energy storage. Even though all of the samples have hierarchical pore distributions, AC3 shows better electrochemical performance than the other AC samples. The reason is that KMnO4 activation considerably improves the porosity in the carbon material, which is required for the electrolyte to reach the entire surface for effective charge storage.36,37 It is understood from Figure 4a, in which the quantity of N2 gas adsorbed is high for the AC3 sample compared to all other AC samples. The chemical reaction and gas produced by the subsequent heat treatment resulted in the creation of mesopores, which altered the original pore structure. Figure 4b displays the pore size distribution of all of the AC samples in the 3−40 nm range; the inset image shows the pore size distribution in the low range of 3−9 nm. In all samples, more pores are distributed in the mesopore range, with the pore size mainly concentrated around 3−9 nm. Mesopores efficiently speed up electrolyte ion transmission and reduce the diffusion path in porous carbon at high current densities, improving electro￾chemical characteristics. Specific surface areas for all samples were carried out using BET analysis; among all of the AC samples, the AC3 sample has a higher BET specific surface area, resulting in higher electrochemical performance. The AC3 sample has a specific surface area of 2333.4 m2 g−1 , with a pore volume of 2.63 cm3 g−1 and an average pore diameter of 4.26 nm. The pore volume, pore radius, and specific surface area of all AC samples are shown in Table 1. X-ray Photoelectron Spectroscopy (XPS) Analysis. XPS was used to examine the surface elemental composition and chemical bonding states of the AC3 sample. Figure 4c depicts the survey spectrum of the AC3 sample; two main peaks at 285 and 532 eV correspond to carbon and oxygen. Figure 4d represents the Gaussian fit C 1s narrow spectrum, which consists of three deconvoluted peaks. The carbonyl group (C−O) was indicated by the peak located at a binding energy of 284.6 eV. The other two peaks at binding energies of 285.7 and 288.4 eV correspond to the ether bonds (C�O� C) and carboxylic groups (C�O), respectively.38−40 The deconvoluted oxygen peak is displayed in Figure 4e with three peaks. The carbonyl groups (O�C�O) have the peak position at the binding energy of 532.1 eV; the carboxylic groups (C�O) have the peak at the binding energy of 533.2 eV; and the hydroxyl groups (C�OH) have the peak at the binding energy of 534.3 eV. The above results suggest that, at a high temperature, the KMnO4 activator strongly oxidizes the carbon materials to boost the oxygen content and etch out the non-oxygen atoms.34,41 It has been established that adding oxygen-functional groups to carbon materials makes them more hydrophilic, maximizing the use of their large specific surface areas and improving their capacity for energy storage.42 Electrochemical Performances of AC. The electro￾chemical and energy storage characteristics of pure AC1, AC2, AC3, AC4, AC5, and AC6 are investigated using a three￾electrode system before building the supercapacitor device. The charge storage performance of the six samples was studied using CV, GCD, and EIS analyses in a 2 M KOH electrolyte solution. The CV curves for six samples within the potential window from −0.5 to 0.0 V at 50 mV s −1 scan rate are shown in Figure 5a. The shape of the CV curve is rectangular with no redox peaks, which reveals the favorable EDLC behavior of the activated carbon materials. The area covered by the CV curve decreases from AC3 to AC6 in the order of AC3 > AC5 > AC4 > AC1 > AC2 > AC6. The AC3 electrode exhibits better electrochemical performance than the other activated-carbon￾coated electrodes. Figure 5b displays the CV curve for the AC3 electrode within the potential window from −0.5 to 0.0 V at different scan rates from 10 to 200 mV s −1 . The CV curves for all other electrodes (AC1, AC2, AC4, AC5, and AC6) within the same potential window are examined and shown in Figure S5 of the Supporting Information. The shape of the CV curve is nearly identical for all scan rates, demonstrating the reversible adsorption−desorption of electrolyte ions on the surface of the electrodes. With the increase of the scan rate, the electrochemical performance of all electrodes improves, which is shown by the increase in the area of the CV curve with an increase in the scan rate.43 The scan rate (ν) retains a linear correlation with the current density i(ν), which is described by the power law equation shown in eqs 1 and 2. i( ) = a b (1) log(i( )) = log(a) + b log( ) (2) i(ν) is the value of the current density at scan rate ν, and a and b are the electrode-material-dependent parameters. The values of parameters b and a are measured from the graph log(ν) versus log i(ν), and the values of b and a are the slope and y intercept of the above graph. The parameter b gives the idea about the charge storage mechanism for the electrode, where b = 1 indicates that the charge storage mechanism is a purely surface-controlled process (ideal EDLC) and b = 0.5 represents that the charge storage mechanism is a purely diffusion-controlled process (ideal PC).44 Generally, the b Table 1. segments.text: materials include graphene,11 carbon nanotubes,12 carbon nanofibers,13 etc. Nonetheless, the intricate fabrication procedure and high costs have hindered their industrial application. On the contrary, biomass-derived activated carbon has emerged as a promising candidate for supercapacitor electrode composites due to its renewability,14 substantial specific surface area,15 exceptional electrochemical durability,16 and superior conductivity.17 Prior investigations have achieved considerable advancements in constructing porous carbon materials derived from diverse biomass resources such as bamboo, olive tree pruning residues, and hazelnut shell, among others.18−20 Notably, activation and carbonization procedures used to develop electrodes using biomass feedstock can induce unique porous and layered pseudo graphite wall morpholo￾gies.21 However, activated carbon used in supercapacitor electrodes should provide ample room for ion storage by micropores and a well-developed pathway for ion transfer by mesopores.22 Therefore, the carbon electrodes should possess an optimal pore distribution, which can be achieved by optimizing the preparation and activation process. H3PO4 is commonly used as an activator due to its ability to create activated carbon materials with an abundance of micropores and mesopores.23 The choice of H3PO4 was strategically guided by its multifaceted advantages in sustainability, pore structure engineering, and electrochemical functionality. Unlike conventional alkaline activators (e.g., KOH) or metal salts (e.g., ZnCl2), H3PO4 provides an environmentally benign activation pathway with minimal generation of corrosive byproducts, aligning with green chemistry principles while reducing postprocessing haz￾ards.24,25 Its unique activation mechanism, involving dehy￾dration and cross-linking reactions at moderate temperatures (≤500 °C), enables the simultaneous development of a hierarchical pore architecture: microporous domains to maximize charge storage capacity and mesoporous channels to facilitate rapid ion diffusion, thereby synergistically enhancing both specific capacitance and rate perform￾ance.26−28 Furthermore, the phosphorus-containing functional groups (e.g., C−O−PO3) introduced during H3PO4 activation not only improve interfacial wettability for efficient electrolyte penetration but also contribute to pseudocapacitance through reversible redox reactions.29 The activating process is divided into one-step and two-step activation.30 During one-step activation, biomass is impregnated with the activator prior to the carbonization process. The activator interacts directly with biomass by cleaving the aryl ether bonds. Concurrently, gas release is accelerated by dehydration and condensation mechanisms associated with hydrolyzed glycosidic bonds present in hemicellulose and cellulose.31 In addition, phosphate and polyphosphate moieties are formed by H3PO4 conjugation with organic components within the biomass source, which subsequently facilitates the expansion of the precursor into the porous structure.32 Alternatively, a two-step activation procedure involves carbonization and subsequent impregnation in the activator, followed by activation at an elevated temperature to produce activated carbon. Throughout the two-step activation protocol, pyrolysis results in the release of volatile components and facilitates the production of pores within activated carbon. However, certain tar constituents partially block the developed pores. The physicochemical characteristics of activated carbon generated by one-step versus two-step activation may show considerable differences, potentially affecting supercapacitors’ performance. However, systematic investigations of the effects of these two methods on the physical and chemical properties of activated carbon are rarely conducted. Eucommia Ulmoides Oliver (EUO) stands as a significant economic tree species exclusively found in China. The cultivated area of this species covers over 95% of the worldwide EUO resources, yielding substantial annual biomass assets.33 However, improper use of these biomass resources can lead to serious resource wastage and environmental contamination dilemmas. Hence, there is a growing need to convert EUO wood into value-added products. Research efforts have been devoted to harnessing EUO wood as a sustainable precursor for high-performance supercapacitor electrodes, with a particular focus on structural and process optimization strategies. These endeavors encompass systematic investigations into pore structure engineering of biomass￾derived activated carbons,34 comparative analyses of thermal activation methodologies,35,36 and mechanistic studies of H3PO4-mediated activation protocols.37 However, critical knowledge gaps persist regarding the fundamental differences between one- and two-step activation approaches in governing the hierarchical porosity and charge storage behavior of EUO wood-derived carbons. A systematic understanding remains essential for rational design of biomass-based electrodes with tailored energy-power characteristics. In this study, we have developed a method using both one￾and two-step activation procedures with H3PO4 as a chemical activator to manufacture EUO activated carbon. The optimal activation technique (one-step or two-step activation) is selected based on the distinct pore structure of the activated carbon, and microwave heating technology is used to investigate the effects of heating time on the pore architecture characteristics of the activated carbon. By contrasting the structural differences between activated carbon and biochar, the intrinsic correlations between the structural properties of activated carbon and its electrochemical performance are unveiled. In a three-electrode system, the electrochemical performance of EUO activated carbon is evaluated using cyclic voltammetry (CV), galvanostatic charge−discharge [galvano￾static charge/discharge (GCD)], and electrochemical impe￾dance spectroscopy (EIS), and key metrics such as specific capacitance, capacitance retention, Coulombic efficiency, and energy density of the activated carbon electrode material are obtained. This work initiates a sustainable strategy to transform underutilized EUO wood biomass into hierarchically porous carbons through H3PO4-microwave synergy, offering a dual advantage of coefficient fabrication and remarkable energy storage performance. Our findings not only advance the rational design of biomass-derived supercapacitor electrodes but also establish a model for converting agricultural forestry residues into high-value carbon materials for next-generation energy devices. 2. EXPERIMENTAL SECTION 2.1. Materials. The EUO wood used for this study was sourced from Yangling City, Shaanxi Province, China. The bark and foliage are carefully removed and subjected to a drying procedure at 105 °C for 24 h. The dried wood is then processed into a wood meal (40−60 mesh sizes). H3PO4 of analytical purity (99.90%) was purchased from Energy Co., Ltd. (Shanghai, China). 2.2. Preparation of Carbon Material via Microwave Heating. 6.00 g portion of feedstock is transferred to a 900 W ACS Omega http://pubs.acs.org/journal/acsodf Article https://doi.org/10.1021/acsomega.4c11529 ACS Omega 2025, 10, 15368−15380 15369

microwave heating reactor for 30 min. N2 gas is introduced into the reactor at a rate of 200 mL/min throughout the heating process. After heating, the substance is treated with 0.1 M HCl and then rinsed repeatedly with deionized water until a neutral pH is reached. This final product is designated as EUC. In a one-step activation process, 25 wt % phosphoric acid is used as a chemical activator. This process involves immersing 6.00 g of EUO wood meal in water for 9 h with a solid/liquid ratio of 1:4. After a 2 h drying period, the precursor undergoes a pyrolysis process in a microwave reactor. The resulting solid product is then washed to generate EUO activated carbon. Microwave heating time varies from 30 to 70 min, and the resulting activated carbon materials are named EUAC1−30, EUAC1−40, EUAC1−50, EUAC1−60, and EUAC1−70, respectively. The two-step activation method involves using EUC as a starting material and subjecting it to a chemical activation process. The resultant material then undergoes a 30 min pyrolysis, followed by immersion in 0.1 M HCl and subsequent water washing to achieve a neutral pH prior to drying. The final product is denoted as EUAC2−30. 2.3. Characterization of Carbon Material. SEM-EDS (TM3000, Hitachi, Japan) is used to analyze the micro morphology and composition of our samples. A special surface area instrument (Tristar II 3020, Micromeritics, USA) is used to measure the surface area and pore diameter distribution to provide deeper insight into pore characteristics through using the multipoint N2 adsorption−desorption process. These results are further determined through BET and DFT models. To determine the chemical properties of the surface, Fourier transform infrared (FT-IR) spectroscopy (Vertex70, Bruker, Germany) is performed over a wide spectral range of 400− 4000 cm−1 . Activated carbon was further examined by XPS analysis using a Veresprobe II spectrometer operated under Al Ka radiation. To evaluate the crystallinity of the sample, XRD patterns were analyzed with a D8 ADVANCE A25 instrument (Bruker, Germany) via Cu-Ka radiation at 30 kV and 20 mA, all processed with JADE software (version 5.0). Raman spectral analysis was carried out using a sophisticated Raman microscope system (Horiba JobinYvon, Longjumeau, France), which incorporated a confocal microscope (Olympus BX51, Tokyo, Japan) together with a motorized X/Y sample stage. This equipment is coupled to an argon ion laser that operates at an optimal excitation wavelength of 532 nm for data collection. 2.4. Electrode Preparation and Electrochemical Assays. The working electrode is created by combining EMAC1−60, carbon black (SUPERT-P, TIMCAL), and polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE, Aldrich) at a uniform weight ratio of 8:1:1. This blend is then coated on a stainless-steel mesh, with an active mass weight per unit area of ∼8.0 mg/ cm2 and thickness of ∼0.05 mm. The electrochemical characterization of the electrode is evaluated using EIS, cyclic voltammetry (CV), and GCD analysis in a three-electrode system under the potential window spanning from −1.0 to 0.2 V. A platinum foil functions as the counter electrode, and a Hg/HgO electrode serves as the reference electrode, with an aqueous 1 M KOH functioning as the electrolyte. The EIS technique was implemented on an electrochemical workstation (Zahner Im6ex). The applied frequency was between 100 kHz and 10 MHz, and the ac signal amplitude was 5 mV. The specific capacitance of activated carbon material is then calculated through GCD measurements at charge/discharge current densities ranging from 0.2 to 5 A/g and CV evaluation with varying scanning rates (5, 10, 20, 50, and 100 mV/s). RESULTS AND DISCUSSION 3.1. Effect of the Activation Method on the Pore Structure. N2 adsorption and desorption methods are used to evaluate the porosity profile of the sample. As demonstrated in Figure 1a, significant volumetric adsorption differences are observed for EUAC1−30 at low relative pressures of 0 and 0.2 P/P0, suggesting a substantial increase in its adsorption capacity compared to both EUAC2−30 and EUC. This finding suggests that EUAC1−30 possesses a more complex microporous structure than EUAC2−30 and EUC. The corresponding micropore volumes (EUAC1−30:0.22 cm3 /g; EUAC2−30:0.02 cm3 /g; EUC: 0.09 cm3 /g) support this conclusion (Table 1). During N2 adsorption and desorption, capillary condensation induces N2 molecules to condense and occupy the mesoporous channels. Nitrogen adsorption occurs from the liquid interface of the pore wall, while desorption is initiated at the pore opening. Notably, the nitrogen adsorption and desorption paths do not align to form a hysteresis loop (Figure 1a). This observation indicates the presence of mesopores in the sample, similar to typical type IV adsorption/desorption patterns exhibiting a characteristic H4 hysteresis loop.38 Specifically, EUAC1−30 exhibits a substan￾tially elevated adsorption capacity in the medium pressure domain, accompanied by a pronounced hysteresis loop compared to both EUAC2−30 and EUC, indicating a more widespread distribution of mesoporous architecture through￾out EUAC1−30. These results are consistent with the observed trends in the measured specific surface area and pore volume. The specific surface area (1178.1 m2 /g), total pore volume (0.57 cm3 /g), and mesopore volume (0.35 cm3 / g) of EUAC1−30 outperform those of EUAC2−30 (66.7 m2 / g, 0.04 cm3 /g, and 0.02 cm3 /g), along with those of EUC (292.8 m2 /g, 0.14 cm3 /g, and 0.05 cm3 /g). The pore dimensionality of carbon can be profoundly altered by the choice of activation protocols. As illustrated in Figure 1b, the pore diameter of EUAC1−30 ranges from 1 to 8 nm, manifesting a significant prevalence of both micropores and mesopores when compared to those of EUC and EUAC2−30. This disparity may result from differences in their phosphoric acid activation strategies (i.e., one- vs two￾step). The one-step method integrates phosphoric acid directly into biomass. The substantial hydroxyl function groups within hemicellulose and cellulose facilitate the penetration and flow of phosphoric acid across the substrate. This results in a beneficial dispersion structure, significantly influencing the subsequent formation of pore architecture. During the subsequent thermal decomposition step, phosphoric acid cross-links with the biopolymer (Figure 1c). The covalent reaction involves condensation of three hydroxyl entities in phosphoric acid with hydroxyl units in polysaccharides, leading to the formation of phosphate ester bonds. This bond prevents cell wall shrinkage during thermal decomposition and is a critical stage in the genesis of mature pore architectures.39 Finally, after cleaning activated carbon, both phosphoric acid and its phosphoric-acid-biomass complex are eliminated, yielding pores of diverse dimensions in the final activated carbon. However, the two-step activation procedure can result in activated carbon with increased crystallinity, impeding phosphoric acid’s ability to copolymerize with the carbon framework, leading to suboptimal penetration.40 In cases where the diminished oxygen functional groups act as a significant obstacle to the effective intercalation of phosphoric acid, this is clearly manifested by the restricted pore development observed in EUAC2−30, as documented in Table 1. Findings from this study are in alignment with the research by Fang et al. (2013) and Ma et al. (2014), which indicates that the delayed Table 1. introduction of the activator leads to a reduction in the Lewis acid−base interactions that are crucial for the templating of mesopores. This disruption can have a profound impact on the pore structure formation.41,42 The outstanding capacitance retention rate of 89.90% achieved under high-rate cycling can be attributed to the optimal hierarchical porosity obtained through the one-step activation method. As elaborated by Khalil et al. (2021) and Meng et al. (2023), the interconnected mesopores play a pivotal role in alleviating the ion diffusion bottlenecks that are typically encountered in purely micro￾porous carbons.43,44 This unique structural feature ensures efficient ion transport and contributes significantly to the enhanced electrochemical performance. Therefore, compared to the two-step activation protocol, the one-step activation method produces activated carbon with superior pore architecture, specific surface area, micropore volume, and mesopore volume, making it more conducive to electrolyte permeation during the battery charge and discharge process. 3.2. Effect of Activation Time on the Porosity Structure. The activation time has a great impact on the penetration of phosphoric acid into the carbon precursor and the porosity of the activated carbon material. However, this has rarely been studied in detail. To reach this goal, a one-step activation procedure involving a 900 W microwave for variable durations of 30, 40, 50, 60, and 70 min is applied. Representative N2 adsorption−desorption isotherms and pore diameter distribution are illustrated in Figure 2. As shown, all samples exhibit type IV adsorption isotherms, indicating a high abundance of micropores and mesopores in the carbon material (Figure 2a). The initial enhancement of the specific surface area from 1178.1 m2 /g (30 min) to 1589.0 m2 /g (60 min) can be attributed to progressive acid penetration and controlled etching of the carbon matrix. This aligns with the mechanism proposed by Wang et al.,45 where extended activation facilitates deeper H3PO4 diffusion into biomass precursors, promoting simultaneous micropore formation and mesopore widening. While the adsorption capacity of the samples initially increased with prolonged activation time, it then decreased slightly, suggesting that a prolonged activation time enhances the N2 adsorption capacity of activated carbon. This finding is consistent with trends in the specific surface area and total pore volume (Table 2). However, excessive activation time can disrupt the pre-existing pore structure, the collapse of the porous network and pore blockage, thereby reducing the adsorption ability.46 The activation process resulted in a maximum specific surface area (1589.0 m2 /g), total pore volume (0.82 cm3 /g), and microporous pore volume (0.28 cm3 /g) over a 60 min period. In addition, the activation time significantly influences the average pore diameter variation of total pores in the activated carbon material. As shown in Figure 2b, the pore size of samples generally falls within 1−10 nm, with 2−4 nm mesopores contributing the most. In particular, EUAC1−60 displays the most advanced pore structure development. Thus, a 60 min activation time is considered optimal for converting EUO to activated carbon material through a one-step activation method. 3.3. Structural Characterization of EUC and EUAC1− 60. The Raman spectrum is used to quantify the degree of disorder and crystalline properties of carbon samples. Both EUC and EUACI-60 display discernible peaks D and G. The peak at 1340 cm−1 corresponds to the lattice defects of carbon atoms, while peak G at 1580 cm−1 represents the inplane contraction vibration of sp2 carbon atoms (Figure 3a). The ratio between the intensity of the D-band and G-band typically indicates the level of graphitization.47 Notably, EUAC1−60 demonstrates a higher ID/IG ratio of 0.92 compared to 0.86 for EUC, revealing that the chemical activation process effectively introduces topological defects and disrupts the long-range graphitic order. The increased defect density in EUAC1−60 can be attributed to two synergistic effects: (1) the one-step activation etches carbon skeletons to form hierarchical pore channels, as evidenced by the enhanced specific surface area in BET analysis; (2) the interfacial defects at crystallite boundaries promote the formation of interconnected ion transport pathways.48,49 In addition, EUACI-60 exhibits a superior degree of defect at the material interface, potentially facilitating interconnected channel structures for the rapid adsorption and desorption of electrolyte ions. This advantage would contribute to minimal internal resistance (IR) and Table 2. enhanced rate performance during the electrochemical reaction of carbon electrodes. Furthermore, XRD spectroscopy was employed to further investigate the crystal structure of all of the samples, as illustrated in Figure 3b. Two distinct peaks, corresponding to (002) and (100) lattice planes, were clearly present at 22−26 and 42−46°. Compared to the sharp and narrow peak in the EUC spectrum, EUAC1−60 exhibits a reduced intensity and considerable breadth, suggesting the minimal graphitization and crystallization.50 These findings correlate well with the abundant defect structure observed in the Raman analysis results. This phenomenon may be attributed to phosphoric acid etching, which damages the uniform, flaky crystal framework present within the EUO wood. This process could yield a more diversified pore architecture and an increase in the specific surface area of the amorphous activated carbon, thereby facilitating the charge storage capacity and amplifying the specific capacitance. These results support the analysis of N2 adsorption−desorption isotherm and pore size distribution curves, demonstrating the appropriate activation time (60 min) for fortifying structural properties. SEM analysis is performed to examine the morphology and microstructure of the carbon samples. SEM images (Figure 4) show that a EUAC1−60 s surface area is rougher than that of EUC, indicating that it undergoes a more intense reaction during the one-step activation process. The pore structure of EUAC1−60 is significantly different from that of EUC. The pore structure of EUAC1−60 showed an increased presence of pores and a reduced graphite layer than EUC. As corroborated in Raman and XRD analysis, the pore structure of EUAC1−60 showed signs of rupture, potentially leading to pore expansion of existing pores. Furthermore, EDS technology is used to examine the distribution of elements on the material surface. The analysis shows that the carbon content of EUAC1−60 (81.98%) is lower than that of EUC (84.84%). This discrepancy could be explained by the consumption of carbon in the precursor during the activation process, which potentially facilitates the progression of the pore development. Figure 4. The chemical composition of carbon materials can significantly affect the electrode−electrolyte interface reaction. The FT-IR technique is employed to scrutinize the oxygen￾bearing functional groups within EUC and EUAC1−60. In the spectrum, the broad band within the range of 3500−3300 cm−1 could be attributed to the −OH group, whereas the adsorption bands at 1045 cm−1 are ascribed to the stretching vibration of the C−O bond.51 In addition, there are strengthened bands of −CH (2875, 1445, and 785 cm−1 ) and C�O (1605 cm−1 ) groups appearing in the EUAC1−60 spectrum. This property is advantageous for the hydrophilicity of carbon electrodes in the three electrode system, thus further enhancing the transmission of electrolyte ions in the pores of the activated carbon material. Furthermore, the relative content of chemical bonds on the carbon material surface was further investigated by using the XRS spectrum. The total survey and fitted core-level XPS spectra showed that C and O are the main surface elements of both the samples. In detail, the relative content of O element (15.39%) on the EUAC1−60 surface is higher than that (12.74%) on EUC in Figure 5b, and the trend of C element was opposite. This may be due to the intensive cross-link reaction between phosphoric acid and biomass precursor, and the consumption of carbon compounds to generate abundant pore structure.52 Specifically, the high-resolution spectra of the C element are deconvoluted into C−C (284.8 eV), C−O (285.7 eV), and C�O (288.7 eV) by the Gaussian method, and the O element spectra are contributed to C�O (531.6 eV), C−O/C−O−C (533.2 eV), and O−C�O (533.8 eV) (Figure 5c and d). Besides, EUAC1−60 exhibits the higher relative content of O−C�O and C�O groups than these on EUC. This phenomenon suggests that the activation of phosphoric acid could not only create numerous pore structure and defect sites, but improve the reaction activity of material surface. It is undeniable that it shall further augment the electrochemical efficiency of the carbon electrode through reinforcing the specific capacitance and mitigating the resistance of ion transmission. 3.4. segments.text: Cotton pulp board was purchased from Anhui Snow Dragon Fibre Technology Co., Ltd without further purification. 1.26 g of cotton pulp board was cut into a square shape with length, width and thickness of about 50 mm, 50 mm and 10 mm, respectively. The square cotton pulp board was placed in a glass dish, and then 10.0 mL of potassium hydroxide (KOH, Aladdin, 1.26 g) aqueous solution was added dropwise. The mixture was first dried at 100 °C for 6 h in a drying oven, and then was carbonized at 600 °C for 2 h in a tube furnace with a heating rate of 5 °C min −1 . The obtained black material was washed by 1 M HCl solution for 24 h, followed by filtration with distilled water, and then dried at 100 °C for 12 h to obtain 0.172 g of MHDHPC-600. MHDHPC-600-100 and MHDHPC-600-400 were obtained when the square areas of the cotton pulp were 100 cm 2 and 400 cm 2 .

For comparison, MHDHPC-500 and MHDHPC-700 were produced at 500 °C and 700 °C, respectively, with the same preparation process as for MHDHPC-600. To prepare other comparative samples, the cotton pulp board was mixed with different amounts of KOH with the same preparation process as for MHDHPC-600, where n (0.5 and 1.5) is the mass ratio of KOH : cotton pulp board. The resultant comparative samples were denoted as KOH–CP n ( n = 0.5, 1.5).
Details of the characterization and electrochemical measurements of MHDHPC-500, MHDHPC-600, MHDHPC-700, MHDHPC-600-100 and MHDHPC-600-400 are given in the SI.
