segments.text: Molecules 2023, 28, 4633 2 of 13 As a result of their environmental friendliness, abundance, and low cost in nature, renewable resources have attracted much attention for the preparation of electrode materials along with sustainable development [11]. Significant studies have been conducted on the subject of using lignin, bacterial cellulose, and cellulose to fabricate biomass-based electrode materials [12]. Biomass carbon material is a carbon-rich solid produced as a by￾product from the thermochemical pyrolysis of biomass in an oxygen-limiting environment, which can serve as the electrode for supercapacitors (SCs) [13–15]. The chemical and physical properties of biomass carbon vary significantly with the feedstock and fabrication conditions [16,17]. Their carbonized network can provide more surface area and provide an ion diffusion pathway for charge storage. Momodu et al. synthesized activated carbon derived from bark through a simple activation and carbonization process, which showed a capacitance of 191 F g−1 at 1 A g−1 [18]. Kesavan et al. fabricated nitrogen-doped carbon nanosheets using peanut shell as a precursor. At a current density of 1 A g−1 , a capacitance of 195 F g−1 could be achieved [19]. An Alpinia officinalis leaf derived porous carbon was reported by Taer et al., and it delivered a capacitance of 161 F g−1 at 1 A g−1 [20]. Kang et al. prepared hierarchical porous carbon materials using peanut bran as raw material through hydrothermal carbonization and a KOH activation reaction, and a capacitance of 188 A g−1 was reached at 0.04 A g−1 [21]. In comparison with other biomass waste such as peel, shell, bacteria, etc., reed straw is rich in cellulose, lignin, and hemicellulose [22]. In addition, about 900 million tons of corn, wheat, rice, and sorghum straw are produced every year in China, which can provide sustainable and abundant raw materials for preparing active carbon. The reed straw derived porous carbon is considered as a promising candidate for charge storage [23]. Such a hollow structure can provide more solid–liquid interface for EDLC. Dai et al. fabricated a hollow activated carbon with through-pore structure derived from reed straw. After the activation process, the prepared carbon electrode possessed a high specific surface area of 2387 m2 g −1 and a capacitance of 290 F g−1 [22]. Xie et al. prepared a porous carbon composite by combining raw reed straw with graphene nanosheets. The prepared composite electrode had a capacitance of 297 F g−1 at 0.1 A g−1 and a good cycling stability with a retention rate of 90% after 6000 cycles [23]. Until now, various natural biomass materials such as bacterial cellulose [24], orange peels [25], rice stems [26], bamboo [27], and carb shell [28] have been reported as the precursors to prepared carbon anodes for SCs. These biomass carbon materials based on EDLC charge storage mechanisms can be improved by increasing their surface area. However, the increased surface area contributing to EDLC is limited, and the capacitance and energy density of carbon materials usually remain poor [11]. Recently, the introduction of electrochemical-active functionalities (e.g., O, N, P, and S containing groups) on the carbon skeleton turned out to be a feasible approach to significantly boost the capacitance of carbon-based SCs [29–32]. These heteroatoms can expand the carbon interlayer distance and allow more transfer of anions and cations. Especially, nitrogen doping of carbon can increase the surface polarity, electric conductivity, and electron-donor affinity for the carbon network. Moreover, some reports demonstrated that the type of doped N configuration (pyrrolic-N, pyridinic-N, or graphitic-N) has a significant effect on the charge storage process, and the content of the active N in carbon networks could be key parameter determining the activity of the electrode. Among them, pyridinic N has been widely considered as more active for adsorbing alkali metal ions [33]. The capacitance of nitrogen￾doped carbons (NPCs) comes not only from EDLC but also from the faradaic reaction at or near the surface of the carbon material [34]. Uppugalla et al. reported a nitrogen and sulfur heteroatom co-doped activated carbon by hydrothermal reaction, which served as an electrode for SCs and delivered an enhanced capacitance of 417 F g−1 at 0.7 A g−1 with a good cycling stability [35]. Llnicka et al. prepared an N-doped porous carbon from gelatin and green algae, and its nitrogen functionalities and microstructure enabled a capacitance of 327 F g−1 with cycle durably [36]. Generally, the preparation of NPCs is achieved through the pyrolysis of biomass waste containing N elements, and the post-treatment of carbon materials with ammonia and urea at high temperatures [37]. Therefore, we anticipated

In this work, a reed straw derived biomass carbon (RSM) was prepared by directly pyrolyzing reed straw and melamine with KOH as the activator. The RSM as the electrode for SCs exhibited an enhanced electrochemical performance by rationally introducing melamine. In addition, the pyrolysis temperature was taken into consideration. Molecules 2023, 28, 4633 9 of 13 3. Experimental Section 3.1. Materials and Methods Reed straw powder (60 mesh) was purchased from Shaanxi Jinhe Agricultural Technol￾ogy Co., Ltd. (Shaanxi, China). Melamine and potassium hydroxide (KOH) were purchased from Shanghai Aladdin Biochemical Technology Co., (Shanghai, China). Polyvinylidene flu￾oride (PVDF), acetylene black, concentrated hydrochloric acid (HCl), N-methylpyrrolidone (NMP), and other chemical reagents were purchased from Chengdu Kelong Chemical Reagent Co., (Chengdu, China). Nitrogen was purchased from Guangdu Gas Business Department (Chengdu, China). All reagents were analytical grade and used as received without further purification. 3.2. Preparation of RSM-y-550 An aliquot of 2 g of reed straw powder was mixed with varying weights of melamine (0 g, 0.66 g, 2 g, and 6 g), and stirred continuously with a glass rod after the addition of 50 mL deionized water until the straw powder no longer floated at the liquid level and was well dispersed in the water. It was then transferred to a 75 mL Teflon stainless steel autoclave and reacted in an oven at 120 ◦C for 2 h to allow good mixing and make it partially carbonize. When cooled to room temperature, a yellowish powder (RSM) was obtained. Subsequently, 1 g of RSM powder and 1 g of KOH were added to 10 mL deionized water with continuous stirring for 4 h, and then dried at 80 ◦C for 12 h. The mixture was transferred in a porcelain boat and put in a tubular furnace for further activation. The activator KOH can react with the carbon precursor at the elevated temperature to form a porous structure. The generated CO, CO2, and K could further etch the carbon network to form the micro- and meso-porous structures. The activation operation was conducted at 550 ◦C for 2 h, with a temperature rising rate of 5 ◦C min−1 under a nitrogen atmosphere. After cooling down to room temperature, the mixture was collected and cleaned with 1 M hydrochloric acid and washed with distilled water several times to remove impurities including K2CO3, KHCO3, and KOH. Finally, the products were dried by vacuum at 60 ◦C for 12 h. The obtained sample was denoted RSM-y-550, where y represents the mass ratio of melamine to reed straw (y = 0, 0.33, 1, and 3). 3.3. Characterization XRD patterns were collected on an X-ray diffractometer (Philip Company, Pw1730) equipped with a Cu Kα radiation (λ = 1.5418 Å). XPS spectra were measured on an X￾ray photoelectron spectrometer (XPS, a Kratos Axis Ultra spectrometer, Kratos Analyti￾cal Inc., Manchester, UK). SEM images were captured on a Hitachi S-4800 field emission scanning electron microscope (Hitachi High-Tech Co., Tokyo, Japan) at an accelerating voltage of 20 kV. Raman spectra were measured on a DXR Raman microscope (Thermo Fisher Scientific Inc., Waltham, MA, USA) with an excitation wavelength of 455 nm. Brunauer–Emmett–Teller (BET) surface area was collected on a Micromeritics TRISTAR II3020 surface area analyzer (Micromeritics Instrument, Norcross, GA, USA). 3.4. Electrochemical Measurement To prepare the RSM-y-550 working electrode, the prepared mixture of active carbon material (80 wt%), polyvinylidene fluoride (10 wt%), and acetylene black (10 wt%) was coated on nickel foam (1.0 × 1.0 cm2 ) and dried at 80 ◦C for 24 h. The three-electrode system was employed to estimate the electrochemical performance of all electrodes. RSM￾y-550 was used as the working electrode (anode), with platinum as the opposite electrode, saturated calomel electrode (SCE) as the reference electrode, and 6 M KOH solution as the electrolyte. Cyclic voltammetry (CV), galvanostatic charge–discharge (GCD) and electrochem￾ical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) were performed on a CHI600E electrochemical workstation (Chenhua Instrument Co., Shanghai, China). The GCD was employed at a current density of 1–10 A g−1 . The CV was conducted at a scan rate of 10–100 mV s−1 . The frequency range of EIS was 0.01–100 kHz, and the potential window was 5 mV. Extensive research suggests that high-performance SCs based on sustainable biomass-derived carbons must possess several key characteristics: (i) A high SSA is essential for optimal electrode performance, as it provides a high density of electrocatalytically active sites and substantially enhances charge storage capacity [33–39]. (ii) A hierarchical pore architecture is equally critical, as it integrates distinct functions across multiple length scales: macropores serve as ion-buffering reservoirs, mesopores facilitate rapid ion transport, and micro￾pores serve as ion-storage sites. This architecture collectively contributes to exceptional electrochemical performance [40–47]. (iii) Heteroatom doping (e.g., N, S, and P) effectively increases the density of active sites and simultaneously enables precise modulations of the electronic structure and surface chemistry of the material [48–53]. Heteroatom doping of carbon matrices can be achieved through either post-treatment or in situ methods. The former, however, is often limited by multiple drawbacks, including a complex synthesis procedure, low doping levels, poor controllability, and heterogeneous distribution of dopants. [44]. In situ doping offers a versatile strategy to tailor both the electrochemical properties and hierarchical porosity of carbon￾based materials by judicious selection of precursors and rational design of heteroatom incorporation pathways. Therefore, the selection of inherent heteroatom-rich precursors combined with tailored preparation techniques constitutes a critical strategy for developing high-performance biomass-derived carbons, which possess simultaneously optimized SSA and hierarchical porosity for advanced energy storage. Chinese herbal medicine residues (CHMRs) are byproducts derived from widely adopted practice of Chinese herbal medicine, which has gained significant global recognition for disease prevent and treatment in recent years. This trend toward inter￾nationalization, however, has concurrently led to the generation of substantial quantities of herbal residues [54], posing grow￾ing environmental and disposal challenges. Global agricultural biomass inventories indicate that the annual generation of such residues exceed 30 million metric tons [55]. Currently, the predominant disposal method for these residues—incineration and landfilling—not only results in significant resource wastage but also contributes to substantial environmental harm [56–58]. Therefore, utilizingCHMRs as precursorsfor SC-activated carbon offers a sustainable approach ensures abundant availability, low cost, and environmental renewability [59–61]. Furthermore, owing to their diverse origins, CHMR possesses intrinsic com￾positional complexity and are inherently rich in heteroatoms. This characteristic allows them to function as self-doping carbon precursors, facilitating in situ heteroatom incorporation that effectively tailors the hierarchical architecture and optimizes the electrochemical performance of the resulting carbon [62– 64]. Consequently, several recent studies have demonstrated the successful fabrication of high-performance carbon materialsfrom herbal residues for application as advanced SC electrodes. Lei et al. [33] demonstrated that carbonization-activation of three types of herbal residues yield carbons with record SSA (3410 m2⋅g−1 ), delivering 291.6 F⋅g−1 at 1 A⋅g−1 . Similarly, Zhang et al. [63] reported N/S co-doped porous carbon derived from gallnut residues, which delivered a specific capacitance of 300 F⋅g−1 at 0.5 A⋅g−1 . Despite these advances, current research predominantly focuses on carbon materials from single-herb residues, whereas studies utilizing mixed-herb residuesremain scarce. Using mixed Chinese herbal residues as the carbon precursor, Huang et al. [64] synthesized multi-heteroatom co-doped porous carbon that achieved a specific capacitance of 486.2 F⋅g−1 at 1 A⋅g−1 . Notably, the residues utilized in Huang’s study comprised a relatively high proportion (∼25%) of animal-derived components, in contrast to conventional herbal residues, which typically contain less than 10%. Therefore, the selection of feedstock that more accurately reflects the typical composition of herbal residues is critical for both the effective valorization of herbal waste and the technological advancement of SC applications. Based on the reasons, we developed a facile method for in situ preparation of N, O-doped carbon materials, using mixed herbal residues with actual composition more closely resembling indus￾trial TCM waste asthe sole precursor. The selection of appropriate preparation methods is crucial to fabricating advanced SCs elec￾trodes, asit enablesthe retention of inherent nitrogen and oxygen elements(achieving in situ N/O self-doping) while constructing a high SSA area and a hierarchical pore structure. In this work,self￾doped N, O-containing porous carbon was prepared from mixed CHMRs through a two-step process involving pre-carbonization followed by chemical activation with KOH under a nitrogen atmosphere. The subsequent KOH activation plays a dual role: It effectively creates a hierarchical porous architecture while the intentionally shortened duration (0.5 h) helps preserve a substan￾tial portion of the inherent N and O elements, thereby achieving in situ self-doping. The resulting carbon exhibits well-balanced electrochemical performance, including a specific capacitance of 344 F⋅g−1 at 1 A⋅g−1 , a retention of 78.5% (270 F⋅g−1 ) at 10 A⋅g−1 , and excellent cycling stability with 96% capacitance reten￾tion after 10,000 cycles at 10 A⋅g−1 . These results demonstrate that the proposed synthesis strategy is pivotal for developing high-performance and economically viable SC systems. 2 Experimental Section 2.1 Materials The raw material is a mixture of herbal residues generated within 1 month by Henan Dadeguang Animal Pharmaceutical Co., Ltd. Potassium hydroxide (KOH, 95%) was sourced from Macklin Biochemical (Shanghai), and hydrochloric acid (HCl, 37%, AR grade) was acquired from Aladdin Biochemical. Laboratory-grade deionized (DI) water was employed for all procedures. 2.2 Fabrication of Porous Carbon Using Mixed CHMRs The mixed CHMRs (labeled as YZ) were ground to 200 mesh and dried overnight at 80◦C. The powder was then pre-carbonized in a tubular furnace under a nitrogen flow (400◦C, 2 h, heating rate 10◦C⋅min−1 ) to obtain the carbonized intermediate, denoted as YZC. The starting material (YZ, Figure 1a) and its pre-carbonized counterpart (YZC, Figure 1b) both display an amorphous bulk morphology, indicating that the initial thermal treatment largely preserved the overall structure framework. Without KOH activation, YZPC-0 (Figure 1c) exhibits a relatively flat surface with only minor carbon particulates and negligible pore formation. In contrast, after KOH activation (Figure 1d– g), the materials develop distinctly dispersed and disordered macropores. As the KOH-to-precursor ratio increases, the poros￾ity becomes progressively more pronounced. However, at a ratio of 4, excessive KOH etching leads to framework collapse and structural degradation. KOH corrodes the carbon atoms in the micro-crystallite graphene. This action not only thins the pore walls but also erodes the primary structural units of the material’s skeleton [75]. Notably, an RKOH/YZC ratio of 3 yields the most uniformly distributed porous architectures for the derived carbons. Corresponding TEM images (Figure 1h) display short￾range ordered curved fringes, indicative of turbostratic disorder structures with sp2-sp3 hybridization. The presence of localized parallel fringes further suggests partial graphitization within the carbon matrix [71]. As observed in the SEM images, KOH activation successfully introduced abundant porosity into the YZPC series. The nitro￾gen adsorption isotherms (Figure 2a) display a combined Type I/IV shape, indicating the coexistence of substantial micropores and mesopores—a feature that facilitates efficient ion inter￾calation/deintercalation during charge storage. Without KOH activation,YZPC-0 shows negligible N2 uptake and a very low SSA of only 167 m2⋅g−1 (Table 1). After activation, both YZPC-1 and YZPC-2 exhibit significantly enhanced N2 adsorption capacity and substantially increased BET surface areas (Table 1). At RKOH/YZC ratio of 3 and above, the isotherms evolve into distinct Type I/IV profiles with pronounced hysteresis loops, confirming the development of a well-defined mesoporous structure. The sharp rise in nitrogen uptake at P/P0 < 0.1for YZPC-3 and YZPC-4 further reflects their abundant microporosity [65]. In the relative pressure range of 0.1–0.4, a steady increase in nitrogen adsorption is observed, consistent with the presence of mesopores. The pore-size distribution curves (Figure 2b) reveal that YZPC-3 and YZPC-4 possess similar micropore distributions below 2 nm, while showing a broader and more intense distribution in the 2–4 nm range as the activation ratio rises. Overall, enhanced elec￾trochemical performance can be attributed to the combination of a high SSA and an optimized pore size distribution. The phase structure of the five YZPC samples, are revealed by their XRD patterns (Figure 3a), are closely linked to the pore architecture developed during KOH activation. All patterns exhibit two broad, weak diffraction peaks at approximately 24◦ and 44◦ (2θ), corresponding to the (002) and (100) planes of turbostratic carbon, respectively [66, 67]. The pronounced low￾angle scattering observed in each sample is a direct signature of their microporous nature, a structure feature quantitatively confirmed by the corresponding BET analysis [15]. Notably, the evolution of (002) peak intensity correlates with the changes in porosity. YZPC-0, which possesses minimal porosity, shows a relatively high intensity around 24◦. As the activation ratio increases from YZPC-1 to YZPC-4, this peak broadens and diminishes in intensity, indicating a progressive loss of long￾range graphitic order. This trend coincides with the development of a more extensive and hierarchical pore network, suggesting that the intense KOH etching not only creates pores but also introduces topological defects that disrupt crystallinity. Raman spectroscopy (Figure 3b) provides further support for this structure evolution. The D band (∼1350 cm−1 ) originates from disordered or defect-containing sp3 carbon, whereas the G band (∼1580 cm−1 ) corresponds to the in-plane vibration of sp2-hybridized carbon in graphitic domains [68, 69]. The ID/IG intensity ratios for YZPC-0, YZPC-1, YZPC-2, YZPC-3, and YZPC-4 are 0.85, 0.96, 0.97, 0.97, and 0.98, respectively. The systematic increase in ID/IG with rising KOH ratio indicates a progressive decline in graphitic ordering and a corresponding rise in structural defects. These defects can act as additional active sites for ion adsorption, a conclusion that aligns well with the XRD observations. Combined on N2-sorption and SEM analyses reveal that YZPC￾3 possesses the most developed porous architecture among the series, exhibiting the highest SSA and an optimal mesopore distribution embedded in a continuous microporous network. This well-defined hierarchical porosity is expected to contribute to superior electrochemical performance. The chemical compo￾sition and bonding states of nitrogen and oxygen heteroatoms in the five YZPCs were further examined by XPS. As shown in the survey spectrum of YZPC-3 (Figure 4a), distinct peaks are observed for O 1s at ∼532 eV, C 1s peak at ∼284.5 eV, and a relatively weaker N 1s peak at ∼400 eV [70], confirming the successful incorporation of heteroatoms into the carbon matrix. Quantitative analysis of the C, O, and N content across all synthesized samples is provided in Table 1 and Figure S1a. It is evident that the distribution of nitrogen species decreases as the RKOH/YZC increases due to excessive etching by KOH [71]. The high-resolution C 1s spectrum of YZPC-3 (Figure 4b) was deconvoluted into four components at 284.6, 285.3, 286.3, and 288.1 eV, corresponding to C═C, C─C, C─O, and C═O bonds, respectively [71]. The O 1s spectrum (Figure 4c) exhibits four fitted peaks assigned to quinone-type C═O (531.0 eV), C─O (532.0 eV), C─O in COO− (533.0 eV), and N─O (534.2 eV) [64]. Deconvolution of the N 1s region (Figure 4d) yields four characteristic contributions: pyridinic N (N-6, 398.2 eV), pyrrolic N (N-5, 399.5 eV), quaternary N (N-Q, 401.0 eV), and pyridinic￾N-oxide (N-X, 403 eV). Previous studies have established that pyrrolic and pyridinic nitrogen act as efficient electron donors with high charge mobility. Their incorporation into the carbon matrix enhances the overall electron-donating capability, pro￾motes electron-transfer processes and boosts catalytic activity-all of which contribute to improve electrochemical performance [69, 72]. Furthermore, quaternary nitrogen (N-Q) doping facil￾itates electron delocalization within the carbon frameworks, leading to enhance charge-transfer kinetics and superior SCs performance. A large number of Kochia is directly discarded, which leads to a waste of resources. The lignin, cellulose, and hemicellulose in the plant are pyrolyzed under high temperatures to retain the pore structure and the volatile components are discharged to make the natural tube bundle structure in the original plant more obvious and stable. Use different proportions of KOH for chem￾ical activation to further optimize the pore structure. The micro￾pore and mesopore structure are fully etched on the original tube-like macroporous wall to obtain a biomass-activated carbon electrode material with a hierarchical pore structure, promoting the storage and rapid transportation of a large number of elec￾trolyte ions, and the increased SSA provides more active sites. So far, there are only a few reports of using Kochia as electrode material for supercapacitors. This study explored the influence on the electrochemical performance of electrode materials by changing the ratio of activators. The electrode material samples exhibit excellent electrochemical performance, high surface area, and effective ion diffusion characteristics. We have also explored the assembly and application of electrode material with electro￾lytes, which is expected to go further in the application of supercapacitors. 2. Results and Discussion Figure 1 is a schematic representation of the entire experimental process including the activation mechanism. The Kochia was car￾bonized at 800 °C making the lignocellulose pyrolysis open mac￾ropores to obtain KC-800. Then chemically etched with different proportions of KOH and KAC-n was obtained. Usually, KOH is completely decomposed at 600 °C. During this period, potassium compounds as a chemical activator with carbon undergo redox reactions to etch the carbon skeleton.[23,33] The process had H2O and CO2 generated for further physical activation. During the activation process, the potassium ions are effectively embedded in the lattice of the carbon matrix causing lattice expansion, which cannot be recovered and therefore results in a large SSA and high porosity.[34] Finally, a symmetric superca￾pacitor was assembled using KAC-5 as the electrode material with optimal performance. The experimental section shows the detailed preparation process. According to the FESEM image of Kochia in Figure 2a, the powder was found to be composed of fibrous lignocellulose and had a very rough surface with no visible pore structure. In contrast to it, Figure 2b,c shows the optimal sample that was first carbonized and then activated by KOH because of the pyrolytic volatilization of lignocellulose, the originally blocked plant tube structure is exposed, the tubes with macropores at both ends are completely opened with pore size distribution in the range of 5-10 μm, and opening tube structure increases the SSA of the entire material. The exposed macropores can be used as channels for rapid electrolyte transfer[35] and facilitate KOH etching of the internal duct walls to form more micropores and mesopores, thus providing a large number of active sites.[36] To further investigate the etching of the KAC-5 surface after KOH treatment, TEM analysis was carried out, and the results could be seen in Figure 2d. The red circles show some of the micropores and the mesopores formed by the interconnection of the etched micropores, and there are a large number of more evenly distributed micropores and some mesopores on the sur￾face, this is the result of etching the surface of the material by KOH activation and etching through the macropores into the tube structure. Figure 2e,f shows the C and O elemental mapping images of KOH-5, respectively. After the activation treatment, the surface is composed of only C and O elements, which indicates that KAC-5 can only be used as an electrode material for a carbon-based double-layer supercapacitor, but the presence of some oxygen increases the surface wettability of the electrode material and provides some pseudo capacitance, which facilitates the higher electrochemical performance of supercapacitors in aqueous electrolytes.[31] Figure 1. To explore the composition of Kochia, the FT-IR spectrum of Kochia is shown in Figure 2g. The absorption peaks of lignin, cellulose, and hemicellulose are obvious. The characteristic absorption peak of lignin occurring at 830 cm1 is ascribed to C-H out-of-plane stretching. The peaks at 1624 cm1 indicate aromatic skeletal vibrations. Moreover, the peaks centered at 2926 and 3357 cm1 can be attributed to the C─H and O─H stretching vibration, respectively.[37] The absorption peaks of cel￾lulose can be found at 895, 1038, 1157, and 1375 cm1 , which correspond to ring vibration, C─O stretching vibration of gluco￾sidic bond, C─O asymmetric stretching vibration, and C─H bending vibration, respectively.[38] As for hemicelluloses, the peaks at 1240 and 1733 cm1 indicate the C─O asymmetric vibrations and C=O stretching vibrations of acetyl.[39,40] The results show that Kochia is composed of lignocellulose. Lignin in most plant cells acts as a binder to wrap around cellulose as a skeleton, and hemicellulose acts as a filler to form a stable structure similar to reinforced concrete in cells.[41,42] Therefore, lignocellulose can be decomposed to form porous carbon through high-temperature pyrolysis, and chemical activation can greatly change the structure of this biomass. The above conditions indicate that rationally optimizing the components of Kochia has certain significance for the preparation of target carbon materials. To select a suitable carbonization temperature, the TGA curve of the above sample is observed in Figure 2h. It is mainly divided into three stages: first, continuous decomposition of free water in the temperature range of 100 °C with about 6.7% of weight loss; the most obvious decline is the second stage of lignocellulose decomposition process with 71.9% of weight loss: hemicellulose is first decomposed in the range of 220 to 315 °C, followed by cellulose in the range of 315 to 400 °C and lignin is completely decomposed at 550 °C.[43] In addition, the third stage was rela￾tively stable with a weight loss of 21.4% from 550 to 900 °C. To determine the carbonation temperature, galvanostatic charge/discharge tests at a current density of 1 A g1 were car￾ried out on KC-600, KC-700, KC-800, and KC-900, and the high￾est specific capacitance of 184 F g1 with a current density of 1Ag1 was obtained at the temperature of 800 °C, as shown in Figure S1, Supporting Information. Therefore, 800 °C was selected as the carbonization temperature. To further investigate the role of KOH as an activator, N2 adsorption/desorption isotherms were used to test KAC-5. Figure 2i shows a type I isotherm with a large increase in the relative pressure P/P0 < 0.1, indicating that KOH activation forms a large number of micropores;[25,44] the existence of hys￾teresis loops and good overlap of the isotherms prove that the pore size distribution of mesopores is very narrow. of Figure 2i shows the pore size distribution, which is mainly in the range of 1–7 nm. From Table 1, the large SSA of KAC-5 reaches 1441.30 m2 g1 . This result is higher than the previously reported SSA of most biomass carbon electrode materials, the comparison results are shown in Figure S2, Supporting Information. The microporosity reaches 82.28% with an average pore size of 1.6632 nm, which is also the reason for the large number of micropores that can be seen in TEM images. A small number of mesopores can be used as a channel to store and transmit electrolytes, while a large number of micropores pro￾vide active sites and increase the SSA and contribute to the improvement of electrochemical performance.[24,45] As shown in Figure 3a from XRD determination, two broad diffraction peaks at a 2θ value of approximately 15° and 23° were observed and ascribed to the diffraction peaks of cellulose and hemicellulose in Kochia.[46] Diffraction peaks of around 23° and 43° can be seen in the curves of KC, KAC-4, KAC-5, and KAC-6, corresponding to the (002) and (100) crystal planes of gra￾phitic carbon, respectively.[47] Compared to KC, the (002) crystal￾line plane of the activated samples is all shifted to the left. Previous studies have demonstrated the redox reaction between KOH and carbon during activation to form potassium-containing compounds as well as the production of gas such as CO2 further physical activation affects the extent of defects and produces more active sites, while the metal potassium ions expand the space of the atomic carbon layer, influencing the degree of graph￾itization.[23] Accordingly, further structural information can also be obtained from the Raman spectra measured in Figure 3b, in which the independent peaks at 1340 cm1 (D-band) and 1580 cm1 (G-band) corresponded to the disordered form of car￾bon materials and graphitic lattice vibrations, respectively.[48] Assessment of the degree of disorder in carbon materials by the intensity ratio of the D-band to the G-band. The ID/IG values for KC, KAC-4, KAC-5, and KAC-6 were 0.96, 0.98, 0.99, and 1.00, indicating an increase in defect density after activation. The abundant disordered and defective carbon in KAC-n was beneficial to the improvement of surface area and the number of activated sites for reactions and promoted ion diffusion and transportation, and these were all positive for the capacitive per￾formance of carbon materials.[45] XPS analysis was performed to determine the surface elemen￾tal composition and content of KAC-5. The presence of C and O can be obtained from Figure 3c. Element C accounted for 91.75% of the total and the element O accounted for 8.25%. The C 1s spectrum of KAC-5 can be fitted into four peaks in Figure 3d, corresponding to the C─C (284.8 eV), C─O (286.4 eV), C = O (287.9 eV), and O─C = O (288.9 eV).[49,50] Similarly, in Figure 3e, the O 1s spectrum could be fitted with three major peaks at 530.8, 532.1, and 533.3 eV, representing C = O, C─O, and O─C─O, respectively.[27,32,51] Surface wettability of electrode materials can be improved by the presence of these oxygen￾containing functional groups, as also evidenced by the contact angle test shown in Figure 3f. A drop of water was transiently absorbed within 1 s of contacting the porous carbon material, and the measured contact angle was 58.25°, indicating that KAC-5 has good hydrophilicity, which is conducive to full contact between electrolyte and electrode material as a way to generate more electrochemical reactions.[49] Due to the porous structure and high SSA of the prepared samples, performances of KC, KAC-4, KAC-5 and KAC-6 were first evaluated using 6.0 M KOH as the electrolyte in a three￾electrode system. Figure 4a compares the CV curves of this acti￾vated carbon at a scan rate of 50 mV s1 . These curves are almost always rectangular in shape and are typical of double-layer capaci￾tors.[2,44,52] After activation by KOH, compared to KC, the CV curves of the others have bulges in the lower potential region around 0.5 V, which is caused by the oxygen content on the surface leading to the formation of pseudo-capacitance. The effect of KOH activation is reflected, KAC-4, KAC-5, and KAC￾6 are accompanied by redox peaks due to the pseudo-capacitance provided by the presence of oxygen after activation, which makes the area surrounded by CV curve larger and the electrochemical performance is better than KC. Compared to the other three materials, KAC-5 has the largest integral area of the CV curve, indicating its highest specific capacitance.[44,47,53] This result is also reflected in the charge/discharge curves in Figure 4b, where KAC-5 has the longest discharge time at a current density of 1Ag1 . The symmetrical GCD curves demonstrate the excellent capacitive performance and high coulomb efficiency of all four materials,[10,19] and this suggests that the appropriate carbon￾base ratio is also particularly important for electrochemical per￾formance. According to Equation (1), the specific capacitances of KC, KAC-4, KAC-5, and KAC-6 are 184, 256, 284, and 239 F g1 , respectively. KAC-5 exhibits the highest specific capacitance and higher than previously reported biomass carbon electrode mate￾rials as shown in Table S1, Supporting Information. Compared with KC, the surface of activated KAC-5 contains certain oxygen elements and is more abundant in microporous structure and mesoporous structure, which will increase the contact area between the electrode material and the electrolyte, so that the active site increases, which are particularly important for porous carbon materials, and reflect a difference of 100 F g1 before and after activation in terms of specific capacitance. A comparative multiplier performance graph is made to test the performance of the material at high current densities, as shown in Figure S3, Supporting Information. The specific capacitance was further calculated from Equation (1) for current densities from 0.5 to 10 A g1 . The maximum specific capacitance of the KAC-5 reaches 288 F g1 (0.5 A g1 ), even at high current densities of 10 A g1 , and KAC-5 still maintains a specific capac￾itance of 227 F g1 with a capacitance retention rate of 78.8%. Based on the Nyquist diagram of the samples in Figure 4c, in the low-frequency region, the straight lines of all three activated specimens are nearly perpendicular to the real axis,[45] in contrast to KC, which has a small slope, and the diffuse resistance of the activated specimens becomes smaller. In addition, the interfacial charge transfer resistances (Rct) were 0.055, 0.05, 0.039, and 0.041 Ω. In summary, KAC-5 had the lowest resistance, which was attributed to the increased SSA due to chemical activation, which facilitated the transport of electrolyte ions in the electrode material, and the presence of oxygen-containing functional groups, which improved the wettability of the surface of the electrode material, resulting in such excellent impedance perfor￾mance. The above electrochemical analysis showed that KAC-5 has the best electrochemical performance, which proves the spe￾cific capacitance of KC is further enhanced followed by chemical activation and that the appropriate carbon-to-alkali ratio is equally important, as excessive KOH will transitionally etch the original carbon skeleton, collapsing the skeleton and impeding the transport of electrolyte ions, reducing the SSA and the number of active sites, making the electrochemical performance poor.[5,45,52] A more comprehensive electrochemical analysis of the optimum sample KAC-5 was carried out. Figure 5e shows the power density versus energy density graph and comparison with other studies.[28,58–64] From the results, the energy density of the miniature symmetrical supercapacitor with 6 M KOH aqueous as the electrolyte can reach 12.3 Wh kg1 when the power density is 300 W kg1 and still reach 8.3 Wh kg1 when the power density is as high as 6000 W kg1 . Figure 5f shows that using three supercapacitors connected in series as a small bulb power source to easily light tricolor LED bulbs. These above results demon￾strated that the prepared biomass activated carbon KAC-5 could be used as excellent electrode materials for supercapacitors. 3. Conclusions Kochia was first used as a precursor in the preparation of activated carbon material for supercapacitors in this work. The results showed that the SSA of the electrode material was increased by opening the natural tube structure originally con￾tained in the plant through the carbonation process, and then further modulating the pore size distribution to create a multi￾scale pore structure by KOH activation to increase the active sites and SSA. Its electrochemical performance as an electrode mate￾rial for supercapacitors was superior to that of other previously reported biomass carbon materials. By adjusting the appropriate carbon-to-base ratio, KAC-5 has a rich microporous structure occupying 82.28% of the pore volume, with a SSA of 1441.30 m2 g1 . In the three-electrode system, the maximum specific capacitance of KAC-5 reaches 284 F g1 when the current density is 1 A g1 , and the capacitance retention for 10 000 cycles is 90.31%. The energy density of the symmetrical supercapacitor assembled with KAC-5 as the active material can reach 12.3 Wh kg1 when the power density is 300 W kg1 . All these excellent properties are derived from its natural tubular structure and its rich lignocellulose. This study provides a sustainable method for the preparation of supercapacitor electrode material from biomass waste. 4. Experimental Section Materials: The following materials, Kochia (Deyang, Sichuan Province, China). potassium hydroxide (KOH, Macklin, AR), hydrochloric acid (HCl, AR), acetylene black (AB, ECP600JD, LION Ketjenblack), polyvinylidene fluoride (PVDF, Arkema), and ethanol (C2H6O, AR), were purchased. Deionized water was employed directly without further treatment. Preparation of Activated Carbon: The purchased Kochia was ultrasoni￾cated with absolute ethanol first to remove surface impurities, then rinsed with deionized water, and then placed in an oven for thorough drying. These dried sticks were crushed and grounded through a 35-mesh sieve. Then the Kochia powder was kept in a tube furnace at 800 °C for 2 h at a heating rate of 5 °C min1 ,N2 was used as the protective gas. The samples were thoroughly washed with deionized water and dried in an oven, recorded as Kochia carbon (KC). KC and KOH were mixed according to a mass ratio of 1:5 and a suspension is prepared, and dried it in a 75 °C oven for 12 h. The mixture after drying was activated in a tube fur￾nace at 600 °C under an N2 atmosphere for 2 h at a heating rate of 5 °C min1 . The product’s excess KOH and soluble salts were removed with 1M hydrochloric acid and then washed with deionized water for neutrality. The resulting carbon material was recorded as Kochia activated carbon (KAC). For comparison, three different carbon-to-base ratios (1:4, 1:5, 1:6) were prepared, respectively, as KAC-4, KAC-5, and KAC-6. Characterization: The powder X-ray diffractometer was performed with an X-ray diffraction instrument to characterize the crystal structure of sam￾ples (XRD, Bruker D8). Raman spectrometer was used to characterize the degree of defects and graphitization. (LabRAM HR Evolution). The micro￾scopic morphology of samples was carried out by field-emission scanning electron microscope (FESEM, GeminiSEM500). The distribution of ele￾ments in the samples was determined through energy-dispersive spectros￾copy (EDS, GeminiSEM500). Transmission electron microscopy (TEM, Talos F200X) was performed to observe the microstructures of the obtained products. The SSA and pore size distribution of the analyzed samples were tested by using a nitrogen adsorption meter (BET, Micromeritics APSP 2460). X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy was per￾formed to analyze chemical composition (XPS, ESCALAB 250 electron spectrometer). The Fourier transform infrared was used to characterize the type of functional group of the raw material (FTIR, ISQ 7000 Nicolet iS50 TGA/DSC3). Electrochemical Performance: The prepared carbon material, polyvinyli￾dene fluoride, and acetylene black were thoroughly mixed in a mass ratio of 8:1:1 to form a slurry, the slurry was coated on the foamed nickel with a size of 1 cm 1 cm and dried at 75 °C after 1 h, and they were pressed at 10 MPa for 1 min. The three-electrode system was assembled with pressed electrode sheets as working electrodes, and the Hg/HgO electrode was used as the reference electrode and the platinum sheet as the counter electrode. The single-electrode sheet active material load of the three￾electrode system was 3 mg cm2 , with 6 M KOH as the electrolyte. CHI605E electrochemical workstation for cyclic voltammetry (CV) tests was recorded from 1.0 to 0 V at a scan rate of 5, 10, 20, 50, 100 mV s1 , and galvanostatic charge–discharge (GCD) tests were recorded from 1.0 to 0 V at a current density of 1,2,3,5,10 A g1 . Supercapacitors, also referred to as electrochemical capacitors, provide unique techni￾cal advantages over traditional energy storage devices like batteries and dielectric capacitors, largely due to their fundamentally different charge storage mecha￾nisms [2–5]. Unlike batteries, which depend on slow, diffusion-based redox reactions, supercapacitors store energy through rapid electrostatic interactions at the electrode-electrolyte interface [6, 7]. This mechanism enables them to achieve extremely high power densi￾ties, allowing rapid charging and discharging within seconds or minutes, a capability that batteries cannot match due to their kinetic limitations [8, 9]. Superca￾pacitors exhibit high power density, rapid charge-dis￾charge capability, and long cycle life, making them attractive for applications such as smart grids, backup power systems, consumer electronics, and renewable energy integration [10, 11]. In recent years, various materials have been explored by the scientific community for superca￾pacitor applications, such as FeCo2O4 [12], SrFeO3 [13], LaMnO3 [14], NiO [15], MnO2 [16], MoS2 [17] and reduced graphene oxide (rGO) [18, 19]. Activated carbon is preferred for supercapacitor electrodes due to its exceptionally high specific surface area, well￾developed porous structure, good electrical conductiv￾ity, chemical stability and low cost [2]. Conventional precursors for activated carbon production, including fossil fuels, coal and petroleum coke, are becoming increasingly limited in availability and are associated with high extraction and processing costs. Therefore, there is a strong demand for alternative sources that are abundant, low cost, renewable and environmen￾tally friendly. In this context, biomass emerges as a highly promising and sustainable feedstock for pro￾ducing activated carbon. Biomass or biowaste is com￾monly derived from plant, animal and marine origins. A diverse range of biomass feedstocks has been inves￾tigated as precursors for the synthesis of activated car￾bon materials, such as bamboo [20], sugarcane [21], rice husk [22], Mangosteen peel [23], coir pith [24], allium cepa peel [25], wood sawdust [26], tea seed shell [27], corncob [28], tobacco waste [29] and orange peel [30]. Subramanian et al. have synthesized acti￾vated carbon using banana fibre, which shows specific capacitance of 74 ­Fg−1 at a current density of 0.02 ­Ag−1 [31]. Sandeep et al. fabricated an electrode of activated carbon from peanut shells, which showed a specific capacitance of 101.6 ­Fg−1 at 1 ­Ag−1 [32]. M. Morad et al. have prepared activated carbon from pomegranate peels, which display a specific capacitance of 126 ­Fg−1 at 0.5 ­Ag−1 [33]. Biomass is abundantly available and renewable, providing an environmentally friendly and low-cost source of carbon. Upon carbonization and activation, biomass naturally forms a hierarchi￾cal porous structure that enhances ion diffusion and maximizes active surface area, both critical for efficient charge storage. These structural and chemical features enable biomass-derived carbons to achieve high spe￾cific capacitance, excellent rate capability and out￾standing cycling stability [2]. Furthermore, utilizing biomass as a precursor provides an effective strategy for waste valorisation, supporting green synthesis approaches and contributing to a circular economy. The Aegle marmelos’s fruit is highly rich in nutri￾tion and medicinal values [34] and normally results in the generation of Aegle marmelos’s fruit shell (AFMS) biowaste (biomass) as large fraction. AMFS was selected as a precursor for activated carbon due to its wide availability, renewable nature and low-cost origin as an agricultural biowaste generated after fruit consumption. Its utilization offers a sustainable waste-to-value approach that reduces environmental burden while avoiding reliance on fossil-based car￾bon sources. Moreover, the absence of prior reports on AMFS-derived activated carbon for supercapaci￾tor applications highlights its scientific novelty and supports its exploration as a promising and sustain￾able electrode material for energy storage devices. To the best of the author’s knowledge, no study has yet explored the electrochemical properties of activated carbon obtained from AMFS for supercapacitor appli￾cation. In the present work, we have successfully syn￾thesized activated carbon from biomass (AMFS) for supercapacitor application. 2 Experimental section 2.1 Materials required Aegle marmelos’s fruit shells were collected locally. Polyvinylidene fluoride (PVDF) (99%), acetylene car￾bon black and potassium hydroxide (KOH) (99.5%) pellets were purchased from Thermo Fisher Scien￾tific. Sulphuric acid (H2SO4, 37% assay), hydrochloric acid (HCl, 37% assay) and N-methyl-2-pyrrolidinone

J Mater Sci: Mater Electron (2026) 37:2204 Page 3 of 18 2204 (NMP) (99.5%) were purchased from Sisco Research Laboratory (SRL). All chemicals were used as received from commercial suppliers without any additional purification or modification. 2.2 Synthesis and characterization of biomass‑derived activated carbon Waste biomass (AMFS) was sonicated with deionized water (DI) for 15 min to remove dust particles. It was dried overnight at 80 ˚C in an oven to eliminate the water content. AMFS was sonicated with ethanol for 15 min to remove the organic/inorganic contaminants and other remaining impurities. It was dried over￾night at 80 ˚C in the oven. AMFS was then ground using a pestle and mortar and converted into a fine powder. Figure S1a shows the schematic diagram of the steps followed for the fabrication of the electrode. The carbonization process was carried out in a closed alumina tube under a flow of Argon gas, schematically as shown in Figure S1b. The complete experimental setup of the activation process is shown in Figure S1b. An alumina tube was used as a reaction chamber in the experiment, which provides a contamination-free environment for the carbonization and activation pro￾cess. The length, inner diameter and outer diameter of the tube were 120 cm, 4 cm and 4.5 cm, respectively. The outlet of the alumina tube was bubbled through a beaker of water. A water bubbler is used at the out￾let to prevent atmospheric air, especially oxygen and moisture, from backflowing into the chamber, which could cause unwanted oxidation or contamination. It also helps trap unreacted or hazardous gases by dis￾solving them in water and providing a simple visual indication of continuous gas flow, ensuring safe and stable operation. Waste biomass (AMFS) powder was collected in an alumina crucible and placed inside the alumina tube of the reaction chamber for carboniza￾tion. The biomass (AMFS) was carbonized at 500 ˚C for 1h (h). The entire carbonization process was carried out under an inert atmosphere of 80 sccm Argon gas flow. The temperature was programmed at a ramp-up rate of 5 ˚C per minute. After the carbonization, the reaction chamber was allowed to cool down to room temperature. The carbonized carbon was mixed with KOH in a 1:1 mass ratio and ground using a pestle and mortar. It was then transferred into an alumina crucible and put inside an alumina tube for activa￾tion. For activation, the temperature was programmed at a ramp-up rate of 5 ˚C per minute. It was set for activation at 700 ˚C for 1h in 100 sccm argon (Ar) gas flow. The purpose of activating carbon is to create a highly porous structure with a large specific surface area, which enhances ion adsorption and charge stor￾age by facilitating electrochemical double-layer forma￾tion and reducing ion diffusion resistance [35]. After the activation, the resulting sample was dispersed into one mole of HCl solution and washed several times via a centrifuge machine until the pH became 7. At last, the sample was dried overnight at 90 ˚C. The final product obtained is the activated carbon (AC). Powder X-ray diffraction (XRD) analysis of AMFS￾derived activated carbon was conducted using a Rigaku SmartLab 9 kW diffractometer (Japan). The measurements employed Cu Kα light (λ = 1.541 Å) as the X-ray source. Data were recorded over a 2θ range of 10˚-80˚, with a scan rate of 4˚ min−1 and a step incre￾ment of 0.04˚. Raman spectra were acquired using a Renishaw Raman spectrometer equipped with a 514 nm He-Ne laser as the excitation source, operated at an incident power of 10 mW. The spectral acquisi￾tion was performed in the range of 500-2500 ­cm−1. Fou￾rier Transform Infrared (FTIR) spectroscopy of AMFS￾derived activated carbon was performed to identify the surface functional groups. Spectra were recorded using a Shimadzu IR Prestige-21 spectrometer (Shi￾madzu Corporation, Japan) within the wavenumber range of 400-4000 ­cm−1. BET measurements were car￾ried out using Quantachrome NovaTouch LXI surface area and porosity analyzer (Quantachrome Instru￾ments, USA). AMFS-derived activated carbon was sub￾jected to a degassing process under vacuum at 150 ˚C for 2 h to eliminate physically adsorbed contaminants, such as moisture and volatile impurities. The surface morphology of the AMFS-derived activated carbon was analysed using field emission scanning electron microscopy (FESEM) with a Carl Zeiss Sigma 300 instrument (Germany), enabling high-resolution imag￾ing of surface texture, particle structure and porosity. Elemental analysis (compositional) of the activated carbon was carried out using an energy-dispersive X-ray (EDX) spectrometer (EMS-850) integrated with FESEM. The thermal stability of biomass-derived acti￾vated carbon was evaluated using a thermogravimet￾ric analyzer (TGA, Shimadzu). For this, AMFS-derived activated carbon (AC) was heated from room tempera￾ture to 1000 ˚C under an air atmosphere at a constant heating rate of 10 ˚C ­min−1. The sample’s weight was continuously monitored, and the percentage weight loss as a function of temperature was analysed to

2204 Page 4 of 18 J Mater Sci: Mater Electron (2026) 37:2204 assess thermal behaviour. X-ray photoelectron spec￾troscopy (XPS) measurements were carried out using a PHI-5000 Versa Probe III system (USA) equipped with a monochromated Al Kα X-ray source (photon energy = 1.4867 keV). The X-ray beam was focused to a spot size in the range of 10-300 µm. Electrochemical measurements of the fabricated electrode of activated carbon were performed in an electrochemical work station (Metrohm Autolab PGSTAT-128, Netherlands, USA). 2.3 Fabrication of supercapacitor and its measurement In the present work, stainless steel (SS) mesh (mesh size 350 micron) was used as a current collector of the working electrode. The current collector in a superca￾pacitor serves as a highly conductive platform, facili￾tating the movement of electrons between the exter￾nal circuit and the active electrode material during charging and discharging. For this, the SS mesh was cut into (2 × 1) cm rectangular pieces. The SS mesh was sonicated in ethanol for 30 min to remove the organic/ inorganic contaminants from it. It was dried in an oven at 80 ˚C for 6 h. A mixture of biomass (AMFS)-derived activated carbon was prepared in a small beaker by mixing activated carbon, PVDF and acetylene carbon black in an 80:10:10 mass ratio. A few drops of NMP were added to the mixture to make a homogeneous slurry. The beaker was kept on a magnetic stirrer for vig￾orous stirring for 8 h. The slurry was coated on the surface of the SS mesh and dried for 10 h at 80 ˚C in an oven. A three-electrode electrochemical setup was used to explore the electrochemical properties of the as-fabricated electrode. A schematic diagram of the standard three-electrode setup used in the experi￾ment is shown in Figure S2a. In the three-electrode setup, activated carbon coated on SS mesh was uti￾lized as the working electrode. The primary role of the working electrodes is to enable efficient storage and release of electrical energy. A silver/silver chloride (Ag/AgCl) electrode was systematically used as the reference electrode during electrochemical testing. It controls the potential of the working electrode during electrochemical measurement. A reference electrode provides a fixed and known potential, allowing for the accurate measurement of the working electrode’s voltage. It does not conduct current but plays a cru￾cial role in precisely monitoring and controlling the electrochemical reactions at the working electrode. A platinum plate was used as a counter electrode, which is used as an anode for the adsorption and desorption of ions during the charge/discharge cycle. In a three￾electrode supercapacitor configuration, the counter electrode (CE) completes the electrical circuit by ena￾bling charge flow between itself and the working elec￾trode (WE). 1 M sulphuric acid (H2SO4) solution was used as an electrolyte during electrochemical measure￾ment via a three-electrode setup. Cyclic voltammetry (CV) of biomass-derived activated carbon electrode was recorded in the scan rates ranging from 10 to 100 mVs−1. Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) was performed within the frequency range of 0.01 Hz to 10,000 Hz. Galvanostatic charge-discharge (GCD) plot of the activated carbon’s electrode was recorded at the current density (Ag−1) of 0.25, 0.50, 1, 2, 3 and 4 Ag−1, respectively. For a two-electrode setup, a symmetric supercapaci￾tor cell was fabricated as shown in Figure S2b. Two activated carbon-coated SS-mesh electrodes were con￾nected in such a way that the activated carbon depos￾ited on both the electrode faces one another. A piece of cellulose paper was immersed in 1 M sulphuric acid (H2SO4) solution (electrolyte) to soak the electrolyte. The cellulose paper was also inserted between the two electrodes to avoid an electrical short circuit. The cel￾lulose paper acts as a separator, physically separating the two electrodes and providing a pathway for the transport of ions from the electrolyte. Cyclic voltam￾metry (CV) of the fabricated symmetric supercapaci￾tor cell was recorded in scan rates ranging from 10 to 100 mVs−1. Electrochemical impedance spectros￾copy (EIS) was performed over a frequency range of 10–2 Hz to 104 Hz. Galvanostatic charge-discharge plot of a symmetric supercapacitor cell was recorded at the current density (Ag−1) of 0.25, 0.50, 1, 2, 3 and 4 Ag−1, respectively. 3 Results and discussion FESEM image of biomass (AMFS)-derived activated carbon at a magnification of 2.50 kX, 5 kX and 50 kX is shown in Fig. 1a–c, respectively. FESEM of biomass￾derived activated carbon has been performed to create highly detailed, magnified images of the material’s sur￾face at high resolution, revealing its topography and morphology. FESEM image reveals the presence of multiple porous structures in biomass-derived activated

J Mater Sci: Mater Electron (2026) 37:2204 Page 5 of 18 2204 carbon. These pores play a crucial role in enhancing the material’s charge storage capacity. This porous structure increases the surface area of AMFS-derived activated carbon, which further increases the surface-active sites of activated carbon. It causes an increase in the elec￾trode’s interaction with the electrolyte at the electrode/ electrolyte interface, which increases the charge storage capacity of the supercapacitor. EDX spectra of biomass (AMRF)-derived activated carbon are shown in Fig. 1d, which is used for elemental composition analysis of biomass-derived activated carbon. The oxygen peaks arise due to the presence of oxygen-containing func￾tional groups such as hydroxyl, carbonyl and carboxyl. A strong carbon peak indicates a high carbon content, which is essential for ensuring good electrical conduc￾tivity and providing a large surface area for charge stor￾age through the electrochemical double-layer capacitor (EDLC). The EDX spectra confirm a predominant car￾bon content, indicating successful carbonization and activation of the biomass precursor. The quantitative elemental distribution obtained from the EDX analysis is provided in Fig. 1d (inset). Powder XRD plot of biomass (AMFS)-derived acti￾vated carbon is shown in Fig. 2a within the 2θ range 10˚-80˚. XRD plot reveals two broad peaks, one of higher intensity and the other of lower intensity. The peaks at diffraction angles (2θ) 24.86˚ and 42.69˚ correspond to reflection through the (002) and (100) planes, respec￾tively. The peak corresponding to the (002) plane rep￾resents a characteristic feature of amorphous or disor￾dered carbon. The peak corresponding to the (100) plane is for graphitic carbon structure. Our XRD data are in accordance with the literature [36]. The average crys￾tallite size of the AMFS-derived activated carbon was estimated using the Scherrer equation [37]. However, achieving a balance between pore size control and main￾taining high surface area, while introducing interconnected mesopores and micropores, presents a significant challenge. Template methods, although capable of precisely controlling pore structure, are costly, involve complex procedures, and present challenges in the selection and adaptation of different template materials. Conventional non-template methods, which use chemical activators such as KOH, H3PO4, and ZnCl2, can achieve a reasonable SSA, however, these methods face sig￾nificant challenges in precisely controlling the pore structure and are limited in their ability to generate interconnected hierarchical pore networks [29,30]. Therefore, developing a cost-effective, simple, effi￾cient, and easily reproducible carbon material that optimizes ultrahigh SSA and interconnected hierarchical pore structures is of great significance. This study employed a non-template method with a simple two-step process that is easy to scale up. Efficient N doping was achieved using supercritical CO2 (SCCO2) as the pretreatment technology and urea as the N source. The resulting material is a hierarchical nanoporous carbon with an ultrahigh SSA derived from walnut shells. This method offers several advantages, including a simple process, low cost, and the availability of abundant raw materials. Furthermore, the material's multifunctional practical value in electrochemical energy storage and direct air carbon capture (DACC) was demonstrated through its appli￾cation in the fabrication of supercapacitor electrodes and CO2 adsor￾bents. The results show that the carbon material with a hierarchical pore structure and ultrahigh SSA not only exhibits excellent electrochemical performance but also demonstrates potential in environmental appli￾cations, offering new possibilities for the development of low-cost, sustainable materials. 2. Feedstocks and methods 2.1. Feedstocks Walnuts shells (WS) were sourced from Henan Province. After thorough washing, they were ground into powder and sieved to obtain WS powder with a particle size of 100-200 mesh. The powder was then dried at 105 ◦C for 48 h. The proximate and ultimate analyses of the raw biomass are provided in the Supporting Information (Table S1). 2.2. Preparation of N-doped carbon materials and derived products WS powder and urea (1:1, mass ratio) were ground, placed in an iron-nickel alloy reactor (1 cm inner diameter, 15 cm length), heated to 200 ◦C at a rate of 10 ◦C/min, and then maintained at 200 ◦C for 0-100 min. The products were washed, filtered, dried, and treated with ul￾trapure water at 70 ◦C to remove residual urea, yielding nitrogen-doped char precursors (NCt, where t is reaction time). A blank sample without urea (Cblankt) was also prepared. NCt was mixed with KOH (1:3, mass ratio), stirred in ultrapure water, dried, and activated in tubular furnace with Ar atmosphere at 700 ◦C for 90 min to obtain nitrogen-doped carbon (NCHUt), with a blank control (ACblankt). For supercapacitor electrodes, NCHU was combined with acetylene black and polytetra￾fluoroethylene (PTFE) (8:1:1, mass ratio) in ethanol, coated onto nickel foam (1 × 1 cm2 ), dried, and pressed at 10 MPa. For amine-loaded ad￾sorbents, tetraethylenepentamine (TEPA) was dissolved in methanol, mixed with NCHU (stirred for 8 h), solvent removed, and vacuum dried to obtain amine-loaded carbon (NCHU-x%, where x is the TEPA mass fraction). Detailed fabrication procedures and a schematic illustration of the preparation process are presented in the Supporting Information (Fig. S1). 2.3. Finally, the sample was cooled to 25 ◦C at a rate of 5 ◦C/min. 3. Results and discussion 3.1. Porosity analysis Fig. 1 shows SEM images of NCHU20 and ACblank20 at different magnifications. At low magnification (5000 × ), both activated carbons consisted of small and irregular particles. Compared with ACblank20, NCHU20 exhibited a rougher surface and a finer particle size, indicating that N doping influenced the carbonization and activation behavior. At higher magnification (30000 × ), distinct differences in pore charac￾teristics were observed. NCHU20 exhibited smaller pore sizes and a higher pore density than ACblank20. In addition, the surface of NCHU20 appeared more uneven and textured, suggesting a more developed nanoscale porous structure. These observations indicate that N doping significantly affected the surface morphology and pore formation of the activated carbon. The corresponding EDS spectra are provided in the Supporting Information (Fig. S2). The pore structure of the samples was characterized using an SSA and porosity analyzer, and the data related to BET surface area, pore volume, and pore size are listed in Table 1. The corresponding N2 adsorption–desorption isotherms are shown in Fig. S4. A comparison of the data for NCHUs and the control group demonstrates that the carbon material doped with N using SCCO2 pretreatment exhibits a markedly high SSA, with NCHU20 reaching an impressive 3784.233 m2 /g. We have reviewed recent reports on the preparation of carbon materials with ultrahigh SSA (Table S2), and our NCHU exhibits one of the highest SSA reported among carbon materials. Under the experimental condi￾tions, even the lowest SSA, NCHU0, reached 1738.070 m2 /g, which is higher than that of all the activated carbons in blank. Furthermore, as the duration of the pretreatment increased, the SSA initially increased and then decreased. This trend is in close accordance with the N content observed in the elemental analysis (Table S3), which directly indicates that the formation of a high SSA is related to N doping during the pre￾treatment process. Additionally, it can be proposed that an excessively lengthy pretreatment may result in the collapse of the pore structure, which is detrimental to the formation of a well-developed pore network. The total pore volume and mesopore volume also increased initially with the pretreatment time and then decreased, with the maximum values observed in NCHU20, reaching 2.211 and 0.994 cm3 /g, respec￾tively. The average pore diameter and mesopore diameter initially decreased with the pretreatment time and then increased, with the minimum values observed in NCHU60 and NCHU40, reaching 2.020 nm and 2.634 nm, respectively.
