This suggests that the NCHUs have superior mass transfer channels, which are advantageous for charge storage and ion diffusion, making them a strong candidate for use in supercapacitors and CO2 adsorbents. The possible reasons for the impact of urea doping pre￾treatment on the pore structure and the increase in SSA can be attributed to the following factors: 1. During the pretreatment stage, urea decomposed to release NH3, which itself had an activating effect, increasing the micropores and surface roughness of the carbon material [34,35]. 2. The high temperature during the activation process caused the preloaded N structures to burn and gasify, creating voids and cav￾ities. The elemental analysis of the carbon precursors (Table S4) con￾firms this observation, indicating that the N content in NCs is significantly higher than that in NCHUs, suggesting that a substantial amount of unstable N structures was destroyed. Furthermore, the NCHU20, which has the highest SSA, also exhibits the highest N content. 3. Including amide and amino groups, the N-containing functional groups enhanced the hydrophilicity or altered the electronic structure of the carbon material, which helped improve its adsorption performance and provided additional reactive sites for KOH activation, the synergy between the N structures and KOH enhanced the activation efficiency [36]. Fig. 2a and S5 display the nanopore size distribution for NCHUs and ACblank. Pores below 2 nm are classified as micropores, while those between 2 and 50 nm are classified as mesopores, as indicated in the figures. As the same analysis from the isotherms, the produced carbon samples have well-developed porosity. The NCHUs have a significantly wider pore size range and a higher pore volume compared to the blank. This indicates that urea modification and N doping played a crucial role in the development of porosity [37]. The pore size distribution of the control group is concentrated solely in the micropore range of less than 2 nm, whereas NCHUs also exhibit significant distribution in the mes￾opore range. Notably, NCHU20 displays distribution not only in narrow mesopores but also in mesopores ranging from 10 to 40 nm. Addition￾ally, the NCHU0 sample shows a distribution of large pores around 90 nm, NCHU20 has mesopores at approximately 20 nm, and NCHU40 predominantly features mesopores around 3 nm. This observation may suggest that with increasing pretreatment time using SCCO2 for N doping, there is a tendency for the activated carbon's pore distribution to shift towards smaller pore sizes. 3.2. Analysis of N doping effects The elemental analysis results of WS, NCHUs and ACblank are pre￾sented in Table S3, and the relative values of H/C, O/C, and N/C have been calculated. In comparison to the feedstock, the C content of the carbonized activated carbon increased, while the amounts of H and O decreased. This reduction can be attributed to the formation of liquid￾phase organic compounds and H- and O-containing gases during the biomass pyrolysis process, as well as the destruction of functional groups. The N content in the NCHUs was markedly higher than that observed in both the feedstock and the control group, thereby indicating the successful doping of N into the activated carbon. As the duration of the pretreatment period increased, the N content in the activated carbon initially increased and then decreased, reaching a maximum of 6.2 wt% at 40 min. This suggests that urea required an adequate time to achieve pyrolysis and loaded N onto the carbon, but extended reaction times could damage the already doped N structure, which may impact the doping efficiency. It is noteworthy that the relative contents of O/C and H/C in the NCHUs were lower than those in the control group. This suggests that the doping of N consumed H and O. Shen and Fan [38] proposed that this was due to the incorporation of N atoms primarily occurring through the substitution of hydroxyl groups and reactions with carboxyl groups to form amides, lactams, and isocyanates. There￾fore, the preparation of NCHU is directly related to the O-containing functional groups present in the material. In our previous research [69], we observed that activated carbon prepared from biomass pretreated in SCCO2 exhibited a more diverse range of O-containing functional groups. This leads us to believe that SCCO2 treatment also had a positive effect on N doping. In order to gain a deeper understanding of the composition and classification of elemental groups in NCHUs, the samples were charac￾terized using XPS. The resulting spectra are presented in Fig. 2b–d, and peak fitting for C, N, and O was performed using deconvolution methods. The spectrum of C1s shows three typical types of carbon bonds: C-C, C-O, and C=O [39]. And O1s is divided into two distinct C=O and C-O bonds [40]. The N1s spectrum is deconvoluted into four peaks, corresponding to oxidized N, graphitic N, pyrrolic N, and pyr￾idinic N. The N1s spectra of the other samples are provided in Fig. S6. Additionally, the positional schematic of structural N on the carbon layers is illustrated in Fig. 2e. Pyridinic and pyrrolic N atoms donate their lone pairs to the carbon conjugated system, inducing an electron-donating effect, while graphitic N facilitates electron transfer within the structure [41]. The functional group structure of NCHUs was characterized using FTIR spectroscopy. The resulting spectra of the samples, together with the corresponding functional group vibration structures at the respective peak positions, are presented in Fig. 2f. The broad band in the range of 1000-1400 cm− 1 includes the functional groups C-O, O-H, C-O-C, C-H, and C-N [42]. In particular, the peak observed at 1031 cm− 1 is attributed to the C-O-C vibration of ethers, while the peak at 1210 cm− 1 is asso￾ciated with the C-O vibration of phenols. As shown in the figure, the proportion of the C-O-C vibration response in the broad spectrum of activated carbon decreased with the extension of pretreatment time, while the proportion of the C-O response increased. This suggests that a substantial number of ether bonds were broken during the reaction, leading to the formation of phenols [43]. The broad peak appearing in the range of 1456-1600 cm− 1 is attributed to the stretching vibration of C=C bonds [44]. The small vibration peak at 1710 cm− 1 is attributed to the contribution of C=O bonds [45]. The absorption band at 2372 cm− 1 corresponds to the out-of-plane stretching vibration of aromatic C=C in AC. Additionally, the band at 3450 cm− 1 represents the stretching vi￾brations associated with N-H and O-H groups [46], as the pretreatment time increased, the corresponding intensity of these bands gradually rose, indicating that extending the pretreatment time can enhance the production of O- and N-containing functional groups. Based on the re￾sults from elemental analysis, XPS, and FT-IR, it was concluded that using urea as an N source and employing SCCO2 pretreatment success￾fully incorporated N into activated carbon in the forms of structural N within carbon layers and chemical N in functional groups. Therefore, by doping N into carbon, the structural characteristics of N itself can not only enhance the pore structure and increase the SSA of carbon, but also provide active sites, as well as improve conductivity and adsorption properties. 3.3. Carbon structure analysis We conducted XRD scans on N-doped carbon NCs and NCHUs over the range of 5-90◦. The resulting curves are shown in Fig. 3a and b. The XRD results for NCs show three principal peaks at 101 (~16◦), 040 (~34◦), and 002 (~24◦). The 101 and 040 peaks are indicative of cel￾lulose in the carbon that has not undergone complete pyrolysis. This finding is corroborated by the thermogravimetric analysis of the feed￾stock (Fig. S3), which suggests that cellulose commences significant pyrolysis at approximately 300 ◦C. Therefore, the char produced under all 200 ◦C pretreatment conditions exhibits discernible cellulose XRD peaks. The broad 002 peak is characteristic of amorphous carbon, which indicates that the biomass underwent pyrolysis and carbonization. Furthermore, the NC0 sample displays distinctive diffraction peaks of urea, indicating that urea did not significantly decompose during the 0- min reaction and remained mainly in the sample, with some urea not fully removed during the washing process. However, as the duration of Z. Zhuang et al. Biomass and Bioenergy 211 (2026) 109160 4

attributed to aliphatic side chains attached to the edges of aromatic rings and other structures. The fitted data were calculated using Equations (1)–(4), resulting in Fig. 3c and Table S5. The figure demonstrates that the crystallite structural parameters of the NCHU samples exhibit distinct variations with different pretreatment reaction times. The diameter (La) of the aromatic layers exhibited an increase at interme￾diate pretreatment times, followed by a decrease at longer reaction durations. While, the average stacking thickness (Lc) of the aromatic layers exhibited an opposite trend. At shorter pretreatment times, biomass decomposition and gasification occurred. Larger aromatic layers were formed. The reduction in stacking thickness might be attributed to the depolymerization of the aromatic structure, which occurred predominantly in the longitudinal direction [47]. With pro￾longed pretreatment, carbon chains and heterocycles were pyrolyzed. Additional aromatic units were generated. These aromatic structures underwent significant lateral polymerization, resulting in the formation of polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons. The aromaticity (fa) continuously decreased with increasing pretreatment time. This decrease was attrib￾uted to sustained reactions between carbon, CO2, and urea, including oxidation, addition, and polymerization, which led to the degradation of aromatic structures [48]. The interlayer spacing between adjacent car￾bon layers (d002) initially increased and then decreased with the extension of pretreatment time. This was due to the extensive N doping, which broadens the carbon layer spacing. This trend was consistent with the variation in N content from elemental analysis. However, at longer pretreatment times, the N-doped structures were disrupted. Stronger π–π stacking occurred. The degree of structural ordering increased. As a result, the interlayer spacing decreased. Meanwhile, the d002 values for the control group were consistently lower than those of the NCHUs, thereby providing further confirmation that the N structures increased the carbon layer spacing. To further investigate the carbon structural characteristics of the NCHUs, Raman spectroscopy was utilized to characterize the samples. In consideration of the heterogeneous nature of the samples, data were collected from three distinct locations on each sample. Fig. 3d shows that all samples exhibited a graphite-like double-peak structure, with the D band at 1350 cm− 1 and the G band at 1580 cm− 1 [49]. Due to the overlap of the D and G peaks, analyzing the carbon microcrystalline structure using only the D and G peaks can lead to incomplete and insufficient structural information. To obtain a more comprehensive understanding of the carbon microcrystalline structure, it is necessary to deconvolute the peaks. As shown in Fig. 3e, the Raman peaks were fitted with Gaussian functions into four components: D1 (~1340 cm− 1 ), D3 (~1480 cm− 1 ), D4 (~1200 cm− 1 ), and G (~1580 cm− 1 ) [50]. D1 is typically associated with disordered structures, sp2 -hybridized carbon atoms, aromatic rings, edge carbon atoms, and in-plane vibrations with structural defects [51]. D3 is associated with amorphous sp2 carbon structures and aromatic structures with 3-5 aromatic rings [52]. D4 is associated with sp3 -hybridized carbon atoms and sp3 -sp2 mixed bonds. The G peak is related to the hexagonal planes composed of sp2 carbon atoms and involves C=C stretching vibrations within the aromatic rings, representing an ordered graphite structure [53]. The peak area ratios can reflect the characteristics of the material. The calculated results for ID1/IG and ID4/IG are provided in Fig. 3f. The ID1/IG ratio is generally used to determine the level of defects present in the carbon microcrys￾talline structure and the extent of graphite-like aromatic structure for￾mation, and it is inversely related to structural ordering [54]. In the first 20 min of the reaction, the biomass macromolecules underwent depo￾lymerization and condensation, resulting in structures with aromatic rings above the six-membered ring [51] and the number of sp2 carbon atoms increased, which led to an incremental ID1/IG. As the reaction time increased, the ID1/IG ratio decreased, indicating that disordered sp2 carbon atoms were converting to ordered sp2 carbon atoms, and the proportion of graphite-like structures increased. The ID4/IG ratio exhibited a similar trend to that of the ID1/IG ratio, initially demon￾strating an increase and subsequently a decline with the pretreatment time. This suggests that the cross-linked structures in the activated carbon initially increased and were subsequently disrupted. It means that after 20 min, the cross-linked bonds between the aromatic struc￾tures were broken, leading to substantial merging and graphitization of the aromatic structures [53]. 3.4. Electrochemical performance testing of the supercapacitor anode materials The cyclic voltammetry (CV) curves of the NCHU samples and blank nickel sheet measured at a scan rate of 10 mV/s within the range of − 1.1 to 0V (Vs. Ag/AgCl) are shown in Fig. 4a. It can be observed that the nickel sheet didn't contribute to capacitance, as it appears as a straight line. The CV curves of all samples exhibit a quasi-rectangular shape, indicating that the samples possess excellent electric double-layer ca￾pacitors (EDLC) characteristics, resulting from charge accumulation at the electrode/electrolyte interface [55]. In the CV curves, redox peaks related to the surface O and N functional groups can also be observed, which are directly associated with the N5 or N6 structures present in the NCHU samples [56]. Using Equation (5), the CV capacitances at different scan rates were calculated based on the area enclosed of the CV curves and specific values are in Table S6. It was determined that NCHU40 exhibited the highest CV capacitance, which is related to its highest N content from elemental analysis. The N structures contributed to an additional pseudo capacitance. From Fig. 4b, it can be seen that the CV curves of NCHU40 at scan rates ranging from 5 to 150 mV showed significant distortion as the scan rate increased, however, the curves generally retain a quasi-rectangular shape. This is attributed to the material's intricate pore structure, which facilitates the expeditious transmission of ions in the electrolyte at elevated scan rates. This sub￾stantiates the assertion that the NCHU produced is an exemplary ma￾terial for EDLC. Compared with physical activation (such as CO2 or water vapor treatment) [17,18] and hydrothermal carbonization [19], chem￾ical activation (such as KOH, K2CO3, etc.) has obvious advantages, and can prepare porous carbon materials with high yield, high specific sur￾face area and rich pore structure in a short time [20,21]. This optimized pore structure not only facilitates rapid electrolyte permeation and ion transport, but also provides more active sites, which significantly im￾proves the specific capacitance, rate performance, and cycling stability of the electrode material [22,23]. For example, Raja [13] et al. reported that the homogeneous fibrous structure of feather finger grass flower facilitates the formation of hollow tubular carbon after KOH activation. The resulting porous carbon offers a high specific surface area and porosity, supplying ample adsorption sites for electrolyte ions and leading to a specific capacitance of 315 F g− 1 at 1 A g− 1 . Qin [15] et al. used gardenia as raw material to produce porous carbon by pre-carbonization, hydrothermal treatment and chemical activation. Its abundance of oxygen and nitrogen heteroatoms not only improves the surface polarity and hydrophilicity, but also significantly increases the specific capacitance (0.5 A g− 1 , 255 F g− 1 ). The material has a large specific surface area (1637 m2 g-1) and a hierarchical microporous-mesoporous structure, which promotes the rapid diffusion of electrolyte ions, resulting in improved rate performance (68.6%) and cycling stability (98.3%, 20000 cycles). Celosia cristata L. (CCL), as a common ornamental plant, is a potential biomass carbon precursor due to its abundant wood fiber composition. CCL-derived carbon has a unique hollow rod-like structure that gives it excellent electrical conductivity and mechanical stability. In addition, CCL-derived carbon contains abundant oxygen and nitrogen atoms. These heteroatoms regulate the surface charge distribution of the carbon material, thereby enhancing its electrochemical performance. However, research on the application of CCL-derived carbon in energy storage remains very limited [24]. Herein, N, O self-doped biomass-derived carbon materials were prepared by one-step carbonization activation method using CCL with hollow rod-like structure and abundant heteroatoms (C: 41.341%, N: 3.153%, O: 30.365%) as raw material, and K2CO3 as the activator. CCL￾derived carbon materials with multi-level pore structure were prepared by precise temperature control strategies. The as-obtained carbon ma￾terial has the high microporosity (88.72%), and retains the hollow rod￾like structure, which is conducive to electrolyte transport and charge storage. In the three-electrode system, the carbon material exhibits excellent electrochemical performance. Its excellent performance is attributed to the rich micropore network, high heteroatom content, and unique hollow rod-like structure, which optimize the charge transport path and create favorable conditions for the rapid transport of electrons and ions. The symmetrical supercapacitors based on CCL-K2CO3-1-700 have an high energy density of 19.5 Wh kg− 1 , which is far superior to most similar carbon-based materials. After 10,000 charge-discharge cycles, the initial capacity retention rate is still as high as 85%. This excellent electrochemical performance is mainly due to the unique hi￾erarchical porous structure and compositional advantages with the ni￾trogen and oxygen co-doping of the electrode material, which makes it of great application value in the field of energy storage and conversion. 2. Experimental section 2.1. Materials K2CO3 was purchased from Aladdin Chemical Reagent Co., Ltd. KOH and PTFE were purchased from Shanghai Macklin Biochemical Tech￾nology Co., Ltd. Conductive carbon black was purchased from Cyber Electrochemical Materials Network. Absolute ethanol was purchased from Tianjin Fuyu Fine Chemical Co., Ltd. HCl was purchased from Sichuan Xilong Science Co., Ltd. Deionized water (DW) was used for preparing all solutions and washing. CCL was collected from the Bozhou medicinal materials market in Anhui Province. 2.2. Synthesis of Celosia cristata L. Derived carbon material Using CCL as the carbon precursor, it was thoroughly ground with K2CO3 in a mortar at a mass ratio of 1:1 to ensure a uniform mixture. Subsequently, the mixed sample was placed in a tube furnace under N2 atmosphere for carbonization and activation. First, the temperature was increased to 400 ◦C at a rate of 10 ◦C min− 1 and held for 1 h; then continued to heat to the target temperatures (700 ◦C, 750 ◦C, and 800 ◦C) at the same rate and maintained for 2 h to ensure sufficient activation. At the end of the reaction, the product was acid-washed with a dilute HCl solution to remove residual impurities, followed by repeated washing with deionized water until the filtrate was neutral (pH = 7). Finally, the samples were dried to constant weight at 105 ◦C, sealed and stored, yielding the CCL-derived carbon material, referred to as CCL-K2CO3-a-b, where a is the activation mass ratio and b is the activation temperature. 2.3. Characterizations EA (Elementar Unicube) was used to evaluate the heteroatom doping and chemical composition of the samples. The thermogravimetric (TG) and differential thermogravimetric (DTG) (STA 449C) explored the relationship between temperature and sample quality throughout the process. The microscopic morphology and structure information of the samples were observed by Scanning electron microscopy (SEM, SU8010) and transmission electron microscopy (TEM, Talos F200x). The chemi￾cal bond type and characteristic functional groups of the sample were analyzed using FT-IR (TENSOR27) testing. The X-ray diffraction (XRD) (D8 ADVAHCE), which records the crystalline properties of the sample. X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) (PHI 5000 Versaprobe III) is used to analyze elemental composition and critical energy information. BET (Micromeritics 3 Flex) obtained the specific surface area parameters and pore structure characteristic distribution of the material. A static water contact angle meter (DSA 25) is used to test the hydrophilicity of a sample. The content of Ca and K elements in CCL was analyzed by ICP￾OES (Agilent ICP-OES 5110). 2.4. Electrode preparation and electrochemical characterizations Electrochemical measurements were performed in an electro￾chemical workstation (CHI760E) using a standard three-electrode sys￾tem with an electrolyte of 6 M KOH, a platinum sheet as the counter electrode, and Ag/AgCl as the reference electrode. The prepared elec￾trode active material was thoroughly mixed with conductive carbon black and PTFE binder at a mass ratio of 8:1:1, dispersed in absolute ethanol, and then made into a film of uniform thickness. After the film is dried at 90 ◦C, it is evenly pressed on the surface of the current collector to obtain working electrodes, and the mass of the sample on each working electrode is maintained between 2.5 and 3.0 mg. Prior to measurement, cyclic voltammetry (CV) activation tests were performed at a scan rate of 100 mV s − 1 between − 0.2 V and 0.8 V. Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) tests an AC disturbance signal with an applied amplitude of 5 mV, measured in the frequency range of 0.01- 100 MHz. Galvanostatic charge-discharge (GCD) measurements were performed in the potential range of − 0.2 V to 0.8 V at current densities ranging from 0.5 to 20 A g− 1 , respectively. Results and discussions 3.1. Morphology, composition and structure of CCL-K2CO3-a-b Fig. 1 shows the preparation technology roadmap of CCL-K2CO3-a-b. According to the results of TG and DTG analysis of the CCL (Fig. S1), the pyrolysis process of the CCL is divided into three stages: (1) the initial stage (20 to 200 ◦C): the TG curve shows a slight decrease in mass, mainly due to the evaporation of the adsorbed water in the sample. (2) Intermediate phase (about 200 ◦C to 400 ◦C): In this temperature range, the TG curve shows a significant mass loss and the DTG curve shows a significant peak. This is usually related to the thermal decomposition of organic matter, mainly caused by the rapid decomposition of cellulose and hemicellulose and the pyrolysis of partial lignin [25], and the mass loss at this stage is also related to the decomposition of polysaccharides, proteins, and other organic components contained in CCL. (3) Late stage (400 ◦C to 1000 ◦C): The TG curve plateaued, indicating that most of the decomposable organic matter had been decomposed, and the remaining mass was mainly carbon materials and inorganic ash [26]. At this stage, the rate of mass change (DTG curve) is close to zero, indicating that no significant decomposition reaction has occurred. At 700 ◦C, the TG curve showed that the residual mass of the sample was about 30%, and the test results showed that the yield of CCL was high after carbonization. The SEM was used to observe and analyze the morphology of the carbon material and CCL, and the CCL in Fig. 2a showed a hollow rod￾like structure, which was derived from the vascular system of its vascular plants (Fig. S2a-c, Fig. 2b–d) clearly shows the microstructure changes of the carbon material at different carbonization temperatures, and it can be clearly seen that the CCL-K2CO3-1-700 (Fig. 2b), CCL￾K2CO3-1-750 (Fig. 2c) and CCL-K2CO3-1-800 (Fig. 2d) samples exhibit porous structures. This is attributed to the fact that the hollow structure of CCL can provide more contact area and reaction sites for the activator during the carbonization process, and its internal hollow structure and abundant pores can significantly improve the utilization rate of the activator. This structure not only facilitates the penetration and diffu￾sion of the activator, but also allows for the formation of more micro￾pores and mesopores [27]. After carbonization and activation at 700 ◦C, the CCL-K2CO3-1-700 sample showed significantly optimized microstructure characteristics, which not only had a well-developed porous network and a clearly visible graphitized carbon layer, but also completely retained the hier￾archical structure of vascular bundles. These structural advantages manifest in three key aspects. Firstly, the significantly expanded specific surface area greatly increases active sites. Secondly, the retained unique hollow rod-like structure constructs fast ion transport channels. Finally, the three-dimensional interconnected carbon skeleton provides excel￾lent mechanical strength and ensures structural stability during long￾term cycling. As the temperature increased, the CCL-K2CO3-1-750 sample showed a more pronounced pore structure and a more homo￾geneous carbon layer, and the size and distribution of the pores were more uniform, indicating that the carbonization process was more adequate. However, at this temperature, despite the further develop￾ment of the pore structure of the carbon material, the unique hollow rod￾like structure is partially destroyed, which may be detrimental to its performance. When the conditioning temperature is further increased to 800 ◦C, the pore structure of the CCL-K2CO3-1-800 sample is further developed, forming more pores, but the hollow rod-like structure is completely destroyed, which may have a greater impact on the prop￾erties of the material. The TEM was used to further characterize microscopic morphology and structure of CCL-K2CO3-1-700. As shown in Fig. 2e–f, a significant macroporous structure can be observed in CCL-K2CO3-1-700. It is likely that these macropores are derived from the original vascular structure of the CCL, which was retained and expanded during the carbonization process, and those macroporous structure is beneficial to act as a buffer/ storage layer to reduce the diffusion distance of ions. Fig. 2g–h further reveal the presence of mesoporous and microporous structures. The formation of mesopores may be related to the decomposition of organic matter and the release of small molecular gases during carbonization. The presence of mesopores provides a fast transport channel for elec￾trolyte ions and provides additional active sites [28]. The formation of micropores is mainly attributed to the small molecular gases produced by the decomposition of K2CO3. The presence of micropores can significantly increase the specific surface area of the material and Fig. 1. Preparation technology roadmap of carbon materials derived from Celosia cristata L. X.-y. Zhao et al. Biomass and Bioenergy 211 (2026) 109168 3

24◦ and 44◦ correspond to the (002) and (100) lattice planes, respec￾tively [29]. However, as shown in Fig. 3a, the XRD patterns of CCL-derived carbons exhibit no distinct diffraction peaks, indicating a low degree of crystallinity and a highly amorphous structure. The further decrease in peak intensity with rising temperature corroborates the enhancement of structural disorder. This amorphous nature facili￾tates the development of a hierarchical pore network and promotes the retention of heteroatoms (N, O), both of which contribute to the improved electrochemical performance of the material. In Raman spectra (Fig. 3b), the D-band (about 1350 cm− 1 ) correlates with defects or disordered structures in the material, while the G-band (about 1580 cm− 1 ) correlates with the degree of graphitization [30]. For CCL-derived carbon materials, the ID/IG ratio increases with the increase of activation temperature, indicating that the degree of disorder of the material is increasing. Specifically, the ID/IG ratios of the samples in￾crease with the activation temperature: 0.99 for CCL-K2CO3-1-700, 1.05 for CCL-K2CO3-1-750, and 1.19 for CCL-K2CO3-1-800. This trend sug￾gests that higher temperatures lead to a lower degree of graphitization and an increase in structural disorder. The specific surface area and pore structure of CCL-derived carbon materials were characterized by BET testing, and the corresponding isotherm and pore size distributions are shown in Fig. 3c–d, respectively. According to the International Union of Pure and Applied Chemistry (IUPAC) classification, the adsorption-desorption isotherms of the CCL￾derived carbons show combined features of Type I and Type IV. This mixed profile indicates the presence of a multi-level (hierarchical) pore structure in the materials [31]. In particular, in the low-pressure region where the relative pressure (P/P0) is less than 0.1, the adsorption ca￾pacity shows a significant sudden increase, which intuitively reflects the existence of abundant microporous structures in the material. In the range of relative pressures 0.4<P/P0 < 0.8, the presence of hysteresis loops reveals the presence of mesopores. However, a slight increase in adsorption capacity at high relative pressures confirms the presence of macropores. The pore size distribution in Fig. 3d shows that the pore distribution trend of the samples is similar, with peaks mainly concentrated between 0.5 and 2.8 nm, indicating that the pores of CCL-derived carbon mate￾rials are mainly microporous and mesoporous, with a small number of macropores. Therefore, it can be concluded that the prepared carbon material has a hierarchical porous structure. Table S3 lists the detailed parameters of the specific surface area and pore structure of CCL-derived carbon materials at different tempera￾tures. With the increase of activation temperature, the specific surface areas of CCL-K2CO3-1-700, CCL-K2CO3-1-750 and CCL-K2CO3-1-800 were 908 m2 g-1, 1367 m2 g-1 and 1600 m2 g-1, respectively, and the specific surface area also increased. Among them, CCL-K2CO3-1-700 had the highest microporosity, reaching 88.7%. With the increase of tem￾perature, the microporosity of carbon materials decreases, and the pore volume and average pore size increase, and carbon materials with high microporosity generally have higher specific capacitance [32]. The surface element composition and chemical valence properties of carbon-based materials were systematically studied by XPS combined with elemental analysis. The full spectrum of CCL-K2CO3-1-700 in Fig. 4a clearly shows the peaks of C1s, O1s, and N1s at 286.4 eV, 532.6 eV, and 400.5 eV, respectively, indicating the presence of C, N, and O in CCL-K2CO3-1-700 [33,34]. As can be seen from Table S4, the oxygen content of CCL-K2CO3-1-700 is very high, reaching 12.33%, while the oxygen content of CCL-K2CO3-1-750 and CCL-K2CO3-1-800 decreases to 8.81% and 6.71%, respectively, with the increase of activation tem￾perature. CCL-K2CO3-1-700 (1.62%) showed higher nitrogen content than those of CCL-K2CO3-1-750 (0.63%) and CCL-K2CO3-1-800 (0.38%). CCL-derived carbon has a higher oxygen content than other biomass, which is due to the fact that CCL itself is rich in oxygen, which is retained during the carbonization process. Both nitrogen and oxygen decreased with the increase of activation temperature, mainly because with the increase of temperature, N and O in the biomass will escape in the form of gas [35]. So CCL-K2CO3-1-700 activated at a lower temperature re￾tains most of the heteroatoms in CCL, which may show better Fig. 4. The XPS spectra of CCL- K2CO3 -a-b: survey spectrum (a), high-resolution O 1s spectrum (b), C 1s spectrum (c), and N 1s spectrum (d). X.-y. Zhao et al. Biomass and Bioenergy 211 (2026) 109168 5

electrochemical performance. The high-resolution O1s spectrum can be fitted to four peaks (Fig. 4b): C=O quinone-type functional group (O-I, binding energy 531.2 eV), C-OH phenolic or C-O-C ether-type functional group (O-II, binding energy 532.6 eV), chemisorption oxygen (COOH), or water molecule (O-III, binding energy 535.5 eV) [36]. The presence of O-I and O-II functional groups not only significantly enhances the surface wettability of the material, but also promotes the rapid transport of ions, thereby improving the utilization of microporous channels. In the acidic electrolyte environment, quinone oxygen (O-I) is the only electro￾chemically active oxygen functional group that can participate in charge storage through reversible redox reactions [37]. In CCL-K2CO3-1-700, the proportion of quinone oxygen (O-I) is as high as 30.06%, which makes it exhibit better electrochemical activity in the acidic electrolyte. The high-resolution C1s spectrum shown in Fig. 4c can be divided into four parts: C-C/C=C (283.3 eV), C-N/C-S (284.6 eV), C-O-C (287.6 eV), and O-C=O (290.5 eV). Since the contribution of nitrogen to pseudocapacitance in different states is different, it needs to be studied in depth. In Fig. 4d, the high-resolution N 1s spectra presents pyridine nitrogen (N-6), pyrrole nitrogen (N-5), graphite nitrogen (N-Q), and pyridine oxide N (N-X) at binding energies of 398.3, 399.5, 400.5, and 401.3 eV. Among them, N-6 and N-5 can participate in Faraday redox reactions to produce additional pseudocapacitance, while N-Q can improve the conductivity of carbon materials as an electron donor or electron acceptor [38]. In the sample, the sum of N-5 and N-6 accounted for 65.40%, and the proportion of N-Q accounted for 26.76%. During the high-temperature activation process, the difference in the thermal stability of heteroatoms directly led to the change of its composition. The elemental analysis data (Table S5) also confirmed that the content of heteroelements in CCL-K2CO3-a-b material was negatively correlated with temperature. Among them, the contents of N and O el￾ements in CCL-K2CO3-1-700 were 1.39% and 19.23%, respectively. Therefore, it can be determined that nitrogen and oxygen are success￾fully and effectively combined into carbon materials, and the synergistic effect between these two heteroatoms can help improve the electrochemical performance of CCL-K2CO3-1-700. In order to further explore the effect of high oxygen content on the wettability of CCL-K2CO3-a-b, the water contact angle of the sample was tested. As shown in Fig. 5, the CCL-K2CO3-1-700 sample showed excel￾lent hydrophilicity, the water contact angle was only 17.6◦, and the excellent hydrophilicity will be conducive to its surface penetration and increase the effective contact with the electrolyte [39]. The water con￾tact angle of CCL-K2CO3-1-750 and CCL-K2CO3-1-800 are 43.3◦ and 53.6◦, respectively. The water contact angles gradually increase, this indicates that the hydrophilicity of the material gradually decreases with the increase of activation temperature, and this trend is consistent with the decrease of oxygen content of the material with the increase of temperature. Indicating that the high oxygen content can greatly improve the wettability of carbon materials, which is conducive to the improvement of the electrochemical properties of materials [40]. 3.2. Electrochemical performance analysis of CCL-K2CO3-a-b In order to explore the differences in the electrochemical properties of carbon materials prepared at different activation temperatures, the electrochemical properties of CCL-K2CO3-a-b carbon materials were studied in a three-electrode system. According to the CV test results (Fig. 6a), all three samples exhibit approximately rectangular charac￾teristic curves during scanning, with significant Faraday redox peaks in specific potential intervals. This phenomenon confirms that the energy storage mechanism of the prepared carbon materials is not a single interfacial electric double-layer effect, but is accompanied by a revers￾ible Faraday redox reaction, showing the synergistic characteristics of electric double-layer capacitance and pseudo-capacitance. The com￾posite energy storage mechanism is attributed to the introduction of nitrogen, oxygen and sulfur in carbon materials, which is conducive to improving the electrochemical properties of materials [40,41]. In particular, it is worth noting that the CCL-K2CO3-1-700 sample exhibits an extremely pronounced redox peak, which is closely related to its extremely high heteroatom content, indicating that it can undergo a Fig. 5. segments.text: Multi-heteroatom-doped Porous Carbon with High Surface Adsorption Energy of Potassium Derived from Biomass Waste for High-performance Supercapacitors Shengshang Lu, Qingquan Xiao, Wensheng Yang, Xinhai Wang, Tong Guo, Quan Xie, Yunjun Ruan* Institute of Advanced Optoelectronic Materials and Technology, College of Big Data and Information Engineering, Guizhou University, Guiyang 550025, China. *Corresponding author. E-mail: yjruan@gzu.edu.cn (Yunjun Ruan) Abstract Sustainable and renewable biomass-derived porous carbon (BPC) have garnered considerable attention owing to their low cost, high specific surface area, and outstanding electrochemical performance. However, the subpar energy density severely restricts the applications of BPC in high-energy-density devices. Herein, a high￾surface-area porous carbon with multiple heteroatoms doping was derived from rapeseed meals by hydrothermal carbonization and high-temperature activation. The rapeseed meal-derived activated carbon (RMAC) exhibits a remarkable surface area of 3291 m2 g -1 and is doped with nitrogen (1.05 at.%), oxygen (7.4 at.%), phosphorus (0.31 at.%), and sulfur, resulting in an impressive specific capacitance of 416 F g -1 at 1 A g -1 . Furthermore, even after 10,000 cycles, the optimized RMAC-800 electrode maintains 92% of its initial capacitance, attesting to its exceptional performance. Through comprehensive density functional theory (DFT) calculations, the elements O, N, P, and S can significantly enhance the electron negativity and density, improving the adsorption and diffusion of K+ to attain a high capacitance. To assess the RMAC-800's practical performance, an asymmetric supercapacitor with 1 M [BMIM]BF4/AN Journal Pre-proof Journal Pre-proof

2 electrolyte was produced that delivered a high energy density of 195.94 Wh kg-1 at a power density of 1125 W kg-1 . Thus, we propose an eco-friendly strategy for producing BPC materials with outstanding electrochemical performance for supercapacitors. Keywords: Rapeseed meal, hydrothermal carbonization, porous carbons, density functional theory, supercapacitor 1 Introduction In today's rapidly developing society, there is an emerging necessity for environmentally conscious and high-performing energy storage systems (ESSs) to combat the dwindling supply of fossil fuels and the degradation of the environment[1- 3]. Supercapacitors (SCs) are highly regarded for their notable environmental sustainability, exceptional power density, rapid charging capabilities, and extensive lifespan[4, 5]. Depending on the electrode materials' charge storage mechanism, SCs are categorized into two main types: electric double-layer capacitors (EDLCs) and pseudocapacitors[6, 7]. The capacitance mechanism in EDLCs is achieved by creating a dual layer consisting of positively and negatively charged ions, which are separated on the surface of the electrode material[8]. In pseudocapacitors, the charge storage mechanism happens via Faradaic redox reactions near the electrode interface[9]. Searching for porous carbon electrodes with a higher specific surface area and multi￾heteroatom doping has been validated as a successful approach to enhancing the electrochemical performance of supercapacitors[10, 11]. Biomass, especially agricultural waste, derived activated carbon has gained much interest due to its wide distribution, abundant resources, sustainability, environmental friendliness, unique porosity, and multi-heteroatom doping[12-14]. Many agricultural and forestry wastes have been converted into activated carbon, such as crop straws, leaves, fruit shells, fruit cores, and rice shells[13, 15]. Biomass stems and leaves with abundant nutrient transport channels possess a significant potential for producing activated carbon due to their highly porous structure and elemental doping[16-19]. To Journal Pre-proof Journal Pre-proof

3 enhance the specific surface area of carbon materials, it is common practice to activate biomass carbon at high temperatures. Alkaline activators, such as KOH and NaOH, have been reported to inhibit tar formation and produce a large number of micropores and a high specific surface area[20-22]. Phosphoric acid activators have been found to catalyze the depolymerization of carbon materials that contain lignocellulosic fiber, resulting in the formation of monosaccharide molecules that subsequently re-form into polymerized phosphate structures[20]. The composition of cellulose, lignin, proteins, oils, and fats in various biomass materials varies significantly, leading to different demands for activators and activation temperatures during the preparation of biomass￾derived carbon materials. Hence, further optimization is still required to achieve an efficient and effective preparation process for such materials. When biomass is converted into activated carbon, it usually becomes self-doped with heteroatoms due to the abundance of components present in it. Furthermore, the type and amount of heteroatom doping can vary depending on the biomass used. Li et al. utilized NaOH activation platanus acerifolia (aiton) willd at different temperatures of 700, 800 and 900 ℃ to prepare O/N-self-doped porous carbon[23]. Wei et al. employed ammonia dopant and K2CO3 activator to transform coal tar pitch into S/N￾self-doped porous carbon[24]. Moerover, utilizing different activators makes it possible to obtain biomass-derived carbon with a high ratio of heteroatom doping. Fang et al. modified betel nut wastes with nitric acid/thiourea to obtain O/N/S-doped carbon, which exhibits a high capacitance (423 F g-1 at 0.5 A g-1 )[25]. Zhao et al. utilized ZnCl2 and Mg(NO3)2·6H2O activators to prepare peanut meal derived N/P/S self-doped hierarchical porous carbon, achieving an ultrahigh specific capacitance of 525 F g-1 (1 A g-1 )[26]. Nevertheless, the controlled synthesis of heteroatom self-doping in carbon derived from biomass and its impact on its physicochemical and electrochemical characteristics remain to be comprehensively understood. A thorough examination of the impact of multi-heteroatom doping on the properties of biomass carbon materials remains a crucial challenge[27, 28]. Journal Pre-proof Journal Pre-proof

4 Rapeseed meal (RM) is a prevalent agricultural byproduct containing a significant quantity of crude, fat, and protein, which is rich in heteroatoms such as oxygen, sulfur, nitrogen, and phosphorus. The utilization of RM precursor was implemented to fabricate N, S, O, and P codoped activated carbon via hydrothermal carbonization and subsequent annealing activation. The optimized rapeseed meal-derived activated carbon (RMAC-800) exhibits an ordered honeycomb-like framework with abundant microporosity, achieving an ultrahigh surface area (3291 m2 g -1 ). Meanwhile, the multi￾heteroatom doping of RMAC-800 produces a highly polarized surface, ensuring good wettability to encourage the effective adsorption of electrolyte ions on the porous surface. Thus, the RMAC-800 electrode gains a high specific capacitance and remarkable cycling stability. Density functional theory (DFT) calculations were utilized to investigate the impact of N, P, O, and S doping on the electronic structure of carbon, elucidating the origin of the exceptional conductivity and capacitance of multi￾heteroatom-doped carbon materials. Moreover, the asymmetric supercapacitors assembled by RMAC-800 anode and NiCoAl-LDH cathode with 1 M [BMIM]BF4/AN and 6 M KOH electrolytes exhibit superior electrochemical performance. 2 Material and Methods 2.1 Materials The rapeseed meal was sourced from local farmer's markets near Guizhou University in Guiyang. Before use, the RM was cleaned with deionized water and subjected to a 24-hour freeze-drying process. All reagents were bought from Sinopharm Chemical Reagent Co., Ltd. without further purification. 2.2 Preparation of RMAC The dried RM pieces underwent hydrothermal carbonization at a temperature of 140 ℃ for 8 hours within a stainless steel container that contained 60 mL of DI water. Journal Pre-proof Journal Pre-proof

5 The resultant carbon product is soaked in a concentrated KOH solution and put into a vacuum-drying oven for 2 hours at 80 ℃. The soaked carbon is activated in a nitrogen atmosphere at varying temperatures (600, 700, and 800 ℃) for 2 hours. The pH value of the product was neutralized to 7 by an HCl solution, followed by repeated rinsing with deionized water. The products obtained are known as RMAC-600, RMAC-700, and RMAC-800. 2.3 Characterization methods Product morphology was examined through scanning electron microscopy (SEM, Hitachi, SU8010) and transmission electron microscopy (TEM, JEOL, JEM-2100f). Structural information was evaluated via X-ray diffraction (XRD, PANalytical, Empyrean), Raman spectroscopy (Horiba, LabRAM HR Evolution), and X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS, Thermo Fisher, K-Alpha Plus). Analysis of pore size distribution and specific surface area was performed using the density function theory (DFT) and Brunauer Emmett Teller (BET) methods, respectively, with the ASAP-2020 surface analyzer (Micromeritics). The thermal decomposition process of the biomass was conducted by the thermogravimetric analysis (TGA). The electrical conductivity of the samples was measured by the RTS-9 four-point probe tester. 2.4 Electrochemical measurement The mixture of RMAC powder, conductive carbon black, and PTFE emulsion (in a mass ratio of 8:1:1) was coated onto a nickel foam (1.0 cm) to prepare the working electrode, which was then dried. The mass of electroactive material on the electrode was controlled to be 2 - 3 mg. The electrodes’ electrochemical performance was evaluated using a workstation (CHI760E), including cyclic voltammetry (CV), galvanostatic charge-discharge (GCD), and electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) measurements. segments.text: porosity and tailored surface chemistry remains a key challenge for improving electrochemical energy storage performance [5,6]. In paral￾lel, hydrogen has attracted considerable attention as a clean energy carrier with high gravimetric energy density and zero carbon emissions during utilization. Among various hydrogen generation strategies, the catalytic methanolysis of sodium borohydride (NaBH₄) is considered an attractive approach because it operates under mild conditions and provides controllable hydrogen release. Nevertheless, the intrinsic sta￾bility of NaBH₄ in alcohols requires highly active catalysts to achieve practical hydrogen generation rates. Most reported catalysts rely on noble or transition metals, which increase costs and may suffer from stability issues. Consequently, the development of efficient, low-cost, and metal-free catalysts remains an important research direction [7]. One of the viable methods for on-demand hydrogen generation is the catalytic methanolysis of NaBH₄, which offers advantages such as high hydrogen content, mild operating conditions, and controllable reaction rates [8–11]. However, the intrinsic stability of NaBH₄ in alcohols re￾quires effective catalysts to accelerate hydrogen release while main￾taining durability and reusability [12–15]. Biomass-derived porous carbons represent a sustainable platform capable of addressing both challenges simultaneously. Their high surface area, tunable pore struc￾tures, and modifiable surface chemistry make them suitable for elec￾trochemical energy storage as well as catalytic applications. In particular, heteroatom doping (e.g., phosphorus, nitrogen, or sulfur) can introduce defect sites and surface functionalities that enhance both charge storage behavior and catalytic activity [16–18]. Carbon-based materials, especially activated carbon derived from biomass waste, have been extensively investigated as electrode materials due to their abundant availability, tunable porosity, high surface area, and chemical stability [19,20]. Chemical activation-assisted pyrolysis, particularly with potassium hydroxide (KOH), is one of the most effective routes for generating highly porous carbon frameworks. During pyrolysis, KOH participates in complex redox and gasification reactions with the biomass carbon matrix, producing potassium metal and potassium compounds (e.g., K₂CO₃) that intercalate into carbon layers, etch the matrix, and promote pore evolution. These reactions also release gaseous species such as CO and CO₂ that act as internal pore-forming agents, significantly enhancing the development of micro- and meso￾pores. Such mechanistic insights have been supported by studies investigating the kinetics and structural evolution during pyrolysis of chemically impregnated biomass [21,22]. Such effects of KOH activa￾tion on porosity and surface area have been extensively reviewed in the literature, showing enhanced capacitance performance with increased surface area and pore connectivity [23–25]. Beyond purely physical activation, the incorporation of heteroatoms—especially P—into the carbon framework has been demonstrated to significantly alter the surface chemistry and electrochemical behavior of porous carbons. P doping introduces polar functional groups (e.g., P–O and P = O) that increase surface wettability and promote stronger electrolyte–electrode interactions, which facilitate faster ion diffusion and more uniform charge distribution [26,27]. Moreover, heteroatom doping can create defect sites and active centers that contribute additional pseudocapa￾citance, thereby complementing the EDLC mechanism and yielding higher overall capacitance [28,29]. Specifically, P-doped porous car￾bons have shown enhanced mesopore formation and improved cycling stability in supercapacitor applications, with significant retention of capacitance over prolonged cycling and increased working voltage windows. This highlights the synergistic effect of combining physical activation with chemical doping to simultaneously optimize pore ar￾chitecture and surface chemistry in carbon electrodes [28]. P doping is especially effective in enhancing pseudo capacitance in porous carbon materials, significantly boosting the capacitance of supercapacitors. Due to their larger atomic size and lower electronegativity compared to carbon atoms, P atoms induce charge delocalization when incorporated into the carbon structure. This process leads to structural defects, which improve electrochemical activity and contribute to higher capacitance. In addition to pore structure regulation, phosphorus treatment in￾troduces phosphorus-containing surface functionalities (such as P–O and P = O groups), which enhance surface polarity, wettability, and elec￾tronic properties of the carbon framework. These chemical features contribute to additional pseudocapacitive charge storage and improved electrode–electrolyte interaction, leading to enhanced capacitive per￾formance even when the BET surface area is reduced. Such behavior has been widely reported for phosphorus-doped carbons, where surface chemistry plays a more critical role than surface area alone in deter￾mining electrochemical performance [26,27,30]. Chestnut shell waste is a suitable and sustainable precursor for electrode materials due to its high carbon content, natural porous structure, and abundant oxygen-containing functional groups formed during pyrolysis [31]. After chemical activation and phosphorus modification, the resulting biochar exhibits stable electrochemical behavior, high capacitance, and good cycling stability, demonstrating its suitability for supercapacitor electrode applications. Moreover, the presence of heteroatom-derived active sites and a stable carbon matrix suggests that this material may also be promising for catalytic applications; however, the present study primarily focuses on its role as an electrode material for supercapacitor. Integrating these two applications, the development of multifunc￾tional carbon materials capable of catalyzing hydrogen generation and serving as supercapacitor electrodes presents a sustainable and cost￾effective strategy. Biomass-derived carbons not only valorize agricul￾tural waste but also reduce environmental burdens, aligning with cir￾cular economic principles [32,33]. Among biomass sources, chestnut shells represent an abundant and underutilized agro-waste, rich in car￾bon content suitable for activation and doping processes. In this context, chemical activation of chestnut shells using potas￾sium hydroxide (KOH) can generate porous activated carbon with desirable textural properties. Subsequent phosphorus doping via phos￾phoric acid treatment introduces surface functionalities that modulate electronic and catalytic properties. The resulting phosphorus-doped mesoporous carbon is hypothesized to exhibit enhanced active sites for both the methanolysis of NaBH₄ and charge storage mechanisms in supercapacitors. Despite several studies focusing individually on biomass-derived carbons for hydrogen generation or supercapacitors, research exploring their dual applicability remains limited. Despite established studies on KOH-activated biomass carbons, systematic un￾derstanding of phosphorus incorporation following pyrolytic activation and its effect on structure-property relationships remains insufficiently explored. In this work, chestnut shells are converted into hierarchical porous carbon through KOH-assisted pyrolysis at 700 ◦C, followed by phosphoric acid functionalization. The resultant phosphorus-doped carbon is systematically evaluated as (i) an electrode for super￾capacitor energy storage and (ii) a metal-free catalyst for hydrogen generation via NaBH₄ methanolysis, demonstrating the dual utility of pyrolysis-derived biomass carbons. Despite numerous studies on biomass-derived carbons for either supercapacitors or hydrogen production separately, investigations exploring their dual functionality remain limited. In this context, the present work introduces a sustainable strategy for converting chestnut shell waste into phosphorus-doped porous carbon through KOH-assisted pyrolysis followed by post-functionalization. The novelty of this work lies in demonstrating the multifunctional capability of the same biomass-derived carbon material as both a high-performance super￾capacitor electrode and a metal-free catalyst for hydrogen generation via NaBH₄ methanolysis. This dual functionality highlights the potential of heteroatom-doped biomass carbons as versatile materials for inte￾grated energy storage and conversion systems. 2. Experimental 2.1. Materials Methanol (CH₃OH, ≥99.9%, Sigma-Aldrich) and sodium C. Saka et al. Journal of Analytical and Applied Pyrolysis 196 (2026) 107754 2

borohydride (NaBH₄, ≥98%, Merck) were used as hydrogen source components in the catalytic tests. Potassium hydroxide (KOH, ≥85%, Merck), sulfuric acid (H₂SO₄, 98%, Merck), hydrochloric acid (HCl, 37%, Merck), and phosphoric acid (H₃PO₄, 85%, Merck) were used during the activation and functionalization steps. All chemicals were of analytical grade and were used as received without further purification. 2.2. Preparation of phosphorus-doped carbon material Initially, the chestnut shells, acquired from a local market, were dried at room temperature. Subsequently, they were ground and sifted to achieve the desired particle size. The ground chestnut shell powder was mixed with potassium hydroxide and distilled water under contin￾uous stirring at 50 ◦C for 24 h to allow effective impregnation of KOH into the biomass structure. After this impregnation step, the slurry-like mixture was directly transferred into porcelain crucibles and subjected to pyrolysis in a tubular furnace under a nitrogen atmosphere at 700 ◦C for 2 h. During the initial heating stage of the pyrolysis process, the remaining water gradually evaporated before the activation reactions occurred. After pyrolysis and chemical activation, the obtained samples were thoroughly washed with a dilute hydrochloric acid solution to remove residual inorganic impurities, followed by repeated rinsing with distilled water until neutral pH was achieved. The washed samples were then dried in an oven at 80 ◦C for 2 h and labeled as CSKOH. Phosphorus doping was subsequently carried out via thermal treatment under continuous stirring using phosphoric acid. In a typical procedure, a known amount of CSKOH was dispersed in 30 mL of 85 wt% H₃PO₄, which was previously diluted with an equal volume (30 mL) of distilled water. The resulting suspension was placed in a sealed glass beaker and magnetically stirred at 100 ◦C for 2 h under atmospheric pressure. After the treatment, the sample was repeatedly washed with distilled water to remove excess acid and unreacted species, followed by drying at 80 ◦C for an additional 2 h. The resulting phosphorus-doped composite was denoted as P-doped CSKOH. A schematic illustration of the fabrication procedure is provided in Fig. 1. Literature reports indicate that temperatures around 700 ◦C are optimal for KOH activation of biomass-derived carbons. Below this range, the formation of metallic potassium species and the gasification reactions that produce CO and CO₂ are significantly limited, resulting in lower pore development and reduced surface areas. As the temperature rises to ~700 ◦C, the mobility of potassium increases, facilitating intercalation into the carbon lattice and enhancing pore formation. Moreover, decomposition of K₂CO₃ and evolution of gaseous products are more pronounced at this temperature, contributing to the generation of hierarchical micro- and mesopores. When the activation temperature increases further (e.g., above ~800 ◦C), surface area may increase more but often at the cost of carbon yield reduction and excessive burn-off, which can negatively affect material yield and structural integrity. These trends are consistent with prior studies demonstrating that the most effective activation temperature for KOH is in the range of 700–800 ◦C, where a balance between pore formation and carbon con￾servation is achieved [34,35]. 2.3. Electrochemical measurements Using a Metrohm Autolab instrument from the Netherlands, elec￾trochemical experiments were performed with a three-electrode setup. The working electrodes consisted of CSKOH and P-doped CSKOH-based carbon materials. An Ag/AgCl electrode served as the reference elec￾trode, while a platinum electrode was used as the auxiliary electrode. To prepare the working electrode, 18 mg of either CSKOH or P-doped CSKOH was combined with 2 mL of N,N-dimethylacetamide and 2 mg of polyvinylidene fluoride. This mixture was then sonicated for 4 h. Sub￾sequently, a 5 μL aliquot of the mixture was applied to a glassy carbon electrode, and an infrared lamp was used to dry the electrode, after which an extra drying step was performed. This process resulted in electrodes that were ready for supercapacitor applications. Electro￾chemical tests, including cyclic CV, EIS, and GCD) methods, were per￾formed using a 1 M H₂SO₄ electrolyte. GCD measurements were conducted at current densities ranging from 0.5 to 5 A/g, with a po￾tential window of − 1–0 V. CV tests were carried out at various scan rates between 2.5 and 50 mV/s. EIS measurements were performed over a frequency range of 100 kHz to 0.1 Hz. Eq. 1 was used to calculate the specific capacitance (Cs) values. Fig. 1. The fabrication steps of P-doped CSKOH material. Characterization of materials The functional groups present in the carbonaceous materials were identified using Fourier Transform Infrared (FTIR) spectroscopy within the wavenumber range of 500–4000 cm− 1 (Nicolet 6700). The synthe￾sized carbon materials' surface morphology was examined using EVO 18 model SEM (Carl Zeiss, Japan). EDS was employed to determine the elemental composition and ratios of the materials. The carbon materials' surface area and porosity were evaluated through nitrogen adsorption analysis conducted with a Micromeritics Tristar II apparatus. An assessment of structural defects in the synthesized carbonaceous mate￾rials was conducted using WiTec alpha 300 model Raman spectroscopy (Germany). Additionally, XPS, Thermo Fisher Co., Escalab 250Xi, USA) was employed to analyze the elemental composition and binding en￾ergies of the materials. 2.5. Hydrogen production experiments The catalytic hydrogen generation via methanolysis of NaBH₄ was performed to evaluate the activity of the synthesized P-doped CSKOH. All chemicals used were of analytical grade and employed without further purification. In a typical experiment, 10 mg of the P-doped CSKOH catalyst was dispersed into 10 mL of methanol in a sealed re￾action vessel equipped with a magnetic stirrer. The mixture was ther￾mostated at 30 ◦C using a water bath to maintain constant temperature throughout the reaction. Subsequently, 0.125 g of NaBH₄ was rapidly added to the reaction mixture to initiate the methanolysis reaction. The volume of hydrogen gas evolved was measured volumetrically using an inverted burette connected to the reaction vessel via a gas-tight tubing system. The reaction was monitored continuously until the hydrogen generation ceased, indicating complete NaBH₄ consumption. Hydrogen generation rates (HGR) were calculated by normalizing the volumetric hydrogen output to catalyst mass and reaction time (mL min⁻¹ g⁻¹). 3. Results and discussion 3.1. Characterization results Fig. 2 presents SEM images illustrating the surface morphologies of CSKOH (panels a, b, c) and P-doped CSKOH (panels d, e, f). The struc￾tures obtained from the activation of chestnut shells with KOH, followed by phosphoric acid treatment (H₃PO₄), exhibit heterogeneous and porous characteristics. Notably, the CSKOH samples demonstrate a more pronounced porous structure. In P-doped CSKOH, porosity decreases as acid particles occupy the pores during the activation process. Such porous structures are crucial for facilitating efficient ion diffusion in electrochemical applications. Elemental composition and ratios for both CSKOH and P-doped CSKOH were analyzed using EDS, with the results shown in panels g and h of Fig. 2. The primary elements identified in both materials are C and O. For the P-doped CSKOH, the presence of P atoms is also confirmed. Specifically, the elemental proportions for CSKOH were found to be 55% C and 28% O, while the P-doped CSKOH showed an increase in carbon content to 75% and a slight decrease in oxygen content to 22%. The proportion of phosphorus in the P-doped CSKOH was measured at 1.97%. Additionally, some impurities were detected in both samples, further corroborating the successful doping of phosphorus. During KOH-assisted pyrolysis, the activation process involves mul￾tiple chemical transformations between KOH and the carbonaceous matrix. At higher temperatures, KOH dehydrates and reacts with carbon to form intermediate potassium salts (e.g., K₂CO₃, K₂O) and metallic potassium. These species then undergo reduction and gasification re￾actions, generating gaseous CO, CO₂, and H₂, which produce internal pressure and etching of the carbon framework. The evolution of these gases facilitates the formation of hierarchical pores, as evidenced in pyrolysis kinetic studies with phosphoric acid-impregnated biomass. The in situ formation of metallic potassium can intercalate into carbon layers, resulting in lattice expansion and structural reorganization, which further enhances porosity and defect generation. Accordingly, KOH-assisted pyrolysis should not be viewed solely as a gasification process, but rather as a combined chemical etching and structural reconfiguration mechanism that determines textural evolution during thermochemical conversion. The porosity characteristics of the CSKOH and P-doped CSKOH samples were evaluated using nitrogen (N₂) adsorption-desorption measurements. The corresponding isotherms for both samples are illustrated in Fig. 3a. The Brunauer-Emmett-Teller (BET) specific surface areas for the CSKOH and P-doped CSKOH samples were determined to be 524 m²/g and 331 m²/g, respectively. After phosphoric acid treat￾ment, the specific surface area of P-doped CSKOH decreased to 331 m²/ g, likely due to partial pore blockage or occupation by phosphorus￾containing functional groups formed during hydrothermal modifica￾tion. The decrease in BET surface area observed after phosphorus doping (from 524 to 331 m² g⁻¹) can mainly be attributed to partial pore blockage and surface coverage by phosphorus-containing functional groups formed during phosphoric acid treatment. Phosphorus species such as P–O, P = O, and C–O–P may occupy micropores or narrow pore entrances, thereby reducing the surface area accessible to nitrogen adsorption. Similar reductions in surface area upon phosphorus doping have been widely reported for biomass-derived porous carbons [26,27]. However, this decrease should not be considered detrimental. Phos￾phorus doping can promote pore widening and increase the mesopore fraction, which is more favorable for electrolyte ion diffusion. Moreover, the introduction of phosphorus-related surface functionalities enhances wettability and provides additional pseudocapacitive active sites, often resulting in improved electrochemical performance despite the lower surface area [36,37] The textural analysis of the prepared materials clearly reflects the decisive role of KOH-assisted pyrolysis in establishing a hierarchical porous network. The high specific surface area of CSKOH (524 m²/ g) is primarily attributed to intensive chemical activation and pore formation during pyrolysis, consistent with other biomass-derived activated car￾bons prepared via similar KOH-pyrolysis protocols. In addition to sur￾face area, the presence of active groups within the material's structure is critical for various applications. The alteration of the electronic struc￾ture and pore characteristics due to phosphorus doping with H₃PO₄ can facilitate ion transport within the electrolyte. The pore size distributions for both CSKOH and P-doped CSKOH are presented in Fig. 3b. The Barrett-Joyner-Halenda (BJH) pore sizes for these samples are 7.61 nm and 8.89 nm, respectively, indicating that both samples fall within the mesoporous category according to IUPAC classification. Comparing the two, it is evident that the mesoporosity of the P-doped CSKOH has increased. These mesopores are beneficial for enhancing electro￾chemical performance by enabling more efficient transport of ions to the sample [38,39]. Such improved pore structures shorten the diffusion lengths and promote the Faraday redox reaction [40]. Although the BET specific surface area decreases after phosphorus doping (from 524 to 331 m² g⁻¹), the relative mesoporosity of the P-doped CSKOH sample increases. This apparent contradiction can be explained by structural C. Saka et al. Journal of Analytical and Applied Pyrolysis 196 (2026) 107754 4

changes induced during the phosphorus treatment. The reduction in surface area is mainly attributed to partial blockage of micropores and narrow pore entrances by phosphorus-containing species, as well as possible thickening of pore walls, which limits nitrogen accessibility during BET measurements. In parallel, phosphorus doping can promote pore widening, merging of adjacent micropores, or partial collapse of ultramicropores into mesopores. Consequently, while the total surface area decreases due to the loss of accessible micropores, the proportion of mesopores increases. This evolution toward a mesopore-rich structure is beneficial for electrolyte ion diffusion and charge transport in electro￾chemical applications and explains the enhanced capacitive perfor￾mance despite the reduced BET surface area. From the structure–function perspective, the combination of pyrolysis-derived hierarchical porosity and phosphorus-related functional sites contrib￾utes synergistically to both electrochemical capacitance and catalytic activity. The CSKOH and P-doped CSKOH samples exhibited pore volumes of 0.37 cm³ /g and 0.26 cm³ /g, respectively. The introduction of phos￾phorus atoms into the CSKOH structure through the creation of meso￾porous pore structures is anticipated to enhance electrochemical performance. The expected outcome of this modification is an enhancement in the wettability and conductivity of the carbonaceous material, which will, in turn, facilitate improved ion transport and overall efficiency in supercapacitor and catalytical applications. The reaction mechanism involving the carbon precursor (chestnut shells) and potassium hydroxide (KOH) during the activation process can be summarized as follows (3)-(6) [41]. 6KOH + 2 C → 2 K + 3H2 + 2K2CO3 (3) K2CO3 + 2C → K2O + 2 CO (4) K2CO3 → K2O + CO2 (5) 2 K +CO2 → K2O + CO (6) Due to the activation of the carbon material with KOH, potassium carbonate (K₂CO₃) starts to form initially at the pyrolysis temperature. As the temperature increases during pyrolysis, K₂CO₃ is completely produced. Subsequently, K₂CO₃ decomposes into potassium oxide (K₂O) through the release of carbon monoxide (CO) and carbon dioxide (CO₂). This activation process facilitates the formation of a porous structure within the carbonaceous material, comprising both micro and meso￾pores, which are essential for enhancing its electrochemical perfor￾mance in supercapacitors [42,43]. Fig. 4a presents the FTIR analysis used to identify the surface func￾tional groups in the CSKOH and P-doped CSKOH samples. The FTIR spectra of the two samples display notable differences, particularly with significant changes in peak intensities and positions following activation with H₃PO₄. These changes indicate an increase in the functional groups present in the P-doped CSKOH sample, as evidenced by the distinct peaks observed in its FTIR spectrum. Fig. 3. Among various biomass sources, waste activated sludge (WAS), owing to its high content of organic matter (e.g., proteins, polysaccharides) and natural heteroatoms (N, S) (Deng et al., 2025), has become an ideal precursor for the preparation of functional carbon materials. Numerous studies have employed various treatment methods to pre-separate organic matter in WAS to mitigate the adverse effects of ash on elec￾trochemical performance (Djandja et al., 2022; Xu et al., 2022). How￾ever, traditional processes typically involve a multi-step carbonization-activation method, which is time-consuming and largely dependent on external activators (e.g. KOH or K2CO3) for pore regula￾tion (Xu et al., 2020; Du et al., 2022). Consequently, the development of a green method that integrates rapid extraction of WAS organic matter and in-situ activation is crucial. In recent years, the biomass reconstruction strategy based on green solvents has offered novel insights into the resource utilization of WAS. The low-temperature NaOH/urea aqueous solution system proposed by Zhang et al. enables efficient cellulose dissolution (Cai and Zhang, 2005). The mechanism is attributed to NaOH disrupting the hydrogen bond network and urea inhibiting the reaggregation of molecular chains (Egal et al., 2008; Li et al., 2019; Qin et al., 2013). Similarly, the proteins and polysaccharides in WAS are rich in hydroxyl and carboxyl groups (Yu, 2020) and could possess solvent–response characteristics similar to those of cellulose. Furthermore, previous studies have confirmed that NaOH treatment can achieve sludge disintegration to a certain extent (Li et al., 2008; Yang et al., 2023b). On the basis of these findings, NaO￾H/urea aqueous solutions hold promise for disrupting the WAS structure and promoting the dissolution of organic matter from WAS. More recently, Dang et al. successfully created a porous carbon material by directly dissolving cellulose in a solvent comprising α-lipoic acid and a NaOH/urea aqueous solution (Dang et al., 2020), which provides important inspiration for the green synthesis of carbon derived from WAS. In view of the compact colloidal structure of sludge (Yin et al., 2023b), the efficiency of NaOH/urea aqueous solution in WAS disinte￾gration can be significantly improved by initially disrupting its floc structure. Research has demonstrated that the shear force induced by ultrasonic cavitation can rapidly disintegrate sludge flocs and microbial cells (Tyagi et al., 2014; Zhang et al., 2024a,b). Moreover, alkali-coupled ultrasonic treatment can synergistically promote the dissolution and release of organic matter in WAS (Li et al., 2010). However, these studies have focused predominantly on sludge disinte￾gration for the promotion of anaerobic biodegradability (Tian et al., 2015) or protein purification (Gao et al., 2021; Yan et al., 2023), thereby neglecting the in-situ utilization potential of the solvent system for WAS organic matter. Hence, this study proposed an innovative strategy for the prepara￾tion of nitrogen-doped porous carbon materials (NPCs) through the integration of an in-situ activation and doping: NaOH/urea aqueous solution combined with ultrasonic treatment was used to produce an organic-enriched mixture (S-NaOH/urea), which was mixed with cellulose to obtain precursors. The objectives of this study were to: 1) optimize the preparation conditions of NPCs, 2) investigate the impact of NaOH and urea on the physical structure and chemical composition of NPCs, 3) evaluate the electrochemical properties of NPCs as super￾capacitor electrodes, and 4) explore the universality of strategies for replacing cellulose with wheat straw (WS) or corncob (CC). 2. Materials and methods 2.1. Materials NaOH (≥96.0 %), urea (≥99.0 %), and Cellulose (≥99.0 %) were obtained from Sichuan Xilong Scientific Co., Ltd., Damao Chemical Regent Factory, and Shanghai Macklin Biochemical Technology Co., Ltd. respectively. The waste activated sludge utilized in this study was dewatered cake with 80 % moisture content collected from the Beishi￾qiao Municipal Wastewater Treatment Plant (BMWTP) located in Shaanxi, China. Before the experiment, the hair, debris, large inorganic particles, and other substances in the sludge that may affect the exper￾imental results were removed. The wheat straw and corncob were crushed and sifted through 100 mesh, followed by drying at 105 ◦C for 24 h. 2.2. Extraction of sludge organic matter A NaOH/urea solvent was prepared at a mass ratio of 7:12:81 (NaOH:urea:H2O) and cooled at − 12 ◦C overnight. A certain amount of sludge cake was subsequently added to 50 g of precooled solvent, after which 50 mL of the mixture was introduced into an ultrasonic reactor for treatment at − 12 ◦C for 20 min. The collected liquid phase was desig￾nated S-NaOH/urea. In addition, the liquid phase obtained by ultrasonic treatment with pure water instead of NaOH/urea aqueous solution was denoted as S-US. 2.3. Preparation of NPCs The experimental procedure typically involved the following steps: a specific quantity of cellulose was uniformly suspended in an S-NaOH/ urea solution and continuously agitated at − 12 ◦C for 30 min to produce a precursor solution. Then, the precursor underwent freeze-drying before being subjected to carbonization in a tube furnace. The thermal treatment involved programmed heating to target temperatures (600–800 ◦C) under a N2 atmosphere, with a 1-h isothermal holding period at peak temperature. Post-carbonization processing included successive washing cycles with diluted HCl (0.2 M) and ultrapure water until neutral pH was achieved, followed by vacuum desiccation at 40 ◦C. The final products were designated as NPC-T-w, where T and w denote the annealing temperature and cellulose proportion, respectively. The process of synthesis is provided in Fig. 1. In particular, the carbonized products obtained using pure water instead of NaOH/urea aqueous so￾lutions and using wheat straw (WS) or corncob (CC) instead of cellulose Fig. 1.
