activation. Raising the calcination temperature to 700 ◦C, the surface of NPC-700-6 developed a distinct honeycomb-like porous network. However, the SEM image of NPC-800-6 revealed a greater number of large pores, suggesting that excessive activation led to partial structural damage. To further investigate the impact of the cellulose content and the NaOH/urea aqueous solution on the morphology of the material, SEM images of NPC-700-4, NPC-700-8, and PW-700-6 were analyzed (Fig. 2(d–f)). Compared with those of NPC-700-4 and NPC-700-6, the extent of cross-linking of the porous networks on the surface of NPC￾700-8 was relatively low, which might be due to the restricted degree of activation. Significantly, the surface of water-pretreated PW-700-6 exhibited folding morphology with absent porosity, further indicating that NaOH and urea in the precursor can activate carbon materials in situ during pyrolysis. This phenomenon aligned with established mechanisms where NaOH etching synergizes with volatile removal during carbonization to create three-dimensional porous networks (Lillo-Rodenas ´ et al., 2003, 2004). The TEM image (Fig. 2(g)) of NPC-700-6 further confirmed its highly porous texture and interconnected structural characteristics, facilitating rapid electrolyte ion transport. Enlarged TEM images (Fig. 2 (h and i)) revealed slot hole-like pores on carbon with partial graphiti￾zation at the edges (red rectangles), which indicated good electrical conductivity (Chen et al., 2017). The concentric circles in the electron diffraction pattern indicated the characteristics of amorphous carbon. As shown in Fig. 3(a), all samples except PW-700-6 exhibited hybrid type-I/IV isotherms (Dang et al., 2020). The sharp rise in these isotherms at lower relative pressures confirmed substantial micro-porosity of NPC-T-w. Moreover, narrow hysteresis loops appeared when P/P0 exceeded 0.45, along with significantly enhanced adsorption at higher relative pressures, indicating limited mesopores and a few macropores (Chen et al., 2021; Jiang et al., 2011). Furthermore, the pore size dis￾tributions of NPC-T-w further revealed the hierarchical porosity network comprising abundant micropores combined with meso- and macropores (Fig. 3(b)). As summarized in Table S2, the structure and pore properties exhibited significant dependence on synthesis parame￾ters. Raising the temperature from 600 ◦C to 700 ◦C led to the increase in both the SSA and total pore volume of NPC-700-6. However, the SSA of NPC-800-6 slightly decreased, which was possibly attributed to the removal of volatiles and activation of the carbon materials during heating (Dang et al., 2020). Furthermore, increasing the cellulose ratio resulted in a decreased SSA and pore volume, which could be related to a decrease in the relative proportion of the activator (NaOH) in the pre￾cursor. The electrochemical implications of these structural features warrant attention. Microporous SSA (1164.51 m2 g− 1 ) and micropore volume contribution (58.65 %) of NPC-700-6 were maximized, creating a proper balance between charge storage capacity (extensive SSA, 2320.39 m2 g− 1 ) and ion transport efficiency (appropriate micro/￾meso/macropore volume ratio, 11.4:7:1). This unique pore architecture is particularly advantageous for electrochemical applications requiring both high capacitance and rapid charge/discharge kinetics. As depicted in Fig. 4(a), the XRD patterns of NPC-600-6 and PW-700- 6 exhibited a distinctly broad peak at approximately 24◦, indicating their features of amorphous carbon. As the calcination temperature increased, sharp peaks appeared in the XRD patterns of NPC-700-6 and Fig. 3. (a). NPC-800-6 at ~26.1◦, which was consistent with graphitized carbon characteristics (Bairi et al., 2019). In addition, the peak intensity of NPC-800-6 at ~26◦ was notably greater than that of NPC-700-6, sug￾gesting temperature-dependent crystallinity enhancement. However, at the same annealing temperature (700 ◦C), NPC-700-4, NPC-700-8, and PW-700-6 showed disordered structures. According to previous studies, Na atoms produced by NaOH decomposition during carbon activation processes played a catalytic role in transforming amorphous carbon into ordered graphitic structures (Nanaji et al., 2021; Wu et al., 2016). In this study, the absence of NaOH in the precursor of PW-700-6 and the relatively low content of NaOH in the precursor of NPC-700-8 resulted in their amorphous carbon characteristics. On the basis of the SEM and BET results above, a relatively large amount of NaOH in the precursor of NPC-700-4 led to many pores and defects and ultimately resulted in its amorphous carbon characteristics. As evident from the Raman spectra (Fig. 4(b)), all samples exhibited characteristic vibrational modes at approximately 1350 cm− 1 (D-band) and 1590 cm− 1 (G-band), attributing to defects or disorder and in-plane sp2 C‒C bond vibrations, respectively (Wang et al., 2024). Quantitative analysis of the intensity ratio (ID/IG) revealed decreasing values from 0.96 (NPC-600-6) to 0.91 (NPC-800-6) with elevated carbonization temperatures (Fig. S2), demonstrating enhanced graphitization at higher thermal treatment conditions. 3.2. Composition characterization of materials The doping of heteroatoms can affect the electrical conductivity of carbon materials and facilitate the occurrence of redox reactions, thereby affecting their electrochemical properties (Li et al., 2021). The wide-scan XPS spectra (Fig. 5(a) and Fig. S3) confirmed successful incorporation of nitrogen, oxygen, and trace sulfur dopants. Because PW-700-6 was created using pure water rather than a NaOH/urea aqueous solution, the nitrogen came from the nitrogen-containing organic matter extracted from the sludge. This meant that the nitrogen-containing organic matter in the sludge introduced nitrogen into the carbon matrix via a series of reactions during the pyrolysis process. Furthermore, NPC-T-w had a higher nitrogen content than did PW-700-6, indicating that the NH3 generated by the urea in the pre￾cursor could react with the carbon skeleton and enter the carbon matrix during the pyrolysis process. However, as the calcination temperature increased, more NH3 escaped, resulting in a relatively lower nitrogen content in NPC-800-6. High-resolution C 1s XPS spectra (Fig. 5(b) and Fig. S4(a)) displayed five distinct components: sp2 C, sp3 C, C=O, O− C=O, and a π–π* satellite at approximately 284.7 eV, 285.9 eV, 286.9 eV, 288.0 eV, and 290.1 eV, respectively (Jackson and Nuzzo, 1995; Tian et al., 2022). Additionally, NPC-700-6 and NPC-800-6 have higher sp2 C contents and sp2 /p3 values than the other samples do (Fig. S5(a)), indicating their superior ordered structure, which was agreed with the analysis above. The fitting spectra of N 1s (Fig. 5(c) and Fig. S4(b)) displayed four characteristic peaks: pyridine-N (N− 6, Fig. 5. electrode after 1 cycle and 50,000 cycles were compared. As depicted in Fig. 8(a), the overall shape of the Nyquist plot remained unchanged after 50,000 cycles compared with that after 1 cycle, indicating that the re￾action mechanism of the charge–discharge process remained consistent. Notably, the diameter of the semicircle in the high-frequency region significantly decreased after 50,000 cycles, suggesting a reduction in the charge transfer resistance. Simultaneously, the slope of the straight line in the low-frequency region slightly increased, implying a reduced diffusion resistance of the electrolyte ions within the electrode material and improved pore uniformity and connectivity. Furthermore, as shown in the Bode plot (Fig. S8(b)), after 50,000 cycles, the characteristic frequency (ƒ0) of the NPC-700-6 electrode at a phase angle of − 45◦ was 0.44 Hz, corresponding to a relaxation time τ0 (1/ƒ0) of 2.27 s, which was 22.79 % shorter than that after 1 cycle (2.94 s). This indicated a significant enhancement in the charge–discharge efficiency. The fitting parameters of the equivalent circuit diagram (Table S3) revealed that the charge transfer resistance Rct value of the NPC-700-6 electrode decreased by 57.3 % after 50,000 cycles. Additionally, the values of both CPE-T and CPE-P increased significantly, indicating an improvement in the interfacial charge storage capacity and that the interfacial capaci￾tance of the material became closer to an ideal capacitor, thereby con￾firming the aforementioned conjecture. To further study the dynamic behavior of the NPC-T-w electrodes, the contributions of surface control and diffusion control were calcu￾lated following Dunn’s method (Choi et al., 2020) (Text S4). Taking NPC-700-6 as an example, the slope of the straight line in Fig. 6(g) derived from its CV curves (Fig. S9) served as the key parameter b for evaluating its electrochemical kinetics. The calculated b value was approximately 0.94, which was close to 1, implying a hybrid charge storage mechanism combining surface control and diffusion control processes, among which the former was dominant (Gao et al., 2024). Fig. 6(h) shows the variation in the contribution rates of these two control processes within the scan rate range of 10–200 mV s − 1 . As the scan rate increasing, the contribution rate of surface control capacitance gradually increased. This could be arised from the reduced diffusion time of the electrolyte at higher scan rates, which resulted in the func￾tional groups on the NPC-700-6 electrode being unable to undergo the redox reaction in a timely manner. Furthermore, at 200 mV s − 1 , the diffusion-controlled capacitance still contributed 4.9 % (Fig. 6(i)), attributable to the electrode’s hierarchical pore architecture which facilitated electrolyte diffusion to some extent. These findings revealed the NPC-700-6 electrode’s ability to rapid surface reactions and sus￾tained ionic accessibility. As evidenced by the aforementioned results, the NPC-700-6 elec￾trode exhibited superior electrochemical performance compared with the other samples in the three-electrode system. This could be because its extensive specific surface area and hierarchical pore network pro￾vided abundant contact points and transmission channels, thereby augmenting charge storage and electrolyte ion transport. Furthermore, appropriate nitrogen doping and calcination temperatures were conducive to enhancing the conductivity of the material. 3.4. Wu et al. hydrothermally carbonized soybean hulls in 10 wt% H3PO4 followed by KOH activation, obtaining a carbon material with a high specific surface area of 2523 m2 /g and a specific capacitance of 301 F/g at 0.1 A/g (Wu et al., 2020). In addition to high specific surface areas, heteroatom doping (e.g., with N or S) represents another effective strategy to enhance the capacitive performance of carbon materials through improving their electronic conductivity and surface wettability (Li et al., 2024). Compared with conventional doping methods that rely on external chemical sources such as thiourea (Liu et al., 2023), urea (Rustamaji et al., 2022), or sulfur-containing precursors (Dang et al., 2020), nitro￾gen- and sulfur-rich wastes offer a sustainable alternative for intrinsic doping (Gopalakrishnan and Badhulika, 2020; Kim et al., 2021). Municipal sewage sludge (MSS), a major sink for organic pollutants during wastewater treatment, yields an aqueous phase (AQ) rich in soluble proteins and other organic N/S compounds after HTC treatment (Xu et al., 2020b), which can serve as inherent dopants. Recently, our team employed different solvents (pure water and ammonia solution) for the hydrothermal hydrolysis of MSS (Djandja et al., 2022a). Upon recovering and reutilizing AQ, the high availability of nitrogen hetero￾cycles within AQ promoted the incorporation of nitrogen into aromatic rings during HTC, whereas excessive nitrogen content could adversely affect the material's electrochemical performance. Research has focused predominantly on optimizing hydrothermal temperature or nitrogen-fixing agents (Xu et al., 2020a,b). Strategies for efficiently utilizing organic matter in the aqueous phase (as N/S sources) to syn￾ergistically construct high-performance carbon materials remain underexplored. In particular, the co-hydrothermal carbonization (co-HTC) process involving organic matter from the aqueous phase and carbon-rich biomass (e.g., cellulose), along with its impact on the structure and properties of the resulting materials, requires systematic investigation. Therefore, this study proposes the utilization of an aqueous phase derived from hydrothermal hydrolysis of MSS for co-HTC with cellulose, with the aim of preparing high-performance N-codoped porous carbon materials. The focus will be on investigating the influence of aqueous phase loading (AQ loading) on yield, pore structure (specific surface area, pore size distribution), and heteroatom doping levels of the co￾HTC-derived porous carbons. Furthermore, the electrochemical perfor￾mance (specific capacitance and cycling stability) of the optimized N￾codoped porous carbon materials as supercapacitor electrodes was evaluated. This research aims to provide a novel strategy for the efficient utilization of sludge-derived organic matter in combination with cellu￾lose to prepare high-performance supercapacitor electrode materials, thereby advancing the sustainable and value-added utilization of biomass waste. 2. Experimental section 2.1. Materials MSS, with a moisture content of 79.5 wt%, was obtained from the Beishi-qiao municipal wastewater treatment plant located in Xi'an, Shanxi Province. This sludge cake was produced after the wastewater underwent a "multistage anaerobic‒aerobic, oxidation ditch + micro￾flocculation filtration" process, followed by a "gravity thickening + mechanical dewatering" process. Before the experiment, hair, large inorganic particles and other foreign substances that may affect the experimental results from the MSS were removed. The polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE; 60 wt %) adhesive and α-cellu￾lose powder (99.0%) used in the experiment were purchased from Shanghai Macklin Biochemical Co., Ltd. Potassium hydroxide (KOH; 99.7%) was obtained from Tianjin Damao Chemical Regent Factory. The supplier of acetylene black BP2000 was Tianjin Cabot Company. Ul￾trapure water was used in all the experiments. 2.2. Aqueous phase preparation The MSS hydrolysis experiments were conducted in a 200 mL stainless-steel reactor heated by a molten-salt bath. The molten salt is a ternary salt mixture of KNO3, NaNO2 and NaNO3 with a mass ratio of 53:40:7. 40 g of MSS and 140 mL of H2O were added into the reactor and thoroughly mixed. The reactor was then sealed, and its outer surface was cleaned to ensure that there was no contamination. The salt bath heater was preheated to 245 ◦C, and the sealed reactor was immersed in a molten salt bath. When the internal temperature of the reactor reached the target temperature of 230 ◦C (approximately 30 min), the reaction time was initiated and maintained for 60 min. During the reaction, the internal temperature was controlled within the range of 230 ± 1 ◦C. After completion of the reaction, the reactor was immediately removed from the bath and cooled to ambient temperature. The reaction mixture was then transferred for solid–liquid separation. The resulting liquid fraction was designated the aqueous phase (AQ). The organic content of AQ was determined after freeze-drying and quantified as 16.97 mg/mL. 2.3. HTC experiments and activation The HTC experiments were conducted in a 100 mL electrically heated stainless-steel reactor. First, the AQ was mixed with H2O at volume ratios of 0, 0.2, 0.5, 0.7, and 1.0 to prepare a series of AQ so￾lutions with a total volume of 70 mL. Subsequently, 5 g of cellulose and 70 mL of each AQ solution were introduced into the reactor and thor￾oughly stirred. The reactor was sealed and heated to 240 ◦C within approximately 30 min. After maintaining this temperature for 60 min, the reactor was removed and allowed to cool to ambient temperature. The obtained biochar was washed and dried at 105 ◦C for 12 h and named BC-X, where X denotes the volume ratio of AQ to water (0, 0.2, 0.5, 0.7, and 1.0). The biochar yield was calculated with Equation (1): YBC = mBC/( mcellulose + morganic matter in AQ) × 100% (1) where YBC is the biochar yield and mBC, mcellulose, and organic matter in AQ represent the weights of BC, cellulose, and organic matter in the AQ solution, respectively. Next, BC-X was activated with KOH. Specifically, a mixture of BC-X and KOH (weight ratio of KOH/BC-X = 3) was thoroughly ground and loaded into a corundum crucible, which was transferred to a tube furnace and heated to 800 ◦C at 10 ◦C/min under an Ar atmosphere. The resulting activated BC-X was repeatedly washed with pure water until the filtrate reached neutrality, dried at 105 ◦C for 12 h, and named A-BC￾X. 2.4. Characterization The total organic carbon (TOC) concentration of the AQ was deter￾mined using a TOC analyzer (TA-200, Neuronbc, China). The total ni￾trogen (TN) and ammonia nitrogen (NH4 +-N) concentrations in the AQ were detected using water quality analyzers (LH-3BN, 5B-3BH, China). The contents of C, H, N, S, and O in the BCs and A-BCs were quantified using an elemental analyzer (Vario EL cube, Germany). X-ray photo￾electron spectroscopy (XPS, Thermo Scientific, USA) was conducted to determine the surface properties of the A-BCs. Fourier transform infrared (FTIR) spectra were obtained with a spectrometer (Nicolet iS50) to analyze the changes in surface functional groups. The surface morphology of the A-BCs was observed via field emission scanning electron microscopy (SEM, Carl Zeiss AG, Oberkochen, Germany). The N2 adsorption and desorption curves and pore size distributions of the A￾BCs were determined via a specific surface area analyzer (JW-BK100, China). The identification of the crystalline phase and defects of the A￾BCs were conducted via X-ray diffraction (XRD, XRD-6100), and Raman spectra were acquired using a Raman spectroscopy (InVia Qontor). 2.5. Electrochemical test The electrochemical performance of A-BC-X was evaluated via an electrochemical workstation (CHI760E, China). The working electrode was prepared according to a previously described method (Yin et al., 2025). A mixture of A-BC-X, acetylene black, and PTFE with a mass ratio of 80:15:5 was compacted and shaped into a circular electrode sheet, which was mechanically pressed onto nickel foam. For various A-BC-X electrodes, the mass of the active substance was approximately 2.5 mg. The three-electrode test was conducted in a 6 M KOH electrolyte solu￾tion, which utilized a Pt plate and Hg/HgO as the counter electrode and reference electrode, respectively. The voltage window ranged from -1–0 V. Cyclic voltammetry (CV), galvanostatic charge/discharge (GCD), and electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) tests were carried out. For the cycling test, the A-BC-0.2 electrode underwent 20,000 cycles at a current density of 10 A/g. The calculation of the specific capacitance of the electrode can be found in the Supplementary data. 3. Results and discussion 3.1. Effect of the AQ volume ratio on the yield of BCs To elucidate the impact of the addition of AQ on the yield of BCs, the organic carbon and nitrogen contents of AQ were quantified. The AQ exhibited a high total organic carbon (TOC) concentration (11,923 mg/ L) and nitrogen content (TN = 10,120 mg/L; NH4 +–N = 5450 mg/L), confirming that a substantial fraction of the sludge-derived organics and nitrogen species were transferred into the liquid phase during thermal hydrolysis. Moreover, our previous work (Djandja et al., 2022b) revealed that pyrazine derivatives were the dominant aqueous-phase compounds at 200–230 ◦C, followed by pyrrole and piperazine de￾rivatives. These N-heterocyclic compounds primarily originate from the hydrolysis of proteins and polysaccharides in sludge, generating ami￾nes/amino acids and reducing sugars, which can subsequently undergo condensation and dehydration reactions to form macromolecular sub￾stances (e.g., Maillard-related intermediates and humic-like substances) (Huang et al., 2021). Collectively, these results indicate that the AQ contains a continuum of reactive species, ranging from low-molecular-weight N-containing intermediates to oligomers, which can participate in carbon formation during co-HTC process. The influence of the AQ volume ratio on the BCs yield is shown in Fig. 1. The BC yield progressively increased from 47.38 wt% to 55.56 wt % with increasing AQ proportion. The formation of BC can be catego￾rized into three pathways: (1) direct cellulose conversion, in which cellulose undergoes solid‒solid transformation through condensation, dehydration, and decarboxylation to produce char enriched in C, H, and O (Sevilla and Fuertes, 2009); (2) intermediate polymerization, in which the polymerization of cellulose degradation intermediates results in the formation of pyrolytic carbon deposits that are mainly composed of carbon; and (3) the Maillard reaction, in which amino acids/amine species from AQ react with sugars generated from cellulose hydrolysis, forming N-containing heterocyclic polymers. Accordingly, increasing the AQ fraction introduced more soluble organics—particularly protein-derived nitrogenous species—that could participate in the Maillard reaction and related condensation/cross-linking reactions, thereby generating additional solid products and enhancing the BC yield. Furthermore, other soluble organic species present in the AQ (e.g., polypeptides and polysaccharide fragments) may also contribute to carbon skeleton construction via polymerization and cross-linking, further increasing the solid yield. However, a higher BC yield does not directly indicate the superior electrochemical performance of the acti￾vated material, which is more strongly governed by pore architecture and ion-accessible surface area. 3.2. Elemental analysis The elemental compositions of the BCs and A-BCs produced with different AQ volume ratios are summarized in Table 1. BC-0 presented the highest carbon content and lowest hydrogen and oxygen contents. With increasing AQ volume ratio from 0.2 to 1.0, the nitrogen content increased significantly from 1.46 wt% to 3.49 wt%, and the sulfur content also slightly increased. This trend can be attributed to the incorporation of nitrogen- and sulfur-containing compounds (e.g., protein-derived species) from the AQ into the BC matrix through chemical pathways such as Maillard reactions and subsequent conden￾sation or crosslinking reaction. The introduction of more N and S het￾eroatoms into BC may enhance electrochemical performance by facilitating charge transfer and generating active sites. In contrast, the carbon content decreased from 69.22 wt% to 66.54 wt%, whereas the hydrogen content increased slightly. This is likely due to the high abundance of hydrogen-rich functional groups (e.g., hydroxyl and carboxyl groups) in AQ, imparting a low-carbon, hydrogen-enriched character to the resulting material. These results demonstrate that the organic constituents of AQ were effectively incorporated into the carbon matrix and promoted the conversion of cellulose into solid carbonaceous products during the co-HTC process. After activation, A-BCs presented a substantially higher carbon content together with reduced hydrogen and oxygen contents compared with the corresponding BCs. This indicates that extensive dehydration and decarboxylation reactions occurred during activation, thereby promoting aromatization and enhancing the stability of the carbon framework. Moreover, the increased N and S contents suggested that the heteroatoms were successfully retained or doped in thermally stable Fig. 1. Effect of AQ volume ratio on the BCs yield. implying enhanced incorporation of nitrogen and oxygen atoms into the carbon framework, leading to the formation of additional C‒O‒C and C‒N bonds. Collectively, these results demonstrated that the introduc￾tion of AQ not only led to surface enrichment of nitrogen- and oxygen-containing functional groups but also induced structural rear￾rangement of the carbon skeleton at loadings above 20 v%, with an increase in hybrid polymers and a significant increase in the degree of aliphaticity, which may influence the electrochemical performance of the resulting carbon materials (Wei and Cai, 2020; Xiao et al., 2012). 3.4. Textural properties and morphology analysis To clarify the influence of AQ loading on the pore characteristics of A-BCs, N2 adsorption/desorption isotherms combined with a density functional theory (DFT) pore size distribution model were used for systematic characterization (Fig. 3 and Table 2). All the samples exhibited typical type I isotherms (Fig. 3(a)), indicating micropore￾dominated structures (Rahbar-Shamskar et al., 2020). The significant nitrogen uptake at low relative pressures (P/P0 < 0.05) suggested the presence of well-developed microporosity. Notably, A-BC-0.2 displayed an ~73% greater adsorption capacity in this region than A-BC-0, demonstrating that an appropriate AQ loading (20 v%) effectively pro￾moted micropore development. This enhancement is likely related to the introduction of oxygen- and nitrogen-containing moieties by AQ, which can generate additional reactive sites and gaseous etchants (e.g., COx) during KOH activation, thereby facilitating pore formation and the widening of micropores. Nitrogen uptake almost reached saturation when P/P0 > 0.2, without an observable hysteresis loop, further sup￾porting the predominance of micropores. A slight increase in adsorption at high relative pressures (P/P0 > 0.9) was ascribed to capillary condensation within a limited number of macropores. With further increases in the AQ loading beyond 20 v%, the low￾pressure uptake gradually decreased compared with that of A-BC-0.2, suggesting that excessive AQ might suppress the development of mi￾cropores. A plausible explanation is that some of the AQ-derived or￾ganics, especially the more condensed fractions formed during co-HTC/ activation, preferentially contribute to carbon skeleton growth and carbon deposition, partially narrowing or blocking micropores and limiting KOH diffusion into the interior. A similar decline in adsorption at high relative pressures (P/P0 > 0.9) indicated an overall reduction in accessible porosity at high AQ ratios. Consequently, the AQ loading significantly influenced both the specific surface area (SSA) and the pore architecture of the A-BCs. A-BC-0.2 presented the highest SSA of 2279.2 m2 /g, followed by A-BC-0.5 (1600.45 m2 /g). In contrast, A-BC-0.7 and A-BC-1.0 presented lower SSA values than A-BC-0. This decrease at high AQ loadings was likely associated with (i) excessive carbon deposition that hindered activator diffusion and reduced the effective activation extent and (ii) a more disordered or aliphatic carbon matrix at high AQ ratios, which was less favorable for maintaining a stable microporous framework under severe activation conditions, leading to partial pore shrinkage or collapse and reduced SSA. The pore size distribution (Fig. 3(b)) further confirmed that A-BC-0.2 had the highest micropore volume. This combination of high SSA and abundant microporosity provided many ion-accessible sites for charge storage, which is advantageous for supercapacitor applications. Although higher AQ loadings can increase nitrogen doping, the concomitant deterioration of the pore structure may impede ion trans￾port and reduce the utilization efficiency of surface sites, thereby limiting further electrochemical improvement. Therefore, optimizing the AQ loading is essential for achieving a synergistic balance between heteroatom incorporation and pore architecture. The microstructural evolution of the A-BCs was examined via SEM (Fig. 4), which strongly agreed with the BET results and pore analysis. As shown in Fig. 4(a), the surface of A-BC-0 presented a typical porous carbon skeleton structure, indicating that KOH activation established a basic pore network. At an AQ loading of 20 v% (Fig. 4(b)), A-BC-0.2 presented more uniformly distributed pores, thinner pore walls, and a significantly higher pore density, directly corresponding to its increased SSA and micropore volume, suggesting that AQ participated in carbon skeleton construction via a "pore-formation-dominant" mechanism under these conditions. When the AQ loading increased to 50 v% (Fig. 4 (c)), A-BC-0.5 presented locally enlarged pores and slightly thickened pore walls compared with A-BC-0.2, suggesting a transition toward a "carbon deposition-dominant" mechanism. This shift was likely attrib￾uted to increased formation of amorphous carbon from AQ-derived precursors, which partially blocked micropore channels and reduced the population of small pores. Moreover, nonuniform accessibility of the activator may have lead to localized overetching, producing irregular larger pores. Notably, at 70 v% AQ loading (Fig. 4(d)), A-BC-0.7 exhibited significant structural collapse of the carbon framework. Compared with that of A-BC-0, the surface roughness of A-BC-0.7 decreased, which was consistent with the lower SSA. This degradation was presumably caused by excessive AQ-derived carbonaceous deposi￾tion forming a more continuous amorphous phase that limits KOH penetration and compromises pore development. observations provided morphological evidence that AQ loading can regulate the competition between pore formation and carbon deposition during activation, enabling controllable pore architectures in A-BCs. 3.5. Crystalline phase and surface defect analysis As shown in Fig. 5(a), the XRD patterns of the A-BCs exhibited a broad and elevated peak at approximately 22◦, indicative of a typical amorphous carbon structure. When the AQ loading exceeded 20 v%, this peak became relatively sharper, suggesting increased structural densi￾fication of the carbon matrix, which was consistent with the SEM ob￾servations. The defect characteristics of the carbon skeleton were further investigated via Raman spectroscopy (Fig. 5(b)). All the samples exhibited two distinct peaks at ~1340 cm− 1 (D band) and ~1590 cm− 1 (G band), corresponding to disordered carbon and graphitic sp2 do￾mains, respectively. The intensity ratio (ID/IG) is commonly used to quantify the defect density of carbon materials (Dang et al., 2020). With increasing AQ loading from 0 to 100 v%, the ID/IG values of the A-BCs were 0.984, 1.188, 1.214, 1.074, and 1.058, respectively, indicating that introducing an appropriate amount of AQ (particularly within 0–50 v%) increased the defect density. This behavior can be attributed to AQ-derived heteroatom incorporation (e.g., pyridinic and pyrrolic N and oxygen-containing groups), which disrupted the continuity of sp2 do￾mains during activation and introduced additional edge sites and topological defects. When the AQ loading exceeded 50 v%, the ID/IG values tended to decrease. A plausible explanation is that excessive organic precursors generate a large amount of amorphous carbon during activation, leading to structural rearrangement in the local defect re￾gions. Importantly, the decrease in ID/IG values at high AQ ratios coin￾cided with the decrease in SSA, suggesting that excessive AQ shifted the system from a defect-rich, highly porous structure toward a more densified/deposition-dominated carbon matrix with reduced accessible porosity. These results, together with the BET and SEM analysis results, confirmed that AQ loading governed the balance between defect gen￾eration and pore development during activation, thereby regulating the microstructure of the A-BCs. 3.6. Electrochemical performance Electrochemical performance tests were performed to investigate the influence of the AQ loading on the electrochemical behavior of the A-BC￾X electrodes. As shown in Fig. 6(a–d), the CV curves of all the A-BC-X electrodes exhibited quasi-rectangular profiles within the scan rate range of 10–200 mV/s, indicating the dominance of the electric double￾layer capacitance (EDLC). Notably, the characteristic humps in the CV curves were attributed to the pseudocapacitance caused by N- and O￾containing functional groups on the A-BC-X surface. segments.text: Quinoa straw (QS) was cleaned by being soaked and washed with water to eliminate surface dust. The cleaned QS was dried in an oven at 60 °C for 48 h. QS was grinded (through a 40-mesh sieve) and placed in a crucible to be precarbonized in an electric resistance furnace at 600 °C for 2 h. In quartz boats, carbonized QSC and K 2 CO 3 were thoroughly ground and mixed in a certain proportion. The mixtures were then placed into a tube furnace and heated at a rate of 5 °C min –1 under a nitrogen atmosphere to 800 °C for 2 h for activation. The resulting activated samples were cooled naturally under a nitrogen gas flow, washed with 1 M HCl and ultrapure water until neutral, and dried at 80 °C for 8 h in a vacuum oven. These final samples were designated as QSC- x , with x (equal to 2, 3, or 4) representing the mass ratio of K 2 CO 3 to QS. The detailed experimental process is shown in Figure 1 .

segments.locator: XML p 13; section Preparation of Supercapacitor Electrodes
segments.text: The working electrode based on QSC was prepared using activated carbon materials, a conductive acetylene black agent, and polytetrafluoroethylene (binder, PTFE) with a mass ratio of 80:10:10. The obtained slurry was uniformly coated on a 1 × 2 cm 2 foam nickel collector. Each sheet of the loaded electrode contained QSC active materials with a mass of about 2–3.0 mg. The coating collector was dried in a vacuum oven at 70 °C for 12 h. Then, the nickel foam sheets were compressed under a pressure of 10 MPa to obtain the working electrode.

segments.text: electronics, electric vehicles, memory devices, photographic flashes, etc.16 Supercapacitors have several advantages over traditional storage devices such as high power density, rapid charging, long life cycle, and wide operating temperatures.17 But, traditional supercapacitors mostly suffer from low energy density, which suppresses their far-reaching applications with regard to the growing need for ultrahigh energy density.18 Bio and plastic waste management are a major challenge for modern civilization. Nowadays, scientists are very much engaged in environmental remediation through conversion of waste materials (such as leaves, crops, waste municipal materials, etc.) to value-added products and its application in harvesting, conversion, and storage of clean energy.19,20 In recent years, transforming waste biomass resources into multifunctional porous carbon materials has gathered immense universal acceptance for energy security due to their distinct advantages in terms of low processing cost, high availability, abundant reservation, recyclability, and great potential for commercial production.21−24 Moreover, managing and recy￾cling biomass waste into value-added carbon could also solve the emerging pollution concerns surrounding disposal problems and improve the decarbonized economic efficiency. Biomass and its corresponding natural waste products enriched internally with heteroatoms (N, O and others) are expected to produce N- and O-rich functionalities in the resultant carbon matrix without introducing any external doping agents.25 The modification of the carbon material by heteroatom doping not only introduces more defects and additional pseudocapacitance from surface faradaic reactions, but also increase the exposed active sites for O2 surface adsorption in ORR by modulating the electronic structure.26−28 Additionally, porous nanostruc￾tures with tailored pore size distribution could accelerate the transport of ions as well as provide accessible active sites, both of which are critical for accomplishing high-performing ORR and supercapacitor activities.29,30 To date, much biomass and biowaste as carbon precursors coupled with appropriate synthesis processes (e.g., pyrolysis, template method, chemical vapor deposition, etc.) have been employed for the fabrication of advanced heteroatom-doped nanostructured carbon materials.31−33 However, most of these reported techniques involve relatively intricate templates, tedious processes, and hazardous organic precursors, which may not necessarily meet the principles of green chemistry.34 Among the many techniques available, chemical activation using KOH is the most preferred approach to efficiently control the composition or structure of a biomass carbon with desirable pores.35,36 Besides KOH, activating agents such as ZnCl2, H3PO4, etc. are also widely employed. However, of the many reagents available, KOH activation takes precedence in terms of delivering higher specific surface area (SSA) and well￾developed microporosity in the resultant porous carbon, apart from minimizing tar formation and improving the activation reaction efficiency.37,38 For example, KOH-activated spruce bark-derived porous carbon presented the highest SSA of 2209 m2 g−1 , followed by ZnCl2 (1019 m2 g−1 ) and MgCl2 (98 m2 g−1 ).39 In another instance, rice-husk-derived graphene-KOH showed better physicochemical properties with regard to pore volume and sp2 carbon content than the carbon material prepared by H3PO4 activation. This observation suggests that KOH as an activating agent is more effective than H3PO4. 40 Moreover, KOH is considered to be less toxic to the environment in comparison to ZnCl2 or H3PO4, making it a reliable choice.41 Lin et al. observed that soybean-derived nitrogen-doped porous carbon as an ORR electrocatalyst demonstrated a current density of 5.09 mA cm−2 . 42 It also exhibits a high specific capacitance of 243.2 F g−1 at a current density of 0.5 A g−1 . 42 Harraz and co-workers reported that nitrogen-doped porous carbon materials from B. vulgaris leaves attributed a current density of 5.74 mA cm−2 and 0.8 V (vs. RHE) onset potential for the ORR electrocatalyst in an alkaline medium.43 Taro stem-derived N-doped porous carbon exhibited excellent stability of 96.5% after 20,000 s for ORR and exceptional power density (5 kW kg−1 at 5.56 Wh kg−1 ).44 Biomass-derived O/N co-doped porous carbon material synthesized by Liu et al. shows a specific capacitance of 251 F g−1 at a current density of 1 A g−1 as well as electrocatalytic activity toward ORR.45 Perez-Salcedo and co-workers reported that KOH-activated biocarbon showed good current density of 5.2 mA cm−2 in an alkaline medium for ORR application along with a high capacitance of 207.3 F g−1 at 0.5 A g−1 . 46 Likewise, mulberry leave-derived N, S-porous carbon presented impres￾sive specific capacitance of 214.5 F g−1 at 0.5 A g−1 , onset potential (Eonset) of 0.86 V, and excellent catalytic selectivity.47 The focus of this work is to synthesize a value-added product from a biowaste precursor for catalytic conversion of clean energy through ORR and capacitive energy storage applications. Agarwood leaves (Aquilaria malaccensis) are mostly a kind of common biowaste in India and are rich in phenolic acids, carbohydrates, and alkanes as well as nitrogen￾rich alkaloids, flavonoids, etc.,48 which make them a valuable and reliable feedstock to prepare heteroatom-doped activated carbon. In this paper, waste agarwood leave-derived N-doped porous carbon (ALPC) was prepared via a template-free chemical activation process using KOH as the activating reagent. As heteroatoms are already there in the chemical composition of agarwood leaves, nitrogen is inherently doped in the synthesized catalyst. In-depth characterization studies revealed that the as-obtained ALPC materials possessed a nanoflake morphology, a favorable degree of graphitization, microporosity, large SSA, and an optimal amount of inherent heteroatoms. Based on the exclusive structural and composi￾tional properties, the porous carbons delivered interesting ORR and supercapacitor characteristics. The synthesized ALPC-800 as an electrocatalyst exhibited excellent ORR efficiency having a current density (6.09 mA cm−2 ) and positive onset potential (0.98 V vs. RHE) which is almost comparable to Pt/C. ALPC-800 also demonstrated maximum efficiency through a four-electron pathway for electrocatalytic ORR activity. Moreover, ALPC-800 showed better efficiency in terms of a stability test (70% retention) and methanol tolerance test compared to a commercially available 10 wt % Pt/C catalyst in a O2-saturated 0.1 M KOH media. In terms of the supercapacitor application, the ALPC sample obtained at 800 °C (ALPC-800) in a three-electrode configuration presented a high specific capacitance of 421 F g−1 at a current density of 1 A g−1 using a 0.5 M H2SO4 aq. electrolyte. Moreover, as a fabricated symmetrical supercapacitor (SSC) device, a high energy density of 21.15 Wh kg−1 and a high power density of 4.93 kW kg−1 along with excellent durability (91% capacitance retention after 6000 cycles at 10 A g−1 ) was achieved. Thus, this work follows an affordable, eco-friendly, and facile approach for the conversion of waste material to the value-added product for the conversion of clean energy and capacitive energy storage applications. ■ EXPERIMENTAL SECTION Preparation of Agarwood Leave-Derived N-Doped Porous Carbon (ALPC). As presented in Figure 1a, the ALPC materials were prepared via a potentially scalable chemical activation process using KOH as an activator. At first, the agarwood leaves were washed thoroughly with double-distilled water and dried at 80 °C for 12 h before being crushed into a fine powder with a high-speed grinder (Philips Hl1631). Secondly, the powdered leaves were mixed with NH4Cl in a mass ratio of 1:1 for 10 mins and kept in a vacuum oven at 80 °C for 24 h. A similar procedure was also followed with KOH. Subsequently, the preactivated reaction mixture was carbonized in a tube furnace at 700 °C (ALPC-700), 800 °C (ALPC-800), and 900 °C (ALPC-900) under Ar atmosphere for 2 h with the heating rate of 5 °C min−1 , releasing no toxic emissions. The carbonized samples were washed several times with 3 M HCl and double-distilled water along with ethanol and finally dried at 90 °C overnight. Electrocatalytic Measurements for ORR. The typical three￾electrode system consisted of a 3 mm polished glassy carbon (GC) disk electrode as the working electrode, a Pt wire as the counter electrode, and Hg/HgO as the reference electrode. The slurry for the working electrode was prepared by mixing 5 mg of the ALPC materials in ethanol and isopropanol (790 μL:200 μL) solution and Nafion solution (10 μL) under ultrasonication for 1 h. A total of 5 μL of the as-prepared ink was drop cast on the GC disk electrode and dried at room temperature. The catalyst ink for the commercial Pt/C (10 wt %) was prepared by the same procedure. The voltammograms were studied in N2- and O2-saturated 0.1 M KOH electrolyte solution within a potential range from −0.8 V to 0.3 V vs. Hg/HgO at a scan rate of 20 mV s −1 at 400 rpm. Before each electrochemical test, the electrolyte was purged with N2/O2 for 30 mins. The linear sweep voltammetry (LSV) measurements were investigated at different rotation speeds (400−2500 rpm) at a scan rate of 10 mV s −1 . The negative value for ΔEads indicates that it is energetically favorable for the adsorbate moieties to adsorb onto N-doped graphene. ■ RESULTS AND DISCUSSION Physical Characterizations. The crystalline nature of the as-obtained ALPC-800 was characterized by a powder X-ray diffraction (PXRD) technique. In Figure 1b, the PXRD pattern exhibits two broad low-intensity peaks centered around 24.9° and 42.4°, which are indexed to the (002) and (100) diffraction planes, respectively, for a typical graphitic carbon.9 In order to further elaborate the structural features of the synthesized carbonaceous materials, the comparative Raman spectra of the ALPC samples carbonized at different temperatures are presented in Figure 1c. Two distinct bands are located at ∼1357 and ∼1591 cm−1 , corresponding to the D band (defect or disordered carbon) and G band (ideal graphitic order). Generally, the value of the relative intensity ratio of the D band and G band (ID/IG) gives the graphitization degree of a carbonaceous material. The appearance of a 2D band (overtone of D band) at ∼2855 cm−1 indicates formation of graphite-like domains, which can provide the ALPCs with superior electrical conductivity.63 It is found that the ID/IG values of ALPC-900, ALPC-800, and ALPC-700 are 0.97, 0.97, and 0.96, respectively, indicating that the defects of sp2 carbons increase with higher carbonization temperature. The presence of structural defects in the carbon framework, which arise either from the heteroatom functional groups or micro/mesoporous formation during the chemical activation, facilitates high electrochemical performances by enhancing the electronic conductivity and number of active sites of the materials.27 The evolutions of the surface morphology of the raw biomass during the carbonization process at different high temperatures and the corresponding derived carbons were systematically studied by field emission scanning electron microscopy (FESEM) analysis. The representative images of the as-obtained ALPC materials (Figure 2a−c) show substantial changes in the morphology of the raw agarwood leaves after the chemical treatment with KOH, resulting in the transformation of the bulk structures of the nontreated precursors (Figure S1) into porous structures. KOH as a chemical activation reagent is known to increase the surface area of a sample as well as introduce tunable porosity via the etching process due to its high solubility and chemical reactivity. During the process of carbonization, different carbonates are formed from the reaction involving KOH and the carbon atoms of the biowaste, while the decomposed metallic K vapor is embedded into the carbon layers, which in turn results in the expansion of the carbon lattice.64 Moreover, as displayed in Figure 2b, ALPC-800 showed interconnected 3D cross-linked nanoflake morphology in comparison to ALPC-900 and ALPC-700, inferring here that an optimal temperature of 800 °C in combination with KOH is most favorable for the formation of a highly porous nanostructure. The subsequent EDX mapping of ALPC-800 confirmed the uniform distribution of C, N, and O elements throughout the carbon framework and is shown in Figure 2d−g and Table S1. The existence of the heteroatoms is due to the natural availability of such elements present in the biomass source, as illustrated in Figure S2. A transmission electron microscopic (TEM) study was performed to further comprehend the nanostructural proper￾ties of the as-obtained ALPC-800 material. Ultrathin nano￾flakes with abundant micropores were observed from the TEM analysis under different magnifications (Figure 2h and i), which support the FESEM results. The micropores are known to provide adsorption sites for ions, which is favorable for the enhancement of the electrochemical performance. Figure 2j shows the diffused ring-like selected area electron diffraction (SAED) pattern of ALPC-800, which is indicative of an amorphous carbon. N2 adsorption−desorption isotherms were conducted to determine the textural properties of the obtained ALPC materials. As can be observed in Figure S3a, ALPC-900 and ALPC-800 showed combined features of mixed Type I and Type IV curves, indicating the existence of micropores/ mesopores. This enables ALPC-900, ALPC-800, and ALPC￾700 with SSA of 375, 718, and 25 m2 g−1 , respectively, as listed in Table S1. Moreover, the ALPC-700 sample exhibits the lowest N2 uptake compared to the others with almost no hysteresis loop. The pore size distribution analysis by the density functional theory (DFT) method comes out mostly in the microporous range of less than 2 nm, especially for the ALPC-800 material (Figure S3b). segments.locator: XML p 11; section Material and methods
segments.text: The preparation process of CA is shown in Fig. 1 . The preparation process of CA is shown in Fig. 1 . In a typical process, 12 g NaOH, 7 g urea and 81 g H 2 O are thoroughly mixed and cooled to −12 °C. Then 3 g cellulose was added into NaOH/urea/H 2 O solution. After violent shaking, mechanically stir for 1 hour to promote cellulose dissolution. Cooling the solution to −12 °C, refreezing, and then stirring again to obtain a translucent cellulose solution. The cellulose solution is placed in an oven at 50 °C until cellulose hydrogel was obtained. Wash the hydrogel with diluted acetic acid solution, tert -butanol solution and deionized water until it is neutral, so as to clean NaOH and urea in the hydrogel, and then let the hydrogel stand in each anti-solvent to replace the water in the hydrogel. A control group was set up to clean the surface of prepared hydrogel without replacing NaOH/urea/H 2 O with anti-solvent. Then, liquid nitrogen was used for rapid freezing, and then freeze-dried in a freeze dryer (−60 °C, 0 mbar) for 48 hours to obtain cellulose aerogel. The cellulose aerogel is put into a tube furnace for two-step heat treatment. In the first stage, the temperature was raised from room temperature to 200 °C in nitrogen atmosphere at a rate of 5 °C min −1 , and the temperature was kept at 200 °C for 2 hours. In the second stage, the sample was heated at 200 °C to 800 °C with a heating rate of 5 °C min −1 , and then kept at 800 °C for 2 hours. CA made of acetic acid, tert -butylalcohol and water anti-solvent were carbonized to obtain CA-AA, carbon aerogel- tert -butanol (CA-TB) and carbon aerogel-water (CA-W). The control group was named carbon aerogels-control (CA-C).

The hierarchical porous structure can not only provide a large effective area to obtain high energy storage capacity, but also improve the electrochemical performance.12 Moreover, in the 3D porous system, microspores provide more active sites for electrolyte ions, mesopores provide transfer electrolyte ion channels, and macropores offer buffer space for electrolyte ions.10 Combined with these characteristics, the capacitance retention rate of carbon materials and the charge storage capacity and magnified performance of SCs can be comprehensively improved.9,18 Element doping has emerged as an efficacious strategy for enriching the surface of biomass carbon materials with a variety of functional groups. This enrichment not only augments their wettability but also significantly amplifies the number of active sites available for electrochemical reactions.19 Such a process enhances not only the additional pseudocapacitance but also the overall electrochemical activity of the material. For instance, elements such as nitrogen (N), phosphorus (P), sulfur (S), boron (B) and oxygen (O) are often employed as heteroatoms for carbon doping.20–25 Wu et al.26 successfully achieved O and N co-doped hierarchical porous carbon with hierarchical porous structures through the synergistic effect of KHCO3 and urea, which showed a high specific capacitance (324 F g1 at 1 A g1 ) and good cyclic stability in 6 M KOH. Herein, we used activation, element doping and acid-modified strategies to convert sawdust to AUACW materials. The obtained AUACW biomass-based carbon material has a 3D porous structure, which facilitates the formation of high-speed ion transport chan￾nels and enhances hydrophilicity, electrical conductivity and addi￾tional pseudocapacitance by introducing N and O heteroatoms. Due to these merits, it can achieve a high specific capacitance of 435.84 F g1 at 0.8 A g1 . Meanwhile, it maintains an impressive capacitance retention rate of 93.6% after 10 000 cycles. Moreover, AUACW was assembled into an SSC, which achieved an energy density of 22.61 W h kg1 and a power density of 533.26 W kg1 at 4Ag1 in a 1 M KOH electrolyte. Experimental section Synthesis of the AUACW materials Information about all chemicals used is listed in the ESI.† In the carbonization part, sawdust was purchased online from solid wood furniture factories. 1 g of sawdust was ground into a fine powder, dried, calcined for 2 h at 700 1C in an N2 atmosphere, washed with deionized water and dried to obtain CW. The other two parts of sawdust were prepared as follows: the first part was added to a 16 (w/v)% KOH aqueous solution (the sawdust to KOH mass ratio was maintained at 1 : 2), stirred, dried, and then calcined in N2 at 700 1C for 2 h. The second part was added to a mixed solution of KOH and urea with sawdust, and the mixture (sawdust: KOH : urea = 1: 2: 1 (mass ratio)) was stirred, dried, and transferred to an N2 atmosphere at 700 1C for calcination for 2 h. Then, 1 M HCl and deionized water were used to wash the calcined products. After drying, the ACW and UACW products were obtained. Finally, 0.1 g UACW was added into a 4 mL mixed concentrated acid solution (H2SO4 :HNO3 = 3:1 (v: v)), followed by ultrasonic treatment for 30 min. The final AUACW sample was obtained after washing and drying. Results and discussion Structure and morphology The synthesis process for AUACW materials is shown in Fig. 1. Pre-UACW was obtained by thoroughly mixing KOH, urea and sawdust, followed by impregnation of KOH and dehydration of the sawdust, which is conducive to the activation of the subsequent step to yield UACW. Additionally, UACW was modified with a strong acid mixture to prepare the pristine black AUACW sample (Fig. S1, ESI†). The morphology and structure of the as-synthesized samples were explored using SEM images. The direct carbonized wood (CW) material presented large-scale nanoplates with a smooth surface morphology and 30–70 mm in size (Fig. 2a and Fig. S2a, ESI†). This is because CW is not fully activated and lacks a porous internal structure. Then, the activated carbonized wood (ACW) material was obtained by activation with KOH before carboniza￾tion. The SEM image of the ACW is shown in Fig. S2b (ESI†). A large number of pores were observed on the surface but they failed to extend into the interior of the material. Due to the activation effect of KOH, carbon forms a porous structure. KOH activates biomass carbon at high temperatures, and a series of reoxidation and reduction reactions occur, etching the carbon skeleton to produce holes while producing H2, CO2, CO and other small molecular gases. A large number of pores are formed in the carbon skeleton structure, but the activation also produces potassium compounds forming blockages. To maximize the effectiveness of the hole structure, it iss essential to thoroughly clean and clear any content within the pores. The mechanism is shown as follows:27 6KOH + 2C - 2K + 3H2 + 2K2CO3 (1) K2CO3 - K2O + CO2 (2) CO2 +C - 2CO (3) K2CO3 + 2C - 2K + 3CO (4) K2O+C - 2K + CO (5) Therefore, in order to further increase the specific surface area of the material and enhance the conductive properties and surface functional groups of the material, urea was added as a nitrogen source to obtain urea-doped activated carbonized wood (UACW). The pore structure of UACW not only exists on the surface but also contains a large number of pores in the interior connected to the surface (Fig. S2c, ESI†), which can promote the transport of electrolyte ions. On the basis of KOH activation, urea was also introduced as an N-doped material. At high temperatures, urea decomposes into NH3 and CO2 gases and continues to etch biomass carbon while generating gas, forming pores at the original location. The equation is as follows:15 CO(NH)2 +H2O - 2NH3 + CO2 (6) NH3 +C - HCN + H2 (7) Ammonia can react with hydroxyl (–OH) and carboxylic (–COOH) groups on the surface of biomass carbon to form functional amino groups. The effect of N addition was remark￾able, and the porous structure was more compact and ordered. As shown in Fig. 2b and Fig. S2d (ESI†), the 3D porous structure of AUACW can be observed.28,29 After the mixed acid treatment, Fig. 2 (a) and (b) SEM images of CW and AUACW. The porous carbon surface obtains more O-containing functional groups and changes the electro￾nic structure of the material, enhancing the electrical conduc￾tivity and surface roughness and increasing the specific surface area of the material. Ultrathin pore walls and staggered pore structures can be observed in the TEM images (Fig. 2c and d), which helps to increase the pore volume and provide more paths for electrolyte ion transport. Large amounts of disordered carbon are present in AUACW, which helps provide more active sites for charge transfer and ion diffusion (Fig. 2e). Subsequently, the elemental distribution of AUACW was obtained by energy-dispersive EDS. As shown in Fig. 2f, N and O were uniformly added to the carbon skeleton. The corresponding N and O contents were 3.59% and 10.94%, respectively (Fig. S3, ESI†). The addition of N and O elements enhances the hydrophilicity and conductivity of the material, providing additional pseudocapacitance. XRD provides the ability to measure the crystalline phase composition of the samples within a certain range of diffrac￾tion angles. The XRD patterns of the four samples showed two wide diffraction peaks at 21.481 and 43.441, corresponding to the graphitized carbon hexagonal crystal planes (002) and (101), respectively (Fig. 3a). The (002) peak of AUACW was narrow and flat, indicating a low degree of graphitization and crystallinity with amorphous characteristics.16,31 Simultaneously, the nar￾row and strong diffraction peak of CW at 26.441 indicated the presence of highly graphitized carbon. This may be attributed to the fact that sawdust rich in lignin is conducive to the formation of highly graphitized carbon.14 Furthermore, Raman spectra were used to investigate the degree of graphitization of the four samples, as shown in Fig. 3b. The samples show two evident peaks at 1338 cm1 and 1589 cm1 , which are defined as the D and G bands. The intensity of the D band represents the degree of disordered and defective carbon structure in the material, while the G band corresponds to the vibration of sp2 carbon atoms, that is, the degree of ordered carbon and graphitization.32,33 The ID/IG of CW of 1.37 indicates that biomass carbon without activation exhibits a high degree of disorder, but a very low degree of graphitization will lead to poor electrical conductivity of the material. The ID/IG values of ACW, UACW and AUACW were 0.99, 1.07 and 1.0, respectively, indicating that these samples had low graphitization and high defectiveness, including good conductivity. In addition, the effect of the AUACW material on the water contact angle was also investigated (Fig. 3c). It was observed that AUACW had a minimum contact angle of 261 with hydrophilic properties, while the water contact angles of the other samples were relatively large, ranging from 621 to 1201. The CW sample exhibited a water contact angle of 1201, Fig. 3 (a) XRD patterns. (b) Raman spectrum. (c) Static water contact angle at t = 0 s. This result indicated that heteroa￾tom doping affected the hydrophilicity of the sample. The structural characteristics of the samples were further studied by N2-sorption measurements. The sorption and desorption isotherm curves of the CW sample belong to the typical type-I isotherm, while the other three samples exhibit the characteristics of type-I and type-IV composite curves, and AUACW has a small hysteresis curve (Fig. 3d). The results show that AUACW has a strong force with N2 in the low-pressure region (P/P0 o 0.1), with more micropores in the material, and the adsorption potential energy inside the micropores is strong. As the relative pressure increases, it quickly enters the adsorp￾tion platform and reaches the saturated adsorption state, and the saturated adsorption value at this time is equal to the filling volume of the micropores.34,35 After entering the medium pressure region (0.3 o P/P0 o 0.8), the curve exhibits a unique H4-type hysteresis loop associated with capillary condensation, indicating the presence of a small mesopore. In the high￾pressure region (0.9 o P/P0 o 1), the isotherm shows an obvious H3 hysteresis loop: when the relative pressure is close to 1, the curve rises sharply, indicating that there are large holes in the material, and the material forms a three￾dimensional aperture structure with a multi-aperture distribu￾tion, which is also illustrated by the aperture distribution diagram.36 In conjunction with Table 1, it is evident that the specific surface area of samples ranging from CW to AUACW exhibited a gradual increase, and a three-dimensional pore structure consisting of micro-, meso- and macropores is formed. Micropores are generated by removing volatile sub￾stances from the biomass and activating KOH during high￾temperature pyrolysis, while the mesoporous pores are gener￾ated by the cavity fusion between the micropores and nanostructures.37 Upon further examination of the aperture distribution diagram (Fig. 3e), it is evident that the majority of the pores in the four samples are concentrated within the 1.56 nm micropores and the 4.35 nm mesopores. The presence of pores in the macropore region was minimal, with only a few pores observed. The elemental composition and bonding state of AUACW were comprehensively analyzed using XPS. In the full survey spectrum (Fig. 3f), peaks corresponding to C 1s, N 1s and O 1s were observed at binding energies of 284.4 eV, 400.4 eV and 532.4 eV, respectively. In the high-resolution spectrum of C 1s (Fig. 3g), three discernible peaks emerged at binding energies of 284.8 eV, 286.4 eV, and 288.4 eV, which can be attributed to different carbon functional groups, including C–C/CQC, C–O/ C–N and O–CQO, respectively, thus confirming the presence of O functional groups and suggesting the incorporation of N element into the AUACW structure. Similarly, in the high￾resolution N 1s spectrum, three characteristic peaks appear at binding energies of 398.8 eV, 400.l eV, and 401.l eV, respec￾tively, which are assigned to pyridinic-N, pyrrolic-N and graphitic-N species (Fig. 3h).38 These N-containing functional groups can enhance the electrochemical performance of the carbon electrode material.39 The pyridinic-N serves as an electrochemically active center to increase capacitance, pyrrolic-N introduces pseudocapacitance to enhance the speci￾fic capacitance, and graphitic-N promotes electron transfer and effectively improves the conductivity of porous carbon. These improvements contribute to the electrochemical performance of the AUACW electrode material. In the O 1s (Fig. 3i), three peaks at 531.9 eV, 532.7 eV and 533.6 eV correspond to the OQO, C–O–C/C–OH and O–CQO bonds, respectively. The O element in AUACW mainly comes from three aspects: the biomass carbon itself contains O that was not lost in the treatment; the O element that was incorporated in the reaction as KOH was activated; and the O introduced on the surface when mixed acid was used for modification. Furthermore, in the FTIR diagram (Fig. S4, ESI†), C–H, N–C, CQC, CQO, C–H and O–H were found at wavelengths of 1046 cm1 , 1225 cm1 , 1402 cm1 , 1612 cm1 , 2918 cm1 and 3432 cm1 , respectively, which is consistent with the XPS analysis results. These results indicate that AUACW has a well-developed pore network (a hierarchical network of micropores, mesopores and macropores), which facilitates the exposure of active sites and diffusion of reactants and electrolytes. Heteroatom doping and O-rich functional groups are beneficial for changing the hydrophilicity of the material and providing additional Faraday capacitance. Meanwhile, a good degree of graphitization helps enhance the electrical conductivity of the material. Electrochemical performance The electrochemical properties of each electrode were evalu￾ated in 1 M KOH using a three-electrode system (Fig. S5, ESI†). The CV curves of the four electrodes are shown in Fig. 4a. It can be observed that most of the CV curves present a quasi￾rectangle at a low scan rate, reflecting the fast ion transfer rate and excellent magnification capacity of the samples. However, the CV curve of the CW electrode has the smallest closed area, which is related to the small specific surface area and also demonstrates a slow electron transfer.15 The integrated CV curve area of AUACW is larger than that of the other electrodes, indicating a larger specific capacitance, faster electron transfer and better electrochemical performance, which is beneficial for expanding the contact area with the electrolyte reaction. Then, the electrodes were employed to execute the GCD test at 0.8 A g1 , as shown in Fig. 4b. segments.text: 2 Abstract: Porous carbon materials as one of the most promising electrodes for energy storage and conversion devices have attracted many attentions because of their large specific surface area, well-developed pore structure, excellent electrical conductivity and low cost. However, the traditional production of porous carbon is often accompanied by complex synthesis conditions, environmental pollution and large energy consumption. Herein, a new kind of B/N/P co-doped porous carbon (OPBNP) were prepared by simple hydrothermal doping method combined with a low-temperature carbonization-activation process using orange peel (OP) as the precursor, boric acid and diammonium phosphate as co-dopant. The careful regulated element doping and low carbonization temperature (600 oC) enable the prepared OPBNP material to have a high specific surface area (1774.8 m2 g-1), microporous-dominated hierarchical structure, larger graphite interlayer spacing (0.392 nm), and more defects. The combination of structurally strategic design and multi-atom doping promotes fast charging and long-lasting stability. As electrodes in supercapacitors (SCs), the OPBNP delivers superior specific capacitance of 289 F g-1 at 5 A g-1 with 93.6% capacitance retention after 10000 cycles. Besides, the assembled OPBNP//OPBNP symmetric supercapacitor could reach a high energy density of 8.9 Wh kg-1 at a power density of 499.7 W kg-1. Furthermore, as anodes for sodium ion batteries (SIBs), the OPBNP also exhibits a high reversible capacity of 292.3 mAh g-1 after 100 cycles at 0.1 A g-1, and excellent cycling performance of 206.6 mAh g-1 after 1000 cycles at 1 A g-1. The B/N/P co-doped porous carbon behaves the characteristics of low cost, simple preparation and excellent properties, making them great potential electrodes for advanced supercapacitors and sodium ion batteries. 3 1. Introduction Supercapacitors (SCs) and sodium-ion batteries (SIBs) have become the most promising energy storage conversion devices today. They have the potentials to significantly alleviate the lithium resource scarcity inherent in traditional lithium-ion batteries (LIBs) and demonstrate promising market prospects.1-3 Developing electrode materials with low cost and high performance is the crux to improve the performance of energy storage and conversion devices (SCs and SIBs).4-6 Porous carbon materials have been extensively studied due to their large specific surface area (SSA), enriched pore structure, excellent electrical conductivity and low cost.7-10 However, the traditional production of porous carbon is often accompanied by complex synthesis conditions, serious environmental pollution and large energy consumption. As a renewable green raw material, biomass is considered to be a very promising precursor for the manufacture of functional carbon because of its rich resources, helping to sustainable energy utilization and environmental protection, low cost, etc. In particular, biomass-based carbon, such as rice husk,11 wheat-straw,12 bagasse,13 pomelo peels,14 waste palm,15 etc. have unique structural properties as bioresidual materials. Besides, their inherent hierarchical porous structure can provide not only a large accessible surface area but also smooth transfer paths for electrolytes ions. Furthermore, most of the biomass contain the elements of N, S, and P, and therefore, heteroatom self-doping can be realized in the synthesis of the materials to form additional active sites in the biomass-based carbon materials. Therefore, the development of high-performance porous carbon-based materials with controlled pore structure and composition using biomass as a precursor can not only save costs and alleviate environmental pollution, but also achieve the high-value utilization of biomass. Activation conditions and heteroatom doping also show significant effects on the pore structure and surface chemistry of porous carbon.16, 17 Traditional porous carbon material is usually obtained by one-step or two-step high temperature pyrolysis (usually above 700 °C) combined with activation, resluting in a high energy consumption.9, 18 In recent years, hydrothermal carbonization technology (HCT) has been used for waste biomass treatment due to its low energy consumption and high efficiency.19-22 At relatively mild temperatures (180-250 °C), waste biomass in the water environment tends to be rich in oxygen-containing functional groups, which has considerable activation potential and can produce porous structures with high porosity. At the same time, hydrothermal method can effectively stabilize heteroatom doping and improve graphitization, Page 3 of 29 Journal of Materials Chemistry A Journal of Materials Chemistry A Accepted Manuscript Published on 17 June 2024. Downloaded by FAC DE QUIMICA on 6/26/2024 1:47:55 PM. View Article Online DOI: 10.1039/D4TA02115K

4 thereby improving the capacitance performance of biomass carbon materials.23 The introduction of other heteroatoms, such as N, P, B, etc., into carbon materials can not only improve significantly the wettability of carbon materials to the electrolyte and promote the ionic transport rate, but also provide more electrochemical active sites to enhance the capacity of the materials, thus effectively improving the energy density and rate capabilities. Wang et al. developed N/P/O heteroatom doped porous activated carbon using durian shells as raw material and (NH4)2HPO4 as doping reagent by hydrothermal method, delivering a high capacitance of 560 F g-1 at 2 A g-1 and good cycle stability (retention rate of 88 % after 10,000 cycles).24 Yue et al. reported B/N/P co-doped cornstalk-based carbon, behaving rich porosity structure and showing a good electrochemical performance (a high specific capacitance of 342.5 F g-1 at 0.5 A g-1).25 In addition, Tao and his co-workers prepared N/P co-doping mesoporous hard carbon derived from soybean root exhibiting high electrochemical performance for both SIBs and potassium ion batteries (PIBs), which can be attributed to the fact that N, P elements can effectively increase the interlayer spacing of the hard carbon and provided more active sites.26 Muruganantham et al. also confirmed that the reversible capacity of N/S co-doped carbon derived from mango peel is significantly higher than that of the un-doped carbon material.27 Orange juice is one of the most widely consumed beverages today. Its large-scale production meets people's needs, but it also produces a large amount of waste orange peel (OP).28,29 OP is mainly composed of cellulose, hemicellulose, pectin and lignin, which are known as good carbon precursors. It is reported that OP-derived carbon materials have been employed in catalysis,30 gas sensors,31 Pb-C mixed SCs,32 LIBs/SIBs,33 PIBs,34 etc. However, most of OP are discarded and burned as waste due to the lack of effective and inexpensive synthesis methods, resulting in the environmental pollution and resource waste. Therefore, it is necessary to explore how to prepare a high-performance biomass carbon material from OP through hydrothermal heteroatom doping and low-temperature activation technology. To our knowledge, there is no report on OP-derived B/N/P co-doped porous carbons as electrodes for SCs and SIBs. Herein, we report a new B/N/P co-doped porous carbon (OPBNP) employing OP as carbon sources, boric acid and (NH4)2HPO4 as dopant, via hydrothermal heteroatom doping and low-temperature KOH activation method. The OPBNP behaves a high SSA of 774.8 m2 g-1, larger interlayer spacing of 0.392 nm, and rich interpenetrate network porous structure, which could facilitate the transport of ions and electrons in the electrodes. At the same time, the synergistic Journal of Materials Chemistry A Page 4 of 29 Journal of Materials Chemistry A Accepted Manuscript Published on 17 June 2024. Downloaded by FAC DE QUIMICA on 6/26/2024 1:47:55 PM. View Article Online DOI: 10.1039/D4TA02115K

5 co-doping of B/N/P atom can greatly promote the physical and chemical properties of carbon and provide an additional pseudopocapitance, high wettability through the occurrence of redox reactions, ensuring high energy density.35 Used as anode electrode for SCs and SIBs, the OPBNP exhibited excellent storage performance, high specific capacity and superior rate performances. This work provides a simple and new preparation method for developing heteroatom-doped carbon, which is helpful to further promote its application in the field of energy storage. 2. Experimental Section 2.1 Materials Orange peels (OP) were collected from Zhenjiang fruit market. The orange peels were first rinsed in deionized water to remove impurities such as fouling and then vacuum dried at 80 oC overnight. After that, the clean OPs were crushed into fine powder by a pulverizer and stored in a clean flask under dry condition for further use. All chemicals in our research were used directly as received without further treatment. Distilled water was used throughout the whole experiment. 2.2 Synthesis of B/N/P co-doped porous carbon Firstly, 2 g of OP powder, 1 g of (NH4)2HPO4, and 1 g of boric acid were added into 60 ml of deionized water to stir for 4 h to receive a suspension. Then, the suspension was transferred into a 100 mL stainless steel sealed high-pressure reaction kettle and kept at 180 °C for 12 h. After natural cooling to room temperature and vacuum filtration, the as-obtained sample were collected by washing with deionized water and dried overnight at 80 °C to obtain hydrothermally doping products. Next, the products and KOH were dissolved in 50 ml of deionized water at a mass ratio of 1:3, after be stirring at room temperature for 10 h then dried at 100 °C for later use. The obtained products were then tiled in a nickel porcelain boat and placed in a tube furnace to calcination activation 3 h at 600 °C with the heating rate of 3 °C min-1 under nitrogen atmosphere obtain. The obtained black samples were washed with 2 M HCl to remove the salt residue then washed with deionized water to neutral, dried overnight at 80 °C to obtain the resultant B/N/P co-doped porous carbon (OPBNP). The detailed synthesis process of OPBNP in this study is shown in Scheme 1. For comparison, the sample prepared via the similar method without the addition of (NH4)2HPO4 and boric acid was denoted as OPC. While the sample synthesized via the similar method with only (NH4)2HPO4 was denoted as OPNP, and the sample with only boric acid was Page 5 of 29 Journal of Materials Chemistry A Journal of Materials Chemistry A Accepted Manuscript Published on 17 June 2024. 6 denoted as OPB. 2.3 Characterizations The phase structure and chemical composition of the porous carbon materials were characterized by X-ray diffraction (XRD, Shimadzu XRD-6000) with Cu Ka radiation (λ=0.15406 nm). The morphology was investigated using scanning electron microscopy (SEM, Quanta FEG 250) and high-resolution transmission electron microscopy (HRTEM, Tecnai G2 F20). The specific surface areas, pore volume and pore diameter of carbon materials were analyzed by nitrogen adsorption-desorption measurements (Micrometric, JW-BK200B), and calculated by Brunauer-Emmett-Teller theory and non-local density functional theory methods, respectively. The chemical states of elements were further investigated by X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS, Thermo Fisher Nexisa). Raman spectra of the as-synthesized sample were carried out on a Renishaw Raman spectrometer. 2.4 Electrochemical measurements for supercapacitors The electrochemical properties of the samples for supercapacitors were evaluated both in three-electrode half-cells and two-electrode systems within 6 M KOH electrolyte. Working electrode were prepared by mixing the active carbonaceous material (80%), the conductive agent acetylene black (10%), and the binder polyvinylidene fluoride (PVDF) (10%) in N-methyl-pyrrolidone (NMP) to produce a uniform thick slurry, then the mixed slurry was coated on nickel foams (1×2 cm2 ) which were pretreated with acetone and hydrochloric acid. The electrode materials were then placed in a vacuum drying oven, dried for 12 h at 80 oC, followed by pressing into a film at a pressure of 10 MPa. The loading mass of active material was 1-2 mg cm-2 . The Pt foil and Hg/HgO electrodes were used as the counter and reference electrodes, respectively. Galvanostatic charge-discharge (GCD) and cyclic voltammetry (CV) measurements were conducted in the voltage range of -1–0 V (vs. Hg/HgO), electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) with the frequency range of 105–10-2 Hz and amplitude of 5 mV were conducted on the electrochemical workstation (CHI660E, Shanghai, China). Cycling stability was tested using a battery test instrument (CT2001A, Wuhan Blue Electronics Co., LTD.). The symmetrical supercapacitors devices were assembled by using two working electrodes with the same mass of active substances (loading weight of about 2 mg cm-2) in the CR2032 button cell, Whatman glass fiber (GF/D) as separator, and 6 M KOH as electrolyte solution. The high-resolution spectra of C 1s (Fig. S3), N 1s, O 1s, B 1s and P 2p (Fig. 2f-i) further prove the existence of C, B, N, P and O elements to understand the chemical bonds formed on the surface of OPBNP. The corresponding valence structures include pyridine N (N-6)/N-B, pyrrole N (N-5) and graphite N/N=P.41,43 N-6 and N-5 mainly act as the electron donor and generate defects to increase the active sites as well as provide pseudocapacitance contribution,44 while graphitic N can increase the conductivity of the material.44 For the O 1s spectrum (Fig. 2g), the characteristic peaks at 532.57, 533.87 and 535.2 eV can be attributed to C-O-C/C-O-H, O-B and -COOH functional groups, respectively.41 The three characteristic peaks of B 1s are shown in Fig. 2h, and the corresponding functional groups are B-C (189.84 eV), B-N (190.97 eV) and B-O (191.82 eV); the P 2p spectrum has three characteristic peaks (Fig. 2i) with binding energies of 131.79 eV P-O group, 133.43 eV C-PO3/C2-PO2 group and 134.66 eV P-C group, respectively.42,46 The doping of heteroatoms can significantly improve the properties of porous carbon materials, in terms of increasing conductivity, modulating disorder and defects of materials, thus promoting the formation of surface pseudocapacitance, which will bring benefits to the application of samples in the field of electrochemistry.5,47,48 3.2 Electrochemical properties The electrochemical performances of the OPC, OPB, OPNP and OPBNP samples for supercapacitor were presented in Fig. 3.
